commentary_summary: Arjun is so confused he cannot determine if victory or defeat is preferable, as killing his own kinsmen would make victory meaningless.
theme: Paralysis of judgment when facing deeply conflicting moral choices

speaker: Arjun
text_sanskrit:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभाव:
पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसम्मूढचेता: |
यच्छ्रेय: स्यान्निश्चितं ब्रूहि तन्मे
शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम् || 7||
transliteration:
kārpaṇya-doṣhopahata-svabhāvaḥ
pṛichchhāmi tvāṁ dharma-sammūḍha-chetāḥ
yach chhreyaḥ syān niśhchitaṁ brūhi tan me
śhiṣhyas te 'haṁ śhādhi māṁ tvāṁ prapannam
translation: I am confused about my duty, and am besieged with anxiety and faintheartedness. I am Your disciple, and am surrendered to You. Please instruct me for certain what is best for me.
commentary_full: This is a landmark verse in the Bhagavad Gita — it marks the formal moment when Arjun surrenders to Shree Krishna as a disciple. The words 'śhiṣhyas te 'ham' — 'I am your disciple' — transform the conversation from a dialogue between friends to a Guru-Shishya (teacher-student) relationship. This surrender is the qualification needed for receiving divine knowledge. Arjun openly admits he is afflicted by kārpaṇya (miserliness of spirit), that his nature has been corrupted by attachment, and that his mind is bewildered about dharma. This honest admission of confusion and helplessness is the first step toward wisdom.
commentary_summary: Arjun formally surrenders to Krishna as his disciple, admitting his confusion about dharma and seeking definitive guidance.
theme: Surrender to the Guru as the starting point of true spiritual knowledge

speaker: Arjun
text_sanskrit:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्
यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् |
अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धं
राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् || 8||
transliteration:
na hi prapaśhyāmi mamāpanudyād
yach chhokam uchchhoṣhaṇam indriyāṇām
avāpya bhūmāv asapatnam ṛiddhaṁ
rājyaṁ surāṇām api chādhipatyam
translation: I can find no means of driving away this anguish that is drying up my senses. Even if I win a prosperous and unrivalled kingdom on the earth, or gain sovereignty like the celestial gods, I will be unable to dispel this grief.
commentary_full: Arjun's grief has reached such a depth that he can see no worldly solution for it. Even the greatest material achievements — a vast kingdom on earth, or the lordship of the celestial realms — appear insufficient to relieve his sorrow. This insight, though born of despair, is actually a profound spiritual truth: material possessions and achievements cannot permanently satisfy the soul. The soul's true hunger is for divine bliss, not worldly prosperity. Arjun's despair is thus simultaneously his darkness and his dawn — the necessary prelude to seeking the eternal solution.
commentary_summary: Arjun confesses that no worldly gain, not even lordship over heaven, can remove his grief — a profound though painful insight into the limits of material life.
theme: The insufficiency of worldly achievements to satisfy the grieving soul

speaker: Sanjay
text_sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच |
एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेश: परन्तप |
न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह || 9||
transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam uktvā hṛiṣhīkeśhaṁ guḍākeśhaḥ parantapa
na yotsya iti govindam uktvā tūṣhṇīṁ babhūva ha
translation: Sanjay said: Having thus spoken, Gudakesh, that chastiser of enemies, addressed Hrishikesh: "Govind, I shall not fight," and became silent.
commentary_full: Arjun's declaration 'I shall not fight' is the culmination of his confused state of mind. Sanjay refers to Arjun as Gudakesh — the conqueror of sleep — a title that highlights the irony of his present inaction. The one who had conquered sleep (signifying full alertness and valor) is now declaring inaction. Shree Krishna is addressed as Hrishikesh (master of the senses) and Govinda (who gives pleasure to the senses and to the earth) — both titles appropriate because Krishna is about to reveal the true science of controlling the senses and finding real pleasure through divine knowledge.
commentary_summary: Arjun declares he will not fight and falls silent — the deepest point of his despondency, which sets the stage for Krishna's teachings.
theme: The absolute nadir of Arjun's resolve, demanding divine intervention

speaker: Sanjay
text_sanskrit:
तमुवाच हृषीकेश: प्रहसन्निव भारत |
सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वच: || 10||
transliteration:
tam uvācha hṛiṣhīkeśhaḥ prahasanniva bhārata
senayorubhayormadhye viṣhīdantam idaṁ vachaḥ
translation: O Dhritarashtra, thereafter, in the midst of both the armies, Shree Krishna smilingly spoke the following words to the grief-stricken Arjun.
commentary_full: The smile of Shree Krishna at this moment is profoundly significant. He is not smiling in mockery of Arjun's grief. Rather, his smile reflects the equanimity and divine wisdom of one who sees the full picture while his dear friend sees only a fragment. Just as a parent smiles upon seeing a child grieving over a broken toy, Shree Krishna smiles because he sees the eternal soul of Arjun, not merely his present bodily turmoil. This gentle smile is the expression of compassion, wisdom, and confidence that the divine truths he is about to share will completely resolve Arjun's confusion.
commentary_summary: Krishna smiles gently at Arjun's grief — not in mockery but with divine compassion and confidence as He prepares to impart eternal wisdom.
theme: The compassionate smile of the Guru who sees beyond the student's momentary confusion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे |
गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिता: || 11||
transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
aśhochyān anvaśhochas tvaṁ prajñā-vādānśh cha bhāṣhase
gatāsūn agatāsūṁśh cha nānuśhochanti paṇḍitāḥ
translation: The Supreme Lord said: While you speak words of wisdom, you are mourning for that which is not worthy of grief. The wise lament neither for the living nor for the dead.
commentary_full: This is the true beginning of Krishna's divine instruction. He gently but firmly points out the central contradiction in Arjun's position — Arjun speaks of wisdom (citing reasons of dharma, family honor, etc.) but acts with ignorance (being overwhelmed by grief for the body). The truly wise do not grieve because they understand the eternal nature of the soul. The body is mortal and subject to change — grief over it is misplaced. The soul is eternal and imperishable — it cannot be harmed. Therefore, grief for either the living or the dead betrays a fundamental confusion about the nature of the self.
commentary_summary: Krishna exposes the contradiction in Arjun — speaking wisely but grieving foolishly. The truly wise grieve neither for the living nor the dead.
theme: True wisdom lies in understanding the eternal soul beyond the mortal body

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपा: |
न चैव न भविष्याम: सर्वे वयमत: परम् || 12||
transliteration:
na tvevāhaṁ jātu nāsaṁ na tvaṁ neme janādhipāḥ
na chaiva na bhaviṣhyāmaḥ sarve vayam ataḥ param
translation: Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor all these kings; nor in the future shall any of us cease to be.
commentary_full: This verse establishes one of the most fundamental teachings of the Bhagavad Gita — the eternal, continuous existence of the individual soul. Shree Krishna is explicitly declaring that he, Arjun, and all the kings assembled on the battlefield have always existed and shall always exist. This statement also subtly reveals that Shree Krishna is not an ordinary mortal but the Supreme Being who is eternal, all-knowing, and omnipresent. For an ordinary person, past lives are veiled from memory by the trauma of death and rebirth. But for the Lord, all of time is transparent. This verse is also an implicit refutation of the materialist view that the soul is born with the body and perishes with it.
commentary_summary: Krishna declares the eternal existence of all souls — none ever was not, none shall ever cease to be — refuting the fear of death.
theme: The eternal, unbroken continuity of the individual soul across all time

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा |
तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति || 13||
transliteration:
dehino 'smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā
tathā dehāntara-prāptir dhīras tatra na muhyati
translation: Just as the embodied soul continuously passes from childhood to youth to old age, similarly, at the time of death, the soul passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna uses a beautiful and accessible analogy to explain the soul's journey through bodies. Just as we do not weep when the child-body grows into a youth-body, or when the youth-body ages into an old-body, we should not weep when the old or worn-out body is cast aside at death for a new one. In each case, it is the same soul continuing its journey — only the outer garment (the body) changes. The term dhīra, meaning 'the wise' or 'the steady one,' refers to those who, by understanding this truth, remain undeluded and undisturbed by the inevitable changes of the body.
commentary_summary: The soul's passage through different bodies at death is like passing from childhood through youth to old age — only the outer form changes, not the soul.
theme: Death as a natural transition of the soul, no different from aging

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदु:खदा: |
आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत || 14||
transliteration:
mātrā-sparśhās tu kaunteya śhītoṣhṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ
āgamāpāyino 'nityās tāṁs titikṣhasva bhārata
translation: O son of Kunti, the contact between the senses and the sense objects gives rise to fleeting perceptions of happiness and distress. These are non-permanent, and come and go like the winter and summer seasons. O descendent of Bharat, one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.
commentary_full: Having established the eternal nature of the soul, Shree Krishna now addresses the practical challenge of living in the world — the inevitable experience of pleasure and pain through sense contact. Just as summer and winter alternate with complete regularity and neither lasts forever, so too happiness and distress come and go in the course of life. The key instruction is titikṣhasva — learn to tolerate them. This does not mean suppression or denial of feelings, but rather the cultivation of inner equanimity that is not shaken by external fluctuations. The wise person experiences both pleasure and pain but remains anchored in the unchanging awareness of the soul.
commentary_summary: Pleasure and pain arising from sense contact are transient, like summer and winter — the wise learn to tolerate them with equanimity.
theme: Cultivating inner stability by tolerating the transient dualities of life

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ |
समदु:खसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते || 15||
transliteration:
yaṁ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣhaṁ puruṣharṣhabha
sama-duḥkha-sukhaṁ dhīraṁ so 'mṛitatvāya kalpate
translation: O Arjun, noblest amongst men, that person who is not affected by happiness and distress, and remains steady in both, becomes eligible for liberation.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna describes the eligibility for liberation — amṛitatva (immortality). The one who remains steady — sama-duḥkha-sukham — equally in joy and sorrow, is qualified for spiritual liberation. This equanimity is not the numbness of the emotionally dead, but the higher steadiness of one who has transcended bodily consciousness and is rooted in the awareness of the eternal soul. When the inner being is grounded in the self, external circumstances — pleasant or unpleasant — cannot fundamentally disturb it. This is the very foundation of the yoga of wisdom that Krishna is about to expound.
commentary_summary: One who remains steady in both happiness and distress, unaffected by life's dualities, becomes eligible for liberation.
theme: Equanimity in pleasure and pain as the qualification for spiritual liberation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सत: |
उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभि: || 16||
transliteration:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ
ubhayorapi dṛiṣhṭo 'ntas tv anayos tattva-darśhibhiḥ
translation: Of the transient there is no endurance, and of the eternal there is no cessation. This has verily been observed and concluded by the seers of the Truth, after studying the nature of both.
commentary_full: This verse is one of the most philosophically profound in the Bhagavad Gita. It establishes the Vedantic principle of the distinction between the real (sat) and the unreal (asat). That which is temporary and changing — the body, the world, sense objects — has no ultimate reality. It appears to exist but is constantly changing and will eventually cease. That which is eternal — the soul, God — cannot cease to exist. The seers of truth (tattva-darśhibhiḥ) who have investigated both the temporary and the eternal have arrived at this definitive conclusion. This verse forms the bedrock of all of Krishna's subsequent teachings about the soul.
commentary_summary: The transient has no permanent existence; the eternal cannot cease to be — this is the conclusion of all seers of truth.
theme: The Vedantic distinction between the real (eternal) and the unreal (transient)

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम् |
विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित्कर्तुमर्हति || 17||
transliteration:
avināśhi tu tad viddhi yena sarvam idaṁ tatam
vināśham avyayasyāsya na kaśhchit kartum arhati
translation: That which pervades the entire body, know it to be indestructible. No one can cause the destruction of the imperishable soul.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna defines the soul as that which pervades the entire body — consciousness that illumines every cell and organ. This pervading consciousness is avināśhi — indestructible. Bodily organs can be damaged, but the consciousness that pervades them cannot be destroyed. This is why doctors can amputate a limb without destroying the person — the person (the soul) remains whole. No weapon, no disease, no natural force can destroy the soul. This is the foundational principle of the Bhagavad Gita's answer to Arjun's grief: those he fears to kill cannot actually be killed, because the soul within them is imperishable.
commentary_summary: The soul pervades the entire body and is indestructible — no one can truly destroy it.
theme: The soul as the indestructible, all-pervading consciousness within the body

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ता: शरीरिण: |
अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत || 18||
transliteration:
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śharīriṇaḥ
anāśhino 'prameyasya tasmād yudhyasva bhārata
translation: Only the material body is perishable; the embodied soul within is indestructible, immeasurable, and eternal. Therefore, fight, O descendent of Bharat.
commentary_full: Having established the indestructibility of the soul, Shree Krishna now draws the practical conclusion: therefore, fight. The bodies of those on the battlefield are perishable (antavanta) — they will die regardless. The souls within them are eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable. So Arjun's grief over killing the bodies of his kinsmen is misplaced — the eternal souls within them cannot be harmed. Additionally, as a Kshatriya, Arjun's duty is to fight for righteousness. By refusing to fight, he would be failing his dharma and grieving over something that does not ultimately matter (the body), while neglecting what truly matters (his eternal duty).
commentary_summary: Only the body perishes; the eternal soul within is indestructible. Therefore Krishna commands Arjun to fight without fear.
theme: The perishable body vs. the imperishable soul as the basis for fearless action

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम् |
उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते || 19||
transliteration:
ya enaṁ vetti hantāraṁ yaśh chainaṁ manyate hatam
ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṁ hanti na hanyate
translation: Neither of them is in knowledge—the one who thinks the soul can slay and the one who thinks the soul can be slain. For truly, the soul neither kills nor can it be killed.
commentary_full: This verse strikes at the very root of Arjun's anxiety. He fears committing the sin of killing. But Krishna reveals that this fear is based on a fundamental misunderstanding. The soul — the true self — can neither kill nor be killed. It is the body, powered by the soul, that acts. The soul itself is a witness. When a person 'kills' another, only the body is affected; the soul within is untouched. This teaching goes beyond the battlefield. In daily life too, people mistakenly identify themselves with the body and its actions. True spiritual knowledge reveals the soul to be a witness — pure consciousness that neither kills nor is killed.
commentary_summary: Both the one who thinks the soul kills and the one who thinks it can be killed are ignorant — the soul neither kills nor can be killed.
theme: The soul as pure witness — beyond the act of killing and being killed

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचि-
न्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूय: |
अजो नित्य: शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे || 20||
transliteration:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadāchin
nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ śhāśhvato 'yaṁ purāṇo
na hanyate hanyamāne śharīre
translation: The soul is neither born, nor does it ever die; nor having once existed, does it ever cease to be. The soul is without birth, eternal, immortal, and ageless. It is not destroyed when the body is destroyed.
commentary_full: This is one of the most celebrated verses of the Bhagavad Gita, presenting the complete description of the soul's nature. The Katopanishad contains an almost identical verse: 'The soul is not born, nor does it die; it did not spring from something, and nothing sprang from it. It is unborn, eternal, immortal, and ageless. It is not destroyed when the body is destroyed.' The soul is aja (unborn), nitya (eternal), śhāśhvata (ever-existing), purāṇa (the most ancient, or primeval). It precedes the body, it outlasts the body, and it remains unchanged through the entire journey of birth and death.
commentary_summary: The soul is unborn, eternal, immortal, and ageless — it is never destroyed even when the body perishes.
theme: The soul's complete independence from birth, death, and bodily destruction

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम् |
कथं स पुरुष: पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम् || 21||
transliteration:
vedāvināśhinaṁ nityaṁ ya enam ajam avyayam
kathaṁ sa puruṣhaḥ pārtha kaṁ ghātayati hanti kam
translation: O Parth, how can one who knows the soul to be imperishable, eternal, unborn, and immutable kill anyone or cause anyone to kill?
commentary_full: This verse is the logical conclusion of the preceding teachings about the soul. If the soul is imperishable, eternal, unborn, and immutable, then it is impossible for it to be killed or to kill. Arjun's fear of sinning by killing is based on his identification with the body. But the one rooted in the knowledge of the self sees beyond bodies to eternal souls. Such a person cannot be a 'killer' in the true sense, because what they act upon — the body — is already perishable, while what truly matters — the soul — is untouchable. This question is Krishna's invitation to Arjun to change his perspective from the bodily to the spiritual level.
commentary_summary: One who truly knows the soul to be eternal and indestructible cannot consider themselves a killer — for the soul can neither kill nor be killed.
theme: True knowledge of the soul dissolves the concept of killing and guilt

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय
नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि |
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा-
न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही || 22||
transliteration:
vāsānsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya
navāni gṛihṇāti naro 'parāṇi
tathā śharīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇāny
anyāni saṁyāti navāni dehī
translation: As a person sheds worn-out garments and wears new ones, likewise, at the time of death, the soul casts off its worn-out body and enters a new one.
commentary_full: This is perhaps the most popular verse of the Bhagavad Gita — the garment analogy for the soul's change of bodies. It makes the profound truth of transmigration accessible through a simple, everyday metaphor. Just as no one grieves when they change their old, worn-out clothes for new ones, there is no reason to grieve when the soul sheds its old body for a new one. The 'person' (the soul) remains the same throughout; only the outer covering changes. The grief of losing a loved one is thus likened to grief over discarded clothing — it confuses the temporary outer garment with the eternal inner being.
commentary_summary: The soul changes bodies at death just as a person changes worn-out clothes — the inner being remains unchanged.
theme: Death as the natural, painless exchange of old body for new, like changing garments

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावक: |
न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुत: || 23||
transliteration:
nainaṁ chhindanti śhastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ
na chainaṁ kledayantyāpo na śhoṣhayati mārutaḥ
translation: Weapons cannot shred the soul, nor can fire burn it. Water cannot wet it, nor can the wind dry it.
commentary_full: This verse describes the soul's invulnerability to all the forces of the material world. The four elements traditionally considered most powerful — weapons (representing solid matter), fire, water, and wind (air) — are all unable to touch the soul. This is because the soul is not material. It is spiritual in nature — beyond the reach of any physical force. The soul does not occupy physical space, does not have material properties, and hence cannot be cut, burned, drenched, or dried. This is a poetic and vivid way of asserting the soul's absolute transcendence of the material realm.
commentary_summary: No weapon can cut the soul, no fire can burn it, no water wet it, no wind dry it — the soul is beyond all material forces.
theme: The soul's complete transcendence of all material forces and elements

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च |
नित्य: सर्वगत: स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातन: || 24||
transliteration:
achchhedyo 'yam adāhyo 'yam akledyo 'śhoṣhya eva cha
nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ sthāṇur achalo 'yaṁ sanātanaḥ
translation: The soul is unbreakable and incombustible; it can neither be dampened nor dried. It is everlasting, in all places, unalterable, immutable, and primordial.
commentary_full: This verse reinforces and expands on the previous one. The soul is achchhedya (unbreakable), adāhya (incombustible), akledya (cannot be dampened), aśhoṣhya (cannot be dried), nitya (eternal), sarva-gata (all-pervading), sthāṇu (stable), achala (immovable), and sanātana (primordial). These nine attributes together paint a comprehensive picture of the soul's absolute indestructibility, omnipresence, and unchanging nature. The word sanātana is particularly significant — it means not just ancient but beyond the very concept of time, having no beginning and no end.
commentary_summary: The soul is unbreakable, incombustible, eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and primordial — nine qualities of its absolute indestructibility.
theme: The nine attributes of the soul's absolute indestructibility and eternal nature

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते |
तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि || 25||
transliteration:
avyakto 'yam achintyo 'yam avikāryo 'yam uchyate
tasmād evaṁ viditvainaṁ nānuśhochitum arhasi
translation: The soul is spoken of as invisible, inconceivable, and unchangeable. Knowing this, you should not grieve for the body.
commentary_full: The soul is avyakta (invisible — it cannot be perceived by the senses), achintya (inconceivable — it cannot be comprehended by the intellect alone), and avikārya (unchangeable — it undergoes no modification). These three qualities reveal that the soul belongs to a dimension beyond both physical and mental perception. It can only be known through the inner awakening of self-realization. Having summarized the nature of the soul through these attributes, Shree Krishna draws the direct practical conclusion: knowing all this, you should not grieve. Grief for the body (whether one's own or others') is misplaced, because the real self — the soul — is beyond all harm.
commentary_summary: The soul is invisible, inconceivable, and unchangeable — knowing this, there is no basis for grief over the body.
theme: The soul's transcendence of perception and intellect as the final reason to release grief

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम् |
तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि || 26||
transliteration:
atha chainaṁ nitya-jātaṁ nityaṁ vā manyase mṛitam
tathāpi tvaṁ mahā-bāho naivaṁ śhochitum arhasi
translation: If, however, you think that the self is subject to constant birth and death, O mighty-armed Arjun, even then you should not grieve like this.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna makes a concession here for the sake of argument. Even if one does not accept the Vedantic teaching that the soul is eternal (perhaps holding the view that it is born and dies with each body), grief is still unjustified. If birth and death are inevitable for all living beings, what purpose does grief serve? One cannot prevent what is inevitable. The teaching of non-attachment to the transient applies regardless of one's philosophical position. This makes the teaching universally applicable — whether one is a Vedantist or not, excessive grief over the inevitable is irrational.
commentary_summary: Even if one believes in constant birth and death (rejecting the eternal soul), grief is still unjustified since birth and death are inevitable.
theme: Grief is unreasonable whether or not one accepts the eternity of the soul

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च |
तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि || 27||
transliteration:
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛityur dhruvaṁ janma mṛitasya cha
tasmād aparihārye 'rthe na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
translation: Death is certain for one who has been born, and rebirth is inevitable for one who has died. Therefore, you should not lament over the inevitable.
commentary_full: This verse states one of the simplest yet most profound truths: death is certain for the living, and birth is certain for the dead. There is a beautiful cyclical inevitability here. No one born has ever escaped death, and no soul in the cycle of rebirth has ever escaped being reborn. Knowing this, what use is grief? To grieve over the inevitable is like lamenting the rising and setting of the sun. The instruction is aparihārye arthe — 'for that which cannot be avoided.' Wisdom lies not in denying the inevitable, but in understanding it and acting in harmony with the higher truths of life.
commentary_summary: Death is certain for the born and rebirth inevitable for the dead — so grief over the inevitable is irrational and purposeless.
theme: Accepting the inevitability of death and birth frees the mind from futile grief

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत |
अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना || 28||
transliteration:
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyakta-madhyāni bhārata
avyakta-nidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā
translation: O scion of Bharat, all created beings are unmanifest before birth, manifest in life, and again unmanifest on death. So why grieve?
commentary_full: This verse presents an elegant three-stage view of existence: unmanifest before birth, manifest during life, unmanifest again after death. All living beings — human, animal, plant — follow this pattern. Before we were born, we were not visible in this world. During life, we are manifest. After death, we return to an unmanifest state. Given this universal pattern, grief seems almost absurd — we are lamenting the return to the same unmanifest state from which all beings came. The underlying reality (the soul) was never truly born and never truly dies; only the manifested form comes and goes.
commentary_summary: All beings are unmanifest before birth, manifest in life, and unmanifest after death — an eternal cycle that makes grief over the inevitable pointless.
theme: The three-stage cycle of unmanifest-manifest-unmanifest as the universal law of existence

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन-
माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्य: |
आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्य: शृणोति
श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित् || 29||
transliteration:
āśhcharyavat paśhyati kaśhchid enam
āśhcharyavad vadati tathaiva chānyaḥ
āśhcharyavach chainam anyaḥ śhṛiṇoti
śhrutvāpy enaṁ veda na chaiva kaśhchit
translation: Some see the soul as amazing, some describe it as amazing, and some hear of the soul as amazing, while others, even on hearing, cannot understand it at all.
commentary_full: The soul is presented here as an object of wonder (āśhcharya). Shree Krishna uses a four-part progression: some who see the soul are struck with wonder, some who describe it speak of it in wonder, some who hear about it hear it with wonder, and yet others, even after hearing, simply cannot understand it at all. This gradation reflects the varying degrees of spiritual receptivity and past merit. The soul being a matter of wonder is not because it is mysterious by nature — it is wonder to us because we are so habituated to identifying with the body that the revelation of the soul's true nature comes as a shock of astonishment.
commentary_summary: The soul is an object of wonder — some see it in awe, some speak of it in awe, some hear of it in awe, yet many, even after hearing, cannot comprehend it.
theme: The soul as a perennial source of wonder, inaccessible to the materially conditioned mind

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत |
तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि || 30||
transliteration:
dehī nityam avadhyo 'yaṁ dehe sarvasya bhārata
tasmāt sarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
translation: O Arjun, the soul that dwells within the body is immortal; therefore, you should not mourn for anyone.
commentary_full: This verse is the practical conclusion of the entire section on the immortality of the soul (verses 12–29). Having established through multiple arguments that the soul is eternal, indestructible, and beyond all harm, Shree Krishna now issues the direct command: do not mourn for anyone. The soul within every body — whether it is the body of Bheeshma, Drona, Duryodhan, or any other being — is immortal and cannot be killed. Therefore, grief for any being is based on a fundamental misconception. This verse completes the first major section of Krishna's teachings in Chapter 2.
commentary_summary: The soul within every body is immortal — therefore, grief for any living being is fundamentally misplaced.
theme: The immortality of the soul in every being as the ultimate reason to release all grief

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि |
धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाच्छ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते || 31||
transliteration:
svadharmam api chāvekṣhya na vikampitum arhasi
dharmyāddhi yuddhāch chhreyo 'nyat kṣhatriyasya na vidyate
translation: Besides, considering your duty as a warrior, you should not waver. Indeed, for a warrior, there is no better engagement than fighting for upholding of righteousness.
commentary_full: Having argued from the perspective of the immortal soul, Shree Krishna now shifts to the perspective of social duty (svadharma). Even setting aside the philosophical arguments about the soul, Arjun has a clear duty as a warrior (Kshatriya). The Kshatriya's highest dharma is to fight for righteousness. To refuse to fight when dharma is at stake is a failure of one's deepest social and cosmic obligation. There is literally no higher calling for a warrior than this. By refusing to fight, Arjun would not only be failing himself but failing the entire society that depends on warriors to uphold righteousness.
commentary_summary: Even from the perspective of social duty, a warrior should not waver — there is no higher engagement for a Kshatriya than fighting for righteousness.
theme: Svadharma — the sacred duty of one's station in life as a call to righteous action

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम् |
सुखिन: क्षत्रिया: पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम् || 32||
transliteration:
yadṛichchhayā chopapannaṁ swarga-dvāram apāvṛitam
sukhinaḥ kṣhatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddham īdṛiśham
translation: O Parth, happy are the warriors to whom such opportunities to defend righteousness come unsought, opening for them the stairway to the celestial abodes.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna now presents this war as a rare and precious opportunity — a gateway to the celestial abodes. The war has come to Arjun unsought (yadṛichchhayā — by chance, or more precisely, by divine arrangement). Such an opportunity to fight for dharma, on such a grand scale, is extraordinarily rare. Warriors who lay down their lives fighting for righteousness attain the celestial abodes. This is why the verse says 'happy are the warriors' — this battle is not a curse but a blessing, a golden stairway to heaven that has opened right at Arjun's feet.
commentary_summary: This war is a rare, divine opportunity — warriors who fight for righteousness gain access to celestial abodes. Arjun should consider himself fortunate.
theme: War in defense of righteousness as a rare divine blessing for the warrior

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अथ चेत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि |
तत: स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि || 33||
transliteration:
atha chet tvam imaṁ dharmyaṁ saṅgrāmaṁ na kariṣhyasi
tataḥ svadharmam kīrtiṁ cha hitvā pāpam avāpsyasi
translation: If, however, you refuse to fight this righteous war, abandoning your social duty and reputation, you will certainly incur sin.
commentary_full: The previous verse presented the positive case — fighting this war leads to glory and heaven. Now Krishna presents the negative case — refusing to fight leads to sin. Specifically, by refusing, Arjun would abandon svadharma (his duty as a warrior) and kīrti (his reputation for valor). The consequence is pāpa — sin or demerit. This is because a Kshatriya who abandons his duty when dharma requires him to fight is not merely failing himself — he is failing the cosmic order that depends on warriors to uphold righteousness. Dereliction of duty is not a neutral act; it has karmic consequences.
commentary_summary: Refusing this righteous war means abandoning duty and reputation — earning sin instead of glory.
theme: Dereliction of righteous duty leads to sin and spiritual degradation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम् |
सम्भावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते || 34||
transliteration:
akīrtiṁ chāpi bhūtāni kathayiṣhyanti te 'vyayām
sambhāvitasya chākīrtir maraṇād atirichyate
translation: People will speak of you as a coward and a deserter. For a respectable person, infamy is worse than death.
commentary_full: Having established the spiritual and dharmic consequences, Shree Krishna now appeals to Arjun's sense of honor. For a Kshatriya of Arjun's stature — celebrated throughout the known world as the greatest archer — to be branded a coward would be a fate worse than death. The verse states that for a person of high standing (sambhāvita — one who is highly regarded), infamy surpasses death in its severity. The memory of a warrior lives in the deeds he performed; to be remembered as a coward is to have one's entire life's worth erased.
commentary_summary: Arjun would be branded a coward, and for a person of honor, infamy is worse than death itself.
theme: For a person of honor, disgrace is a fate worse than death

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथा: |
येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम् || 35||
transliteration:
bhayād raṇād uparataṁ maṁsyante tvāṁ mahā-rathāḥ
yeṣhāṁ cha tvaṁ bahu-mato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam
translation: The great generals who hold you in high esteem will think that you fled from the battlefield out of fear, and thus will lose their respect for you.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna continues the appeal to Arjun's warrior ego. The great commanders (mahā-rathāḥ) — heroes like Drona, Karna, Bhishma, and others — hold Arjun in the highest regard. Arjun is acknowledged as the greatest archer of his time. If he now retreats from the battlefield, all of them will conclude that he did so out of fear (bhayāt). The one they regarded with the highest admiration will fall to the lowest esteem. This argument is particularly aimed at the warrior's sense of self-worth, which is inseparable from his reputation in battle.
commentary_summary: The great warriors who respect Arjun will conclude he fled out of fear, losing all the respect they held for him.
theme: Loss of respect from fellow warriors as a consequence of cowardice on the battlefield

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून्वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिता: |
निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दु:खतरं नु किम् || 36||
transliteration:
avāchya-vādānśh cha bahūn vadiṣhyanti tavāhitāḥ
nindantas tava sāmarthyaṁ tato duḥkhataraṁ nu kim
translation: Your enemies will defame and humiliate you with unkind words, disparaging your might. Alas, what could be more painful than that?
commentary_full: The enemies who could not defeat Arjun on the battlefield would gleefully defame him if he retreated. They would slander his name, mock his legendary valor, and celebrate his humiliation. For a proud warrior who has earned his reputation through a lifetime of extraordinary feats, to be mocked by enemies would be an unbearable agony. Shree Krishna uses this to highlight the irony of Arjun's 'compassionate' choice — in trying to avoid hurting others, he would end up in a far more painful situation himself, both in terms of reputation and inner guilt.
commentary_summary: Enemies would mock and slander Arjun's valor — and what pain is greater than being defamed by those you could have defeated?
theme: The humiliation of being mocked by enemies one could have rightfully defeated

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम् |
तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चय: || 37||
transliteration:
hato vā prāpsyasi swargaṁ jitvā vā bhokṣhyase mahīm
tasmād uttiṣhṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛita-niśhchayaḥ
translation: If you fight, you will either be slain on the battlefield and go to the celestial abodes, or you will gain victory and enjoy the kingdom on earth. Therefore arise with determination, O son of Kunti, and be prepared to fight.
commentary_full: This verse presents the classical Kshatriya logic — either way, Arjun wins. If he dies fighting righteously, he gains heaven. If he wins, he enjoys the earth. It is a win-win from the perspective of a warrior's dharma. The only losing outcome is to refuse to fight — that leads to infamy, sin, and spiritual degradation (as established in the previous verses). Having presented both the spiritual arguments (soul is immortal) and the practical arguments (duty, reputation, the two outcomes), Shree Krishna now issues the direct command: 'arise with determination.'
commentary_summary: In battle Arjun either wins heaven through death or wins the kingdom through victory — both are gains; therefore arise with determination.
theme: The win-win logic of fighting righteously — victory leads to glory, defeat leads to heaven

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सुखदु:खे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ |
ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि || 38||
transliteration:
sukha-duḥkhe same kṛitvā lābhālābhau jayājayau
tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṁ pāpam avāpsyasi
translation: Fight for the sake of duty, treating alike happiness and distress, loss and gain, victory and defeat. Fulfilling your responsibility in this way, you will never incur sin.
commentary_full: This verse introduces the concept of equanimity in action — one of the core principles of Karma Yoga. By treating happiness and distress, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, the warrior (or any person performing their duty) remains unattached to the outcomes. This equanimity is not indifference but a higher engagement — performing one's duty fully while remaining inwardly untouched by results. When action is performed with this equanimous spirit, it does not generate karma (bondage). This is why Shree Krishna says 'you will not incur sin' — action performed without ego-driven attachment to outcomes is spiritually liberating.
commentary_summary: Fight treating victory and defeat, gain and loss, pleasure and pain as equal — such equanimous duty never incurs sin.
theme: Equanimity in action as the foundation of karma yoga and spiritual liberation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां शृणु |
बुद्ध्या युक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि || 39||
transliteration:
eṣhā te 'bhihitā sānkhye buddhir yoge tv imāṁ śhṛiṇu
buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha karma-bandhaṁ prahāsyasi
translation: Hitherto, I have explained to you Sānkhya Yog, or analytic knowledge regarding the nature of the soul. Now listen, O Parth, as I reveal Buddhi Yog, or the Yog of Intellect. When you work with such understanding, you will be freed from the bondage of karma.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna marks a transition in his teaching. The first section (verses 11–38) dealt with Sankhya Yoga — the analytical knowledge of the soul's nature. Now he introduces Buddhi Yoga — the yoga of the intellect, or working with divine wisdom. The key difference is the application: Sankhya is theoretical knowledge about the soul; Buddhi Yoga is the practical science of how to act in the world based on that knowledge. By working with the intellect aligned with divine wisdom, one breaks free from karma-bandha — the bondage of action. This is the beginning of the famous Karma Yoga teaching.
commentary_summary: Having explained Sankhya Yoga (knowledge of the soul), Krishna now introduces Buddhi Yoga — working with divine intellect to break free from karmic bondage.
theme: The transition from theoretical soul-knowledge to the practical science of karma yoga

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते |
स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात् || 40||
transliteration:
nehābhikrama-nāśho 'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate
svalpam apyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt
translation: Working in this state of consciousness, there is no loss or adverse result, and even a little effort saves one from great danger.
commentary_full: This verse describes the unique characteristics of Buddhi Yoga (Karma Yoga with equanimity and divine consciousness). Unlike material endeavors where partial effort may yield no results, even a small effort on the spiritual path has permanent value. The spiritual path is progressive and cumulative — no sincere effort is ever wasted, and one never has to restart from zero. Additionally, even a little practice of this path protects one from the greatest fear — the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. This encouraging assurance is one of the reasons why the Bhagavad Gita's teachings on karma yoga are so empowering.
commentary_summary: On this path, no effort is ever lost — even a little practice of karma yoga saves one from great spiritual danger.
theme: The irreversible, cumulative nature of spiritual effort on the path of karma yoga

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन |
बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम् || 41||
transliteration:
vyavasāyātmikā buddhir ekeha kuru-nandana
bahu-śhākhā hy anantāśh cha buddhayo 'vyavasāyinām
translation: O descendent of the Kurus, the intellect of those who are on this path is resolute, and their aim is one-pointed. But the intellect of those who are irresolute is many-branched.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna describes the quality of intellect required for Buddhi Yoga — vyavasāyātmikā buddhi, the resolute intellect with a single, unwavering aim. Those who follow this path with determination have a one-pointed focus: God-realization and the fulfillment of their duty in a spirit of divine offering. By contrast, the intellect of the irresolute is bahu-śhākhā — many-branched, scattered in innumerable directions by desires, doubts, and wavering plans. The image is of a tree: the resolute intellect is like a straight trunk going directly upward, while the irresolute mind branches in countless directions, dissipating its energy.
commentary_summary: The resolute intellect on the spiritual path is one-pointed; the irresolute mind branches in countless directions, dissipating its energy.
theme: One-pointed resolute intellect as the essential quality for progress on the spiritual path

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चित: |
वेदवादरता: पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिन: || 42||
transliteration:
yām imāṁ puṣhpitāṁ vāchaṁ pravadanty avipaśhchitaḥ
veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ
translation: Those with limited understanding, get attracted to the flowery words of the Vedas, which advocate ostentatious rituals for elevation to the celestial abodes, and presume no higher principle is described in them. They glorify only those portions of the Vedas that please their senses, and perform pompous ritualistic ceremonies for attaining high birth, opulence, sensual enjoyment, and elevation to the heavenly planets.
commentary_full: This verse (and verse 43) critique a particular misuse of Vedic knowledge — using the Vedic injunctions for ritualistic ceremonies as an end in themselves, rather than as a means to God-realization. The word puṣhpitāṁ vācham means 'flowery speech' — attractive, elaborate, and appealing to the senses, but ultimately leading away from liberation. Those who are avipaśhchitaḥ — of limited understanding — get captivated by the ornate rituals and promises of sensory rewards in the celestial abodes, and fail to go beyond to the deeper spiritual truths of the Vedas. They mistake the finger pointing to the moon for the moon itself. The Vedas, like a river, have shallow banks (ritualistic sections) and deep waters (the Upanishads and their teachings on Brahman). These individuals wade in the shallows, presuming there is nothing deeper.
commentary_summary: Those of limited understanding are seduced by the flowery promises of Vedic rituals for heavenly pleasures, missing the deeper spiritual truths of the Vedas entirely.
theme: The danger of mistaking Vedic rituals and sensory rewards for the ultimate spiritual goal

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
इमं विवस्वते योगं प्रोक्तवानहमव्ययम् |
विवस्वान्मनवे प्राह मनुरिक्ष्वाकवेऽब्रवीत् || 1||
Transliteration:
imaṁ vivasvate yogaṁ proktavān aham avyayam |
vivasvān manave prāha manur ikṣhvākave ’bravīt ||
Translation: I taught this imperishable yoga to the Sun-god Vivasvan; Vivasvan taught it to Manu, and Manu taught it to Ikshvaku.
commentary_full: Krishna begins by establishing the ancient and divine origin of this knowledge. This yoga is not a new philosophy but eternal wisdom passed down through a sacred lineage. By tracing its transmission from the Sun-god to kings, Krishna emphasizes that spiritual knowledge was traditionally integrated with righteous leadership and governance.
commentary_summary: Krishna reveals the eternal origin of yoga.
theme: Eternal transmission of spiritual wisdom

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
एवं परम्पराप्राप्तमिमं राजर्षयो विदुः |
स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप || 2||
Transliteration:
evaṁ paramparā-prāptam imaṁ rājarṣhayo viduḥ |
sa kāleneha mahatā yogo naṣhṭaḥ parantapa ||
Translation: This knowledge was received through disciplic succession, but over time it was lost.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that when spiritual knowledge is not properly preserved or practiced, it becomes distorted or forgotten. The loss of true understanding leads to moral and spiritual decline, making divine intervention necessary.
commentary_summary: Breakdown of tradition causes loss of true yoga.
theme: Decline of spiritual tradition

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
स एवायं मया तेऽद्य योगः प्रोक्तः पुरातनः |
भक्तोऽसि मे सखा चेति रहस्यं ह्येतदुत्तमम् || 3||
Transliteration:
sa evāyaṁ mayā te ’dya yogaḥ proktaḥ purātanaḥ |
bhakto ’si me sakhā cheti rahasyaṁ hyetad uttamam ||
Translation: That same ancient yoga I am teaching you today, because you are My devotee and friend.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals that devotion and trust qualify one to receive higher knowledge. Spiritual truth is not merely intellectual but relational, transmitted through love, faith, and surrender.
commentary_summary: Devotion makes Arjuna eligible for divine knowledge.
theme: Qualification for spiritual knowledge

speaker: Arjuna
Sanskrit text:
अपरं भवतो जन्म परं जन्म विवस्वतः |
कथमेतद्विजानीयां त्वमादौ प्रोक्तवानिति || 4||
Transliteration:
aparaṁ bhavato janma paraṁ janma vivasvataḥ |
katham etad vijānīyāṁ tvam ādau proktavān iti ||
Translation: You were born recently, but Vivasvan lived long ago. How am I to understand this?
commentary_full: Arjuna’s doubt arises from seeing Krishna in human form. This represents the limitation of material perception when confronted with divine reality.
commentary_summary: Arjuna questions Krishna’s divine nature.
theme: Human limitation in understanding God

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
बहूनि मे व्यतीतानि जन्मानि तव चार्जुन |
तान्यहं वेद सर्वाणि न त्वं वेत्थ परन्तप || 5||
Transliteration:
bahūni me vyatītāni janmāni tava chārjuna |
tāny ahaṁ veda sarvāṇi na tvaṁ vettha parantapa ||
Translation: Both you and I have had many births, but I remember them all.
commentary_full: Krishna distinguishes divine omniscience from human forgetfulness. God remains fully conscious across all incarnations.
commentary_summary: Krishna remembers all His incarnations.
theme: Divine consciousness

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
अजोऽपि सन्नव्ययात्मा भूतानामीश्वरोऽपि सन् |
प्रकृतिं स्वामधिष्ठाय सम्भवाम्यात्ममायया || 6||
Transliteration:
ajo ’pi sann avyayātmā bhūtānām īśvaro ’pi san |
prakṛitiṁ svām adhiṣhṭhāya sambhavāmy ātma-māyayā ||
Translation: Though unborn and imperishable, I appear by My own divine power.
commentary_full: Krishna explains the mystery of incarnation. He does not take birth due to karma but manifests through His divine will.
commentary_summary: God incarnates by divine will.
theme: Mystery of incarnation

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत |
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् || 7||
Transliteration:
yadā yadā hi dharmasya glānir bhavati bhārata |
abhyutthānam adharmasya tadātmānaṁ sṛijāmy aham ||
Translation: Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, I manifest Myself.
commentary_full: Krishna declares divine intervention as a response to moral imbalance.
commentary_summary: God appears to restore dharma.
theme: Restoration of righteousness

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम् |
धर्मसंस्थापनार्थाय सम्भवामि युगे युगे || 8||
Transliteration:
paritrāṇāya sādhūnāṁ vināśhāya cha duṣhkṛitām |
dharma-saṁsthāpanārthāya sambhavāmi yuge yuge ||
Translation: To protect the righteous, destroy evil, and reestablish dharma, I appear age after age.
commentary_full: This verse defines the mission of divine incarnation across ages.
commentary_summary: God protects the good and destroys evil.
theme: Purpose of incarnation

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
जन्म कर्म च मे दिव्यमेवं यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः |
त्यक्त्वा देहं पुनर्जन्म नैति मामेति सोऽर्जुन || 9||
Transliteration:
janma karma cha me divyam evaṁ yo vetti tattvataḥ |
tyaktvā dehaṁ punar janma naiti mām eti so ’rjuna ||
Translation: One who understands My divine birth and actions is liberated.
commentary_full: True realization of Krishna’s divinity frees one from rebirth.
commentary_summary: Knowledge of Krishna leads to liberation.
theme: Liberation through divine understanding

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
वीतरागभयक्रोधा मन्मया मामुपाश्रिताः |
बहवो ज्ञानतपसा पूता मद्भावमागताः || 10||
Transliteration:
vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhā man-mayā mām upāśritāḥ |
bahavo jñāna-tapasā pūtā mad-bhāvam āgatāḥ ||
Translation: Freed from attachment, fear, and anger, many have attained My state through knowledge.
commentary_full: Knowledge purifies the mind and removes emotional disturbances, leading to liberation.
commentary_summary: Detachment through knowledge leads to liberation.
theme: Purification through knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
ये यथा मां प्रपद्यन्ते तांस्तथैव भजाम्यहम् |
मम वर्त्मानुवर्तन्ते मनुष्याः पार्थ सर्वशः || 11||
Transliteration:
ye yathā māṁ prapadyante tāṁs tathaiva bhajāmy aham |
mama vartmānuvartante manuṣhyāḥ pārtha sarvaśhaḥ ||
Translation: As people surrender unto Me, I reciprocate accordingly.
commentary_full: Krishna responds to each soul based on their level of surrender.
commentary_summary: God reciprocates with surrender.
theme: Divine reciprocity

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
काङ्क्षन्तः कर्मणां सिद्धिं यजन्त इह देवताः |
क्षिप्रं हि मानुषे लोके सिद्धिर्भवति कर्मजा || 12||
Transliteration:
kāṅkṣhantaḥ karmaṇāṁ siddhiṁ yajanta iha devatāḥ |
kṣhipraṁ hi mānuṣhe loke siddhir bhavati karma-jā ||
Translation: Those seeking material success worship demigods.
commentary_full: Material desires yield quick but temporary results.
commentary_summary: Material worship gives temporary success.
theme: Temporary nature of material gains

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
चातुर्वर्ण्यं मया सृष्टं गुणकर्मविभागशः |
तस्य कर्तारमपि मां विद्ध्यकर्तारमव्ययम् || 13||
Transliteration:
chātur-varṇyaṁ mayā sṛiṣhṭaṁ guṇa-karma-vibhāgaśhaḥ |
tasya kartāram api māṁ viddhy akartāram avyayam ||
Translation: The four social orders were created based on qualities and actions.
commentary_full: Social roles are determined by nature and work, not birth.
commentary_summary: Duties depend on qualities and actions.
theme: Division of work by nature

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
न मां कर्माणि लिम्पन्ति न मे कर्मफले स्पृहा |
इति मां योऽभिजानाति कर्मभिर्न स बध्यते || 14||
Transliteration:
na māṁ karmāṇi limpanti na me karma-phale spṛihā |
iti māṁ yo ’bhijānāti karmabhir na sa badhyate ||
Translation: Actions do not bind Me, nor those who understand Me.
commentary_full: Detachment from results frees one from bondage.
commentary_summary: Detached action leads to freedom.
theme: Action without bondage

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
एवं ज्ञात्वा कृतं कर्म पूर्वैरपि मुमुक्षुभिः |
कुरु कर्मैव तस्मात्त्वं पूर्वैः पूर्वतरं कृतम् || 15||
Transliteration:
evaṁ jñātvā kṛitaṁ karma pūrvair api mumukṣhubhiḥ |
kuru karmaiva tasmāt tvaṁ pūrvaiḥ pūrvataraṁ kṛitam ||
Translation: Knowing this, the wise acted accordingly.
commentary_full: Liberation is attained through enlightened action.
commentary_summary: Follow the path of wise action.
theme: Path of enlightened action

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
किं कर्म किमकर्मेति कवयोऽप्यत्र मोहिताः |
तत्ते कर्म प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् || 16||
Transliteration:
kiṁ karma kim akarmeti kavayo ’py atra mohitāḥ |
tat te karma pravakṣhyāmi yaj jñātvā mokṣhyase ’śhubhāt ||
Translation: Even the wise are confused about action and inaction.
commentary_full: Krishna introduces the subtle science of karma.
commentary_summary: Action must be properly understood.
theme: Subtlety of karma

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
कर्मणो ह्यपि बोद्धव्यं बोद्धव्यं च विकर्मणः |
अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गतिः || 17||
Transliteration:
karmaṇo hy api boddhavyaṁ boddhavyaṁ cha vikarmaṇaḥ |
akarmaṇaśh cha boddhavyaṁ gahanā karmaṇo gatiḥ ||
Translation: One must understand action, forbidden action, and inaction.
commentary_full: True understanding of karma requires discernment.
commentary_summary: Karma is subtle and complex.
theme: Depth of karmic law

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
कर्मण्यकर्म यः पश्येदकर्मणि च कर्म यः |
स बुद्धिमान्मनुष्येषु स युक्तः कृत्स्नकर्मकृत् || 18||
Transliteration:
karmaṇy akarma yaḥ paśhyed akarmaṇi cha karma yaḥ |
sa buddhimān manuṣhyeṣhu sa yuktaḥ kṛitsna-karma-kṛit ||
Translation: One who sees inaction in action and action in inaction is wise.
commentary_full: Detached action is true inaction.
commentary_summary: Wisdom lies in detached action.
theme: Action in inaction

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
यस्य सर्वे समारम्भाः कामसङ्कल्पवर्जिताः |
ज्ञानाग्निदग्धकर्माणं तमाहुः पण्डितं बुधाः || 19||
Transliteration:
yasya sarve samārambhāḥ kāma-saṅkalpa-varjitāḥ |
jñānāgni-dagdha-karmāṇaṁ tam āhuḥ paṇḍitaṁ budhāḥ ||
Translation: One whose actions are free from desire is truly wise.
commentary_full: Desireless action purified by knowledge leads to wisdom.
commentary_summary: Freedom from desire defines wisdom.
theme: Wisdom through freedom from desire

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
त्यक्त्वा कर्मफलासङ्गं नित्यतृप्तो निराश्रयः |
कर्मण्यभिप्रवृत्तोऽपि नैव किञ्चित्करोति सः || 20||
Transliteration: tyaktvā karma-phala-saṅgaṁ nitya-tṛipto nirāśhrayaḥ |\karmaṇy abhipravṛitto ’pi naiva kiñchit karoti saḥ ||
Translation: Giving up attachment to results, one remains free even while acting.
commentary_full: Renunciation within action is the ideal yogic state.
commentary_summary: Inner renunciation leads to freedom.
theme: Renunciation through action

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
निराशीर्यतचित्तात्मा त्यक्तसर्वपरिग्रहः |
शारीरं केवलं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् || 21||
Transliteration:
nirāśhīr yata-chittātmā tyakta-sarva-parigrahaḥ |
śhārīraṁ kevalaṁ karma kurvan nāpnoti kilbiṣham ||
Translation: Free from desires, controlling the mind and senses, and abandoning all sense of ownership, one incurs no sin by performing bodily actions.
commentary_full: Krishna explains the state of a self-realized person who performs actions without personal desire or attachment. Such a person is free from expectations of reward and has renounced possessiveness over material objects and outcomes. Although they continue to perform necessary bodily duties, these actions do not bind them with karma because they are not motivated by ego or selfish intent. The absence of desire and ownership dissolves karmic reactions, making the action spiritually neutral and purifying.
commentary_summary: Desireless action without attachment does not bind one to sin.
theme: Freedom from bondage through desireless action

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
यदृच्छालाभसंतुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः |
समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते || 22||
Transliteration:
yadṛichchhā-lābha-santuṣhṭo dvandvātīto vimatsaraḥ |
amaḥ siddhāv asiddhau cha kṛitvāpi na nibadhyate ||
Translation: Content with whatever comes naturally, free from duality and envy, balanced in success and failure, such a person is not bound by actions.
commentary_full: Krishna highlights the inner stability of a liberated individual. Such a person remains satisfied with whatever comes by destiny and does not chase outcomes. Rising above dualities like pleasure and pain, success and failure, they act without jealousy or competition. Because their mind remains balanced in all situations, their actions do not generate karmic bondage. Equanimity becomes the key to spiritual freedom.
commentary_summary: Equanimity and contentment free one from karmic bondage.
theme: Equanimity as the path to freedom

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
गतसङ्गस्य मुक्तस्य ज्ञानावस्थितचेतसः |
यज्ञायाचरतः कर्म समग्रं प्रविलीयते || 23||
Transliteration:
gata-saṅgasya muktasya jñānāvasthita-chetasaḥ |
yajñāyācharataḥ karma samagraṁ pravilīyate ||
Translation: The actions of one who is detached, liberated, and established in knowledge, performed as sacrifice, are fully dissolved.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that when actions are performed as yajna (sacrifice) rather than for personal gain, they lose their binding power. A person rooted in knowledge and free from attachment performs duties as offerings to the Divine. Such actions do not accumulate karma; instead, they dissolve past karmic impressions. This verse establishes the spiritual principle that intention, not action itself, determines bondage or liberation.
commentary_summary: Actions offered as sacrifice dissolve all karma.
theme: Sacrificial action and dissolution of karma

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
ब्रह्मार्पणं ब्रह्म हविर्ब्रह्माग्नौ ब्रह्मणा हुतम् |
ब्रह्मैव तेन गन्तव्यं ब्रह्मकर्मसमाधिना || 24||
Transliteration:
brahmārpaṇaṁ brahma havir brahmāgnau brahmaṇā hutam |
brahmaiva tena gantavyaṁ brahma-karma-samādhinā ||
Translation: For one who sees everything as Brahman, the offering, the fire, the act, and the goal are all Brahman.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals the highest vision of non-duality. When one realizes Brahman as the ultimate reality, every aspect of action becomes sacred. The doer, the action, and the result merge into a single divine consciousness. Such perception transforms ordinary work into spiritual meditation, leading inevitably to liberation.
commentary_summary: Seeing all actions as Brahman leads to liberation.
theme: Non-dual vision in action

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
दैवमेवापरे यज्ञं योगिनः पर्युपासते |
ब्रह्माग्नावपरे यज्ञं यज्ञेनैवोपजुह्वति || 25||
Transliteration:
daivam evāpare yajñaṁ yoginaḥ paryupāsate |
brahmāgnāv apare yajñaṁ yajñenaivopajuhvati ||
Translation: Some yogis worship the gods through sacrifice, while others offer sacrifice into the fire of Brahman.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that spiritual aspirants follow different paths according to their understanding. Some perform ritual sacrifices to deities, while others engage in inner spiritual sacrifice rooted in self-knowledge. Both approaches, when done with sincerity, contribute to spiritual progress, though knowledge-based sacrifice is superior.
commentary_summary: Different forms of sacrifice suit different seekers.
theme: Variety of spiritual practices

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
श्रोत्रादीनीन्द्रियाण्यन्ये संयमाग्निषु जुह्वति |
शब्दादीन्विषयानन्य इन्द्रियाग्निषु जुह्वति || 26||
Transliteration:
śhrotrādīnīndriyāṇy anye saṁyamāgniṣhu juhvati |
śhabdādīn viṣhayān anya indriyāgniṣhu juhvati ||
Translation: Some offer the senses into the fire of self-control, while others offer sense objects into the fire of the senses.
commentary_full: Krishna describes yogic discipline as an inner sacrifice. Some restrain the senses through self-control, while others regulate sensory engagement mindfully. Both approaches aim to master desire and prevent the senses from dominating consciousness.
commentary_summary: Sense control itself becomes a spiritual sacrifice.
theme: Discipline as spiritual sacrifice

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
सर्वाणीन्द्रियकर्माणि प्राणकर्माणि चापरे |
आत्मसंयमयोगाग्नौ जुह्वति ज्ञानदीपिते || 27||
Transliteration:
sarvāṇīndriya-karmāṇi prāṇa-karmāṇi chāpare |
ātma-saṁyama-yogāgnau juhvati jñāna-dīpite ||
Translation: Others offer all sensory and vital actions into the fire of self-control illuminated by knowledge.
commentary_full: This verse presents a higher yogic state where all actions—physical and mental—are consciously surrendered into disciplined awareness guided by knowledge. Such integration leads to purification and inner mastery.
commentary_summary: All actions are offered into disciplined self-awareness.
theme: Integration of action through knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
द्रव्ययज्ञास्तपोयज्ञा योगयज्ञास्तथापरे |
स्वाध्यायज्ञानयज्ञाश्च यतयः संशितव्रताः || 28||
Transliteration:
dravya-yajñās tapo-yajñā yoga-yajñās tathāpare |
svādhyāya-jñāna-yajñāśh cha yatayaḥ saṁśhita-vratāḥ ||
Translation: Some perform sacrifice through wealth, austerity, yoga, or study of sacred knowledge.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that sacrifice can take many forms—charity, austerity, meditation, and study. What matters is sincerity and discipline. All such sacrifices contribute to purification when aligned with spiritual purpose.
commentary_summary: Spiritual sacrifice takes many valid forms.
theme: Multiple paths of sacrifice

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
अपाने जुह्वति प्राणं प्राणेऽपानं तथापरे |
प्राणापानगती रुद्ध्वा प्राणायामपरायणाः || 29||
Transliteration:
apāne juhvati prāṇaṁ prāṇe ’pānaṁ tathāpare |
prāṇāpāna-gatī ruddhvā prāṇāyāma-parāyaṇāḥ ||
Translation: Some practice breath control by offering inhalation into exhalation and vice versa.
commentary_full: Krishna describes pranayama as a form of inner sacrifice. By regulating breath, practitioners gain control over the mind and life energy, preparing themselves for higher realization.
commentary_summary: Breath control is a powerful spiritual discipline.
theme: Breath regulation as spiritual practice

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
सर्वेऽप्येते यज्ञविदो यज्ञक्षपितकल्मषाः |
यज्ञशिष्टामृतभुजो यान्ति ब्रह्म सनातनम् || 30||
Transliteration:
sarve ’py ete yajña-vido yajña-kṣhapita-kalmaṣhāḥ |
yajña-śhiṣhṭāmṛita-bhujo yānti brahma sanātanam ||
Translation: All these practitioners of sacrifice are purified and attain the eternal Absolute.
commentary_full: Krishna concludes that sincere spiritual practice—regardless of form—purifies the heart. When sacrifice is performed with knowledge and devotion, it leads to realization of the eternal truth, Brahman.
commentary_summary: All sincere sacrifices lead to liberation.
theme: Liberation through sincere sacrifice

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text: नायं लोकोऽस्त्ययज्ञस्य कुतोऽन्यः कुरुसत्तम || 31||
Transliteration: nāyaṁ loko ’sty ayajñasya kuto ’nyaḥ kuru-sattama ||
Translation: O best of the Kurus, one who does not perform sacrifice cannot be happy in this world or the next.
commentary_full: Krishna emphasizes the necessity of sacrifice (yajna) in human life. Sacrifice here does not only mean ritual offerings, but selfless action performed for a higher purpose. A life centered purely on selfish enjoyment leads to dissatisfaction and spiritual stagnation. Without sacrifice, harmony with society, nature, and the Divine is impossible, resulting in suffering both materially and spiritually.
commentary_summary: Without sacrifice, true happiness cannot be attained.
theme: Necessity of sacrifice for fulfillment

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
एवं बहुविधा यज्ञा वितता ब्रह्मणो मुखे |
कर्मजान्विद्धि तान्सर्वानेवं ज्ञात्वा विमोक्ष्यसे || 32||
Transliteration:
evaṁ bahu-vidhā yajñā vitatā brahmaṇo mukhe |
karma-jān viddhi tān sarvān evaṁ jñātvā vimokṣhyase ||
Translation: All these various sacrifices originate from action; knowing this, you will be liberated.
commentary_full: Krishna clarifies that all forms of sacrifice are rooted in action. When action is understood as a means of spiritual growth rather than personal gain, it becomes liberating. Knowledge of this truth removes ignorance and frees one from bondage. Thus, action guided by wisdom becomes the doorway to liberation.
commentary_summary: Understanding action as sacrifice leads to liberation.
theme: Liberation through understanding action

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
श्रेयान्द्रव्यमयाद्यज्ञाज्ज्ञानयज्ञः परन्तप |
सर्वं कर्माखिलं पार्थ ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते || 33||
Transliteration:
śhreyān dravya-mayād yajñāj jñāna-yajñaḥ parantapa |
sarvaṁ karmākhilaṁ pārtha jñāne parisamāpyate ||
Translation: O conqueror of enemies, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to material sacrifice.
commentary_full: Krishna declares that offering knowledge is the highest form of sacrifice. While material sacrifices purify temporarily, knowledge destroys ignorance at its root. When actions are guided by true understanding, they lose their binding effect and culminate in liberation.
commentary_summary: Knowledge is the highest and most powerful sacrifice.
theme: Supremacy of knowledge over ritual

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
तद्विद्धि प्रणिपातेन परिप्रश्नेन सेवया |
उपदेक्ष्यन्ति ते ज्ञानं ज्ञानिनस्तत्त्वदर्शिनः || 34||
Transliteration:
tad viddhi praṇipātena paripraśhnena sevayā |
upadekṣhyanti te jñānaṁ jñāninas tattva-darśhinaḥ ||
Translation: Learn the truth by approaching a Guru with humility, inquiry, and service.
commentary_full: Krishna explains the proper method for acquiring spiritual knowledge. Intellectual effort alone is insufficient. One must approach a realized teacher with humility, sincere questioning, and a service attitude. Such a Guru transmits knowledge born of direct realization, not mere theory.
commentary_summary: True knowledge is received through a realized Guru.
theme: Guru–disciple relationship

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
यज्ज्ञात्वा न पुनर्मोहमेवं यास्यसि पाण्डव |
येन भूतान्यशेषेण द्रक्ष्यस्यात्मन्यथो मयि || 35||
Transliteration:
yaj jñātvā na punar moham evaṁ yāsyasi pāṇḍava |
yena bhūtāny aśheṣheṇa drakṣhyasy ātmany atho mayi ||
Translation: By knowing this knowledge, you will no longer fall into illusion.
commentary_full: Krishna assures Arjuna that true knowledge permanently removes delusion. Once ignorance is destroyed, one perceives all beings as manifestations of the same spiritual reality. This vision dissolves fear, hatred, and attachment.
commentary_summary: Knowledge removes illusion permanently.
theme: Freedom from illusion through knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
अपि चेदसि पापेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः पापकृत्तमः |
सर्वं ज्ञानप्लवेनैव वृजिनं सन्तरिष्यसि || 36||
Transliteration:
api ched asi pāpebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ pāpa-kṛittamaḥ |
sarvaṁ jñāna-plavenaiva vṛijinaṁ santariṣhyasi ||
Translation: Even the greatest sinner can cross all sin by the boat of knowledge.
commentary_full: Krishna declares the redemptive power of knowledge. No matter how sinful one’s past actions may be, sincere spiritual wisdom has the power to purify completely. Knowledge acts like a boat that carries one safely across the ocean of sin.
commentary_summary: Knowledge has the power to redeem all sins.
theme: Redemptive power of knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
यथैधांसि समिद्धोऽग्निर्भस्मसात्कुरुतेऽर्जुन |
ज्ञानाग्निः सर्वकर्माणि भस्मसात्कुरुते तथा || 37||
Transliteration:
yathaidhāṁsi samiddho ’gnir bhasma-sāt kurute ’rjuna |
jñānāgniḥ sarva-karmāṇi bhasma-sāt kurute tathā ||
Translation: Just as fire burns wood to ashes, knowledge burns all karma.
commentary_full: Krishna compares knowledge to fire. Just as fire completely reduces fuel to ash, true knowledge destroys all karmic reactions. This illustrates that knowledge does not merely suppress karma but annihilates it entirely.
commentary_summary: Knowledge destroys karma completely.
theme: Knowledge as destroyer of karma

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
न हि ज्ञानेन सदृशं पवित्रमिह विद्यते |
तत्स्वयं योगसंसिद्धः कालेनात्मनि विन्दति || 38||
Transliteration:
na hi jñānena sadṛiśhaṁ pavitram iha vidyate |
tat svayaṁ yoga-saṁsiddhaḥ kālenātmani vindati ||
Translation: There is nothing as purifying as knowledge.
commentary_full: Krishna states that among all purifying forces, knowledge is supreme. Through disciplined practice and time, a sincere seeker naturally realizes this knowledge within the heart.
commentary_summary: Knowledge is the highest purifier.
theme: Supreme purity of knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
श्रद्धावाँल्लभते ज्ञानं तत्परः संयतेन्द्रियः |
ज्ञानं लब्ध्वा परां शान्तिमचिरेणाधिगच्छति || 39||
Transliteration:
śhraddhāvān labhate jñānaṁ tat-paraḥ saṁyatendriyaḥ |
jñānaṁ labdhvā parāṁ śhāntim achireṇādhigachchhati ||
Translation: The faithful, self-controlled person attains knowledge and supreme peace.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that faith, discipline, and dedication are essential for gaining knowledge. Once knowledge is attained, inner peace naturally follows, free from doubt and disturbance.
commentary_summary: Faith and discipline lead to knowledge and peace.
theme: Path to peace through knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
अज्ञश्चाश्रद्दधानश्च संशयात्मा विनश्यति |
नायं लोकोऽस्ति न परो न सुखं संशयात्मनः || 40||
Transliteration:
ajñaśh chāśhraddadhānaśh cha saṁśhayātmā vinaśhyati |
nāyaṁ loko ’sti na paro na sukhaṁ saṁśhayātmanaḥ ||
Translation: The ignorant, faithless, and doubting person is ruined.
commentary_full: Krishna warns against doubt and lack of faith. Such a mindset prevents spiritual progress and inner happiness. Doubt paralyzes action and blocks realization.
commentary_summary: Doubt and lack of faith destroy progress.
theme: Destructive nature of doubt

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
योगसंन्यस्तकर्माणं ज्ञानसञ्छिन्नसंशयम् |
आत्मवन्तं न कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय || 41||
Transliteration:
yoga-sannyasta-karmāṇaṁ jñāna-sañchhinna-saṁśhayam |
ātmavantaṁ na karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanañjaya ||
Translation: One who has renounced action through yoga and cut doubt with knowledge is not bound by karma.
commentary_full: Krishna describes the liberated individual whose doubts are destroyed by knowledge and whose actions are surrendered through yoga. Such a person remains untouched by karmic reactions.
commentary_summary: Knowledge and yoga free one from karmic bondage.
theme: Freedom from karma through wisdom

speaker: Shree Krishna
Sanskrit text:
तस्मादज्ञानसम्भूतं हृत्स्थं ज्ञानासिनात्मनः |
छित्त्वैनं संशयं योगमातिष्ठोत्तिष्ठ भारत || 42||
Transliteration:
tasmād ajñāna-sambhūtaṁ hṛit-sthaṁ jñānāsinātmanaḥ |
chhittvainaṁ saṁśhayaṁ yogam ātiṣhṭhottiṣhṭha bhārata ||
Translation: Cut ignorance-born doubt with the sword of knowledge and arise, O Bharata.
commentary_full: Krishna concludes Chapter 4 with a powerful call to action. Ignorance creates doubt that binds the soul. Knowledge is the sword that destroys this doubt. Once clarity is achieved, one must rise and act decisively in yoga, fulfilling duty with wisdom.
commentary_summary: Destroy doubt with knowledge and rise to action.
theme: Final call to rise with wisdom

speaker: Arjuna
text_sanskrit: अर्जुन उवाच | संन्यासं कर्मणां कृष्ण पुनर्योगं च शंससि | यच्छ्रेय एतयोरेकं तन्मे ब्रूहि सुनिश्चितम् ||1||
transliteration: arjuna uvācha | sannyāsaṁ karmaṇāṁ kṛiṣhṇa punar yogaṁ cha śhansasi | yach chhreya etayor ekaṁ tan me brūhi su-niśhchitam ||
translation: Arjun said: O Shree Krishna, You praise karm sanyās (renunciation of actions), and You also recommend karm yog (performing actions with devotion). Please tell me clearly which of the two is more beneficial.
commentary_full:
Arjun asks his fifth question to Shree Krishna. Previously, Krishna praised both the renunciation of actions (karm sanyās) and the path of performing actions with devotion (karm yog). This seems contradictory to Arjun, which creates confusion in his mind. He wishes to understand which path is superior and more suitable for him.

In the first chapter, Arjun’s grief and confusion were described, setting the stage for Krishna’s teachings. In the second chapter, Krishna explained the nature of the soul, stating that the soul is immortal and cannot be destroyed. Therefore, lamenting over death is misguided. Krishna also reminded Arjun of his duty as a warrior to fight for righteousness and advised him to perform his duty without attachment to the results, dedicating the fruits of his actions to God.

In the third chapter, Krishna explained the importance of performing one’s duties to purify the mind. However, He also mentioned that a person who has already attained purity and self-realization is not obligated to perform social duties.

In the fourth chapter, Krishna discussed different types of sacrifices and explained that sacrifice performed with knowledge is superior to mechanical rituals. He also introduced the concept of karm sanyās, where one renounces ritualistic duties and engages fully in devotion to God through body, mind, and soul.

Because of these teachings, Arjun feels puzzled. He believes that karm sanyās (renunciation of actions) and karm yog (performing actions with devotion) appear to be opposite paths and wonders how both can be practiced together. Therefore, he asks Krishna to clarify which path is truly better.
commentary_summary: Arjun is confused because Krishna praised both renunciation of actions and performing actions with devotion. He asks Krishna to clearly explain which path is superior and more beneficial.
theme: Arjuna’s doubt about the superiority of renunciation versus selfless action

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: श्रीभगवानुवाच | संन्यास: कर्मयोगश्च नि:श्रेयसकरावुभौ | तयोस्तु कर्मसंन्यासात्कर्मयोगो विशिष्यते ||2||
transliteration: śhrī bhagavān uvācha | sannyāsaḥ karma-yogaśh cha niḥśhreyasa-karāvubhau | tayos tu karma-sannyāsāt karma-yogo viśhiṣhyate ||
translation: The Supreme Lord said: Both the path of karm sanyās (renunciation of actions) and karm yog (working with devotion) lead to the highest spiritual goal. However, karm yog is superior to karm sanyās.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna explains the relationship between karm sanyās (renunciation of actions) and karm yog (performing actions with devotion). Both paths ultimately lead to the supreme spiritual goal, which is union with God. However, Krishna clarifies that karm yog is generally the better path for most people.

A karm yogi performs both worldly and spiritual duties. The person continues performing social responsibilities while keeping the mind focused on God. Every action is performed with the awareness that it is being offered to God. This practice gradually purifies the mind and helps elevate the individual from bodily consciousness to spiritual consciousness.

Karm sanyās, on the other hand, is meant for highly advanced souls who have already transcended bodily identification. A karm sanyāsī renounces social duties completely because the mind is fully absorbed in devotion to God. Such individuals dedicate their entire time and energy to spiritual practice.

However, Krishna warns that karm sanyās carries a risk. If someone renounces worldly duties prematurely but cannot maintain constant absorption in God, they may fall into confusion and spiritual stagnation. Without worldly responsibilities and without genuine spiritual absorption, such individuals may drift away from discipline and purpose.

Karm yog, therefore, becomes the safer and more practical path for most people. Even if one's spiritual focus weakens temporarily, worldly duties still provide structure and purpose. By performing work selflessly and offering the results to God, the practitioner continues progressing spiritually while fulfilling responsibilities in the world.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that both renunciation and selfless action lead to spiritual liberation. However, performing one's duties with devotion (karm yog) is the safer and more practical path for most people.
theme: Krishna explains that selfless action with devotion is superior to mere renunciation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: ज्ञेय: स नित्यसंन्यासी यो न द्वेष्टि न काङ् क्षति | निर्द्वन्द्वो हि महाबाहो सुखं बन्धात्प्रमुच्यते ||3||
transliteration: jñeyaḥ sa nitya-sannyāsī yo na dveṣhṭi na kāṅkṣhati | nirdvandvo hi mahā-bāho sukhaṁ bandhāt pramuchyate ||
translation: The karm yogis, who neither hate nor desire anything, should be regarded as always renounced. Free from the dualities of life, O mighty-armed Arjun, they easily become liberated from the bondage of the material world.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that true renunciation does not necessarily mean abandoning actions. A person who performs duties without attachment, without hatred, and without selfish desires is already living in the spirit of renunciation.
