By understanding that all material objects are temporary manifestations of nature and ultimately belong to God, the yogi remains detached from worldly attractions. This spiritual vision allows the practitioner to remain constantly united with the Supreme and experience inner stability and peace.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that a true yogi, satisfied with spiritual knowledge and realization, remains steady and sees material objects like dirt, stone, and gold with equal detachment.
theme: True yogis remain steady and detached after attaining both knowledge and realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: सुहृन्मित्रार्युदासीनमध्यस्थद्वेष्यबन्धुषु | साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते ||9||
transliteration: suhṛin-mitrāryudāsīna-madhyastha-dveṣhya-bandhuṣhu | sādhuṣhvapi cha pāpeṣhu sama-buddhir viśhiṣhyate ||
translation: The yogi who maintains an equal attitude toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutrals, mediators, relatives, the righteous, and even sinners is considered superior.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna describes another quality of an advanced yogi—the ability to maintain equal vision toward all people. Ordinarily, the human mind reacts differently toward different individuals. We naturally feel affection for friends, hostility toward enemies, and indifference toward strangers. However, the enlightened yogi transcends these partial attitudes.

A realized yogi understands that all living beings are essentially souls, and each soul is a part of the Supreme. Because of this spiritual understanding, the yogi does not judge people based merely on their external behavior, social role, or relationship.

Krishna lists several categories of people to emphasize this point: well-wishers, friends, enemies, neutral persons, mediators, relatives, virtuous people, and even sinners. The yogi maintains balance and impartiality toward all of them.

This equality of vision arises from spiritual realization. When the yogi perceives that every being is connected to God, distinctions based on personal likes and dislikes gradually disappear. Instead of reacting emotionally, the yogi develops a calm, compassionate, and balanced attitude.

Spiritual texts describe different levels of this equal vision. At a basic level, one recognizes that all beings are souls and therefore equal in essence. At a deeper level, one understands that God resides within every being. At the highest level of realization, the yogi sees the entire universe as a manifestation of the divine.

Because of this elevated awareness, the yogi's mind remains steady and impartial. Such a person is considered highly distinguished among spiritual practitioners.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that an advanced yogi maintains equal vision toward all people—friends, enemies, the virtuous, and even sinners—because they see all beings as spiritual souls connected to God.
theme: The advanced yogi sees all beings with equal vision and impartial understanding

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थित: | एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रह: ||10||
transliteration: yogī yuñjīta satatam ātmānaṁ rahasi sthitaḥ | ekākī yata-chittātmā nirāśhīr aparigrahaḥ ||
translation: A yogi should constantly engage the mind in meditation, living in seclusion, alone, with a controlled mind and body, free from desires and possessions.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna begins explaining the practical discipline required to attain the state of Yog. After describing the qualities of an advanced yogi, he now outlines the method by which a seeker can train the mind through regular meditation.

Krishna emphasizes that spiritual mastery requires consistent practice. Just as excellence in any field demands continuous training, progress in meditation and spiritual realization also requires steady effort. Occasional practice is not sufficient; the yogi must regularly engage the mind in meditation.

One important condition for meditation is seclusion. Throughout daily life, the mind becomes absorbed in worldly activities, conversations, and sensory experiences. These influences constantly pull the mind toward material thoughts. Therefore, spending time in a quiet and secluded place helps withdraw the mind from external distractions and direct it toward spiritual awareness.

Krishna also recommends practicing meditation alone, with self-discipline. The practitioner should control the mind and senses so that attention remains focused on spiritual contemplation rather than wandering toward worldly desires.

Another important aspect is freedom from expectations and possessiveness. When the mind is filled with desires for material enjoyment or attachment to possessions, it becomes restless and distracted. By reducing these attachments, the mind becomes calm and better suited for meditation.

Through regular spiritual practice in a peaceful environment, the mind gradually becomes purified and steady. Over time, this discipline enables the practitioner to maintain spiritual awareness even while living and working in the world.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that seekers should practice meditation regularly in a quiet place with a controlled mind, free from worldly desires and attachments.
theme: Regular meditation in seclusion helps purify the mind and lead the seeker toward spiritual realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: शुचौ देशे प्रतिष्ठाप्य स्थिरमासनमात्मन: | नात्युच्छ्रितं नातिनीचं चैलाजिनकुशोत्तरम् ||11||
transliteration: śhuchau deśhe pratiṣhṭhāpya sthiram āsanam ātmanaḥ | nātyuchchhritaṁ nāti-nīchaṁ chailājina-kuśhottaram ||
translation: To practice Yog, one should establish a steady seat in a clean place, placing kuśha grass, deer skin, and a cloth one over another. The seat should be neither too high nor too low.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna describes the proper external arrangement for meditation practice. Before beginning the internal discipline of controlling the mind, the practitioner should prepare a suitable physical environment that supports concentration.

Krishna first emphasizes the importance of a clean and sanctified place. A pure environment helps create a calm mental atmosphere that is conducive to meditation. In the early stages of spiritual practice, the external surroundings strongly influence the mind. A peaceful and clean place reduces distractions and supports inward focus.

Next, Krishna explains how the meditation seat should be prepared. Traditionally, kuśha grass was placed on the ground to provide insulation from the earth and maintain bodily stability. On top of it, a deer skin was placed to protect the practitioner from insects and other disturbances while sitting in meditation for long periods. Finally, a cloth was placed above the deer skin to create a comfortable surface.

The height of the seat is also important. It should not be too high, which might make the practitioner unstable or cause discomfort, and it should not be too low, which may expose the person to disturbances from the ground.

Although these specific materials belonged to the cultural context of ancient India, the underlying principle remains relevant today. The essential idea is to create a stable, comfortable, and undisturbed place for meditation where the mind can easily turn inward toward spiritual contemplation.

Thus, by preparing a proper seat and environment, the practitioner lays the foundation for deeper meditation and steady spiritual practice.
commentary_summary: Krishna instructs that meditation should be practiced in a clean, peaceful place with a stable seat, creating an environment that supports concentration and spiritual practice.
theme: Proper preparation of the meditation environment supports steady spiritual practice

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: तत्रैकाग्रं मन: कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रिय: | उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये ||12||
transliteration: tatraikāgraṁ manaḥ kṛitvā yata-chittendriya-kriyaḥ | upaviśhyāsane yuñjyād yogam ātma-viśhuddhaye ||
translation: Seated on that seat, the yogi should concentrate the mind with one-pointed attention, controlling the mind and senses, and practice meditation for the purification of the self.
commentary_full:
After describing the proper meditation seat, Shree Krishna now explains the internal practice of meditation. The yogi should sit on the prepared seat and bring the mind to a state of one-pointed concentration. Instead of allowing the mind to wander toward worldly thoughts, the practitioner should direct it toward spiritual contemplation.

Controlling the mind and senses is essential in this process. The senses naturally pull the mind outward toward objects of enjoyment. Through discipline and practice, the yogi gradually withdraws attention from these distractions and focuses inward.

The purpose of meditation is purification of the mind. Over many lifetimes the mind accumulates impressions, attachments, and distractions. Meditation helps cleanse these impurities and makes the mind calm and steady. When the mind becomes purified, it becomes capable of perceiving higher spiritual truths.

Through consistent meditation, the practitioner develops concentration, inner clarity, and self-awareness. This practice gradually transforms the mind, allowing it to become focused on higher spiritual realities rather than temporary worldly attractions.
commentary_summary: Krishna instructs the yogi to sit in meditation with one-pointed concentration, controlling the mind and senses to purify the inner self.
theme: Meditation with one-pointed concentration purifies the mind and prepares it for spiritual realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिर: | सम्प्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ||13||
transliteration: samaṁ kāya-śhiro-grīvaṁ dhārayann achalaṁ sthiraḥ | samprekṣhya nāsikāgraṁ svaṁ diśhaśh chānavalokayan ||
translation: The yogi should hold the body, head, and neck straight and steady, gazing at the tip of the nose without letting the eyes wander in other directions.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna explains the proper posture that supports meditation. The body, neck, and head should be held straight in a stable position. This upright posture helps maintain alertness and prevents the practitioner from becoming lazy or falling asleep during meditation.

Meditation requires steadiness of both body and mind. If the body moves frequently or becomes relaxed in a careless manner, the mind also tends to lose focus. By sitting still and upright, the yogi creates the physical stability necessary for mental concentration.

Krishna also advises that the gaze should be directed toward the tip of the nose, without letting the eyes wander in different directions. This technique helps withdraw attention from external objects and reduces distractions from the surrounding environment.

Such discipline in posture and gaze supports deeper concentration. Over time, the body becomes steady and the mind becomes more focused, allowing the practitioner to enter deeper states of meditation.

Although the external posture is important, the true purpose of meditation is inner transformation. Through consistent practice, meditation helps organize the mind, strengthen determination, eliminate negative tendencies, and awaken deeper spiritual awareness.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that a steady upright posture and controlled gaze help maintain focus and support deep meditation.
theme: Proper posture and controlled attention support steady meditation and spiritual awareness

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थित: | मन: संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्पर: ||14||
transliteration: praśhāntātmā vigata-bhīr brahmachāri-vrate sthitaḥ | manaḥ sanyamya mach-chitto yukta āsīta mat-paraḥ ||
translation: With a peaceful mind, free from fear, firmly established in the vow of celibacy, and controlling the mind, the yogi should meditate upon Me, considering Me the supreme goal.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna continues explaining the inner discipline required for successful meditation. He emphasizes that the yogi must cultivate a calm and fearless state of mind. Fear and anxiety disturb concentration and prevent the mind from becoming steady. When the practitioner develops inner peace and trust in the divine, the mind becomes more stable for meditation.

Krishna also stresses the importance of brahmacharya, or the disciplined control of sensual energy. In traditional spiritual practice, brahmacharya refers to regulating and conserving one's physical and mental energies so they can be directed toward spiritual growth. When a person's energy is scattered through uncontrolled desires, the mind becomes restless and difficult to focus.

By practicing self-restraint, the practitioner preserves physical vitality, strengthens mental clarity, and develops greater determination. This disciplined lifestyle supports deeper meditation and spiritual awareness.

Another essential instruction given in this verse is that the mind should be fixed on God. Meditation in the yogic path is not merely an exercise in mental quietness; its true purpose is to focus consciousness on the Supreme. When the mind is directed toward God with devotion and dedication, meditation becomes a means of spiritual union.

Krishna therefore instructs the yogi to sit in meditation with a controlled mind, free from fear and distractions, firmly devoted to the divine as the highest goal of life. Such focused devotion gradually leads the practitioner toward deeper spiritual realization.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that meditation should be practiced with a calm, fearless mind, disciplined senses, and complete focus on God as the ultimate goal.
theme: A peaceful, disciplined mind focused on God enables deeper meditation and spiritual realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी नियतमानस: | शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति ||15||
transliteration: yuñjann evaṁ sadātmānaṁ yogī niyata-mānasaḥ | śhāntiṁ nirvāṇa-paramāṁ mat-sansthām adhigachchhati ||
translation: Thus, constantly keeping the mind absorbed in Me, the yogi with a disciplined mind attains supreme peace, liberation from material bondage, and abides in Me.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna explains the ultimate result of practicing meditation in the manner described earlier. When a yogi consistently disciplines the mind and focuses it upon God, the practitioner gradually attains a state of deep inner peace and spiritual realization.

Krishna emphasizes that the mind must remain constantly absorbed in the divine. Meditation is not merely an exercise for concentration or mental calmness; its true goal is to connect the individual consciousness with the Supreme. When the mind repeatedly turns toward God, it becomes purified and detached from worldly distractions.

Many meditation techniques exist across different traditions, focusing on breath, symbols, or abstract ideas. While such practices may help develop concentration, Krishna explains that true spiritual purification occurs when the mind is fixed upon God, who is completely pure and transcendental.

Devotional meditation may take different forms. A practitioner may meditate upon the divine names, forms, virtues, pastimes, or abodes of God. All these aspects are considered spiritually powerful and capable of elevating the consciousness toward the divine. Through such contemplation, the mind becomes deeply connected with God.

As the mind becomes steadily absorbed in divine remembrance, the practitioner experiences increasing inner peace and freedom from material attachments. This state leads to liberation from the cycle of worldly bondage and allows the yogi to abide in the divine presence.

Thus, Krishna teaches that the ultimate fruit of disciplined meditation is liberation and the attainment of supreme peace through union with God.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that by constantly focusing the mind on God through meditation, the yogi attains liberation and supreme inner peace.
theme: Constant meditation on God leads to liberation and supreme peace

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नत: | न चाति स्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन ||16||
transliteration: nātyaśhnatastu yogo ’sti na chaikāntam anaśhnataḥ | na chāti-svapna-śhīlasya jāgrato naiva chārjuna ||
translation: O Arjun, Yoga cannot be attained by one who eats too much or too little, nor by one who sleeps too much or sleeps too little.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna explains the importance of balance and moderation in spiritual practice. Success in meditation and Yoga does not come from extreme behavior, but from maintaining harmony in daily habits.

Krishna points out that both excess and deficiency can disturb spiritual progress. Eating too much makes the body heavy and dull, while eating too little weakens the body and reduces energy needed for meditation. Similarly, excessive sleep leads to laziness and dullness of mind, whereas insufficient sleep results in restlessness and lack of mental clarity.

Although the soul is distinct from the body, the body remains the instrument through which spiritual practice is performed. If the body becomes unhealthy or exhausted, it becomes difficult to focus the mind on higher spiritual goals. Therefore, maintaining proper care of the body is necessary for steady progress in Yog.

Ancient spiritual traditions recognized that both material knowledge and spiritual knowledge are important. Material knowledge helps maintain the body and physical well-being, while spiritual knowledge helps awaken the inner self. A balanced approach allows both to support each other.

Krishna therefore advises practitioners to avoid extremes and cultivate disciplined habits. Proper diet, adequate rest, and balanced activity help keep the body healthy and the mind stable, creating favorable conditions for meditation and spiritual growth.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that moderation in eating, sleeping, and daily habits is essential for success in meditation and Yoga.
theme: Spiritual progress requires moderation and balance in daily habits

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु | युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दु:खहा ||17||
transliteration: yuktāhāra-vihārasya yukta-cheṣhṭasya karmasu | yukta-svapnāvabodhasya yogo bhavati duḥkha-hā ||
translation: For those who are moderate in eating and recreation, balanced in work, and regulated in sleep and wakefulness, the practice of Yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna continues emphasizing the importance of moderation in daily life for successful spiritual practice. A balanced lifestyle helps create the physical and mental stability required for meditation and Yog.

Krishna explains that a person should maintain moderation in several aspects of life: eating, recreation, work, sleep, and wakefulness. When these activities are performed in proper measure, the body remains healthy and the mind remains calm and steady.

Excessive indulgence in sensory pleasures, known as bhog, disturbs the natural harmony of the body and mind. Such indulgence often leads to physical illness and mental agitation. When the body becomes unhealthy and the mind restless, it becomes difficult to focus on spiritual practice.

On the other hand, extreme austerity can also become harmful. Excessive fasting, overexertion, or sleep deprivation weakens the body and reduces the energy needed for meditation. Therefore, Krishna advises following a balanced path that avoids both extremes.

When a person maintains moderation in daily habits and practices Yog with discipline, the mind gradually becomes purified and stable. In such a condition, Yog helps remove the sorrows and disturbances of the mind and leads the practitioner toward inner peace and spiritual fulfillment.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that moderation in eating, work, recreation, sleep, and daily activities enables Yoga to remove suffering and bring inner peace.
theme: A balanced and disciplined lifestyle supports Yoga and helps remove suffering

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते | नि:स्पृह: सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा ||18||
transliteration: yadā viniyataṁ chittam ātmanyevāvatiṣhṭhate | niḥspṛihaḥ sarva-kāmebhyo yukta ityuchyate tadā ||
translation: When the disciplined mind becomes firmly fixed on the self and remains free from all desires for sense pleasures, then one is said to be established in Yoga.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna explains the state in which a practitioner can be considered firmly established in Yoga. This occurs when the mind, through consistent discipline and practice, becomes fully controlled and remains steadily focused on the higher self or the divine reality.

Ordinarily, the mind is constantly drawn toward sense objects and worldly desires. These cravings create restlessness and prevent the mind from attaining inner stability. Through meditation and self-discipline, however, the practitioner gradually learns to withdraw the mind from these distractions.

When the mind becomes detached from the constant pursuit of sensory pleasures and settles within the self, it experiences a deeper form of fulfillment. At this stage, worldly cravings naturally diminish because the mind begins to experience a higher spiritual satisfaction.

Krishna explains that this state marks the true establishment in Yoga. The mind is no longer scattered by desires but remains steadily anchored in spiritual awareness. Such a person becomes free from the restless yearning for external pleasures and attains inner steadiness.

Thus, the completion of Yoga practice is not merely physical discipline or meditation techniques, but the transformation of the mind into a state of inner stability where it naturally rests in the divine.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that when the disciplined mind withdraws from worldly desires and rests steadily in the self, the practitioner is truly established in Yoga.
theme: True Yoga is attained when the disciplined mind becomes free from desires and rests steadily in the self

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता | योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मन: ||19||
transliteration: yathā dīpo nivāta-stho neṅgate sopamā smṛitā | yogino yata-chittasya yuñjato yogam ātmanaḥ ||
translation: Just as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so the disciplined mind of a yogi remains steady while meditating on the Supreme.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna provides a vivid analogy to explain the state of a yogi’s mind during deep meditation. He compares it to the steady flame of a lamp placed in a windless location.

When a lamp is exposed to wind, its flame flickers constantly and cannot remain steady. Similarly, the human mind is naturally restless and easily disturbed by desires, distractions, and sensory impressions. These disturbances cause the mind to wander and prevent deep concentration.

However, when the mind is disciplined through spiritual practice and absorbed in meditation on the Supreme, it becomes stable and calm. Just as the absence of wind allows a lamp to burn steadily, freedom from desires and distractions allows the mind to remain steady in meditation.

The yogi achieves this steadiness by controlling the senses and focusing the mind on God. When devotion and concentration deepen, the restless movements of the mind gradually diminish. The mind then becomes firmly anchored in spiritual awareness.

Krishna uses this simple yet powerful image to illustrate the goal of meditation: a mind that is calm, unwavering, and completely absorbed in the divine.
commentary_summary: Krishna compares the steady mind of a meditating yogi to a lamp flame that does not flicker in a windless place.
theme: A disciplined mind becomes steady in meditation like a lamp flame protected from the wind

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया | यत्र चैवात्मनात्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति ||20||
transliteration: yatroparamate chittaṁ niruddhaṁ yoga-sevayā | yatra chaivātmanātmānaṁ paśhyann ātmani tuṣhyati ||
translation: When the mind, restrained through the practice of Yoga, becomes calm and free from material distractions, the yogi perceives the self through the purified mind and experiences inner joy.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna describes the inner experience that arises from deep meditation. When the practitioner steadily practices Yoga, the mind gradually becomes restrained from its constant engagement with material thoughts and sensory distractions.

Normally, the mind is restless and continuously occupied with worldly activities, desires, and worries. Such agitation prevents a person from perceiving deeper spiritual truths. Through disciplined meditation, however, the mind becomes calm and controlled.

When the mind reaches this state of stillness, the practitioner begins to perceive the true self. The soul is realized as distinct from the body, mind, and intellect. This realization does not come merely from intellectual understanding but from direct inner experience.

Krishna explains that when the mind becomes purified, it functions like clear water through which objects can be seen clearly. If water is muddy, one cannot see through it; but when the impurities settle, the water becomes transparent. Similarly, when the impurities of the mind—such as desires, attachments, and distractions—are removed through meditation, the soul becomes clearly perceived.

This realization brings a deep sense of inner joy and satisfaction. The happiness experienced at this stage is not dependent on external circumstances but arises from the awareness of one's true spiritual nature.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that when the mind becomes calm and purified through Yoga, the yogi realizes the soul and experiences deep inner joy.
theme: Through meditation and mind purification, the yogi realizes the self and experiences inner spiritual joy

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद्बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम् | वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वत: ||21||
transliteration: sukham ātyantikaṁ yat tad buddhi-grāhyam atīndriyam | vetti yatra na chaivāyaṁ sthitaśh chalati tattvataḥ ||
translation: In that state of Yoga, one experiences supreme and boundless happiness, which is grasped by the intellect and is beyond the senses. Established in this state, one never departs from the Eternal Truth.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna describes the profound spiritual experience attained through deep meditation. When the yogi becomes fully absorbed in meditation and the mind is united with the Supreme, the practitioner experiences a form of happiness that is beyond ordinary sensory pleasure.

This bliss is described as 'atyantika sukham', meaning limitless and supreme happiness. Unlike worldly pleasures that depend on the senses and external objects, this happiness is experienced internally through the purified intellect. It transcends sensory perception and arises from direct contact with spiritual reality.

Human beings constantly seek happiness through various material experiences, believing that fulfillment lies in external objects. However, such pleasures are temporary and cannot fully satisfy the deeper longing of the soul. The soul naturally seeks the infinite bliss that originates from God.

When the mind becomes absorbed in divine consciousness through meditation, the yogi experiences this higher bliss directly. This state is often described as samadhi, where the mind becomes completely unified with spiritual awareness.

In this condition, the practitioner experiences complete satisfaction and inner fulfillment. Since this bliss surpasses all worldly pleasures, the yogi no longer feels attracted toward temporary sensory enjoyments. Thus, the person remains firmly established in spiritual truth and does not deviate from it.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that deep meditation leads to a transcendental bliss beyond the senses, and one who experiences it remains firmly established in spiritual truth.
theme: Union with the divine through meditation leads to supreme bliss beyond sensory experience

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं तत: | यस्मिन्स्थितो न दु:खेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते ||22||
transliteration: yaṁ labdhvā chāparaṁ lābhaṁ manyate nādhikaṁ tataḥ | yasmin sthito na duḥkhena guruṇāpi vichālyate ||
translation: Having attained this state, one does not consider any other gain to be greater. Being established in it, one is not shaken even by the greatest sorrow.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna further explains the nature of the spiritual bliss experienced through Yoga. When a yogi attains union with the divine and experiences the supreme inner happiness, that realization becomes the highest possible achievement.

In ordinary life, people constantly seek greater gains and pleasures. Even after achieving wealth, status, or success, the mind continues to search for something greater. Material achievements never completely satisfy the soul because they are limited and temporary.

However, the bliss experienced through spiritual realization is infinite and complete. Once a person experiences this divine happiness, nothing else appears more valuable. The soul recognizes that it has attained the highest fulfillment.

Krishna also explains that this realization gives extraordinary inner stability. Even in the face of severe difficulties, suffering, or external misfortune, the person remains inwardly steady. The mind no longer becomes disturbed by the fluctuations of worldly circumstances.

This is because the yogi’s happiness is no longer dependent on external conditions but arises from the connection with the divine. Therefore, even great sorrow cannot shake the inner peace of one who is firmly established in this spiritual state.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that the bliss of union with God is the highest attainment, and one who realizes it remains unshaken even by great suffering.
theme: The bliss of spiritual realization is the highest gain and gives unshakable inner stability

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: तं विद्याद् दु:खसंयोगवियोगं योगसञ्ज्ञितम् | स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा ||23||
transliteration: taṁ vidyād duḥkha-sanyoga-viyogaṁ yogasaṅjñitam | sa niśhchayena yoktavyo yogo ’nirviṇṇa-chetasā ||
translation: One should understand that Yoga is the state of separation from union with sorrow. This Yoga must be practiced with firm determination and a steady, undiscouraged mind.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna defines Yoga in a practical and philosophical way. He explains that Yoga is the state in which a person becomes free from the connection with suffering. Since the material world naturally contains pain, uncertainty, and impermanence, true Yoga lifts the individual consciousness beyond these limitations.

Krishna describes the material world as a place where misery arises from attachment, ignorance, and identification with temporary things. When the mind remains absorbed in worldly desires, it becomes vulnerable to sorrow and dissatisfaction.

Through the practice of Yoga—especially meditation and devotion—the mind gradually turns toward the divine. As the consciousness becomes connected with God, the influence of material suffering diminishes. The bliss of spiritual realization naturally dispels the darkness of ignorance, just as light removes darkness.

Krishna therefore explains that Yoga brings two results simultaneously: the attainment of divine happiness and the freedom from the misery of worldly existence.

However, reaching this state requires determined practice. The seeker must approach spiritual discipline with perseverance and confidence. Doubt, discouragement, or impatience can weaken the effort. Instead, Yoga should be practiced steadily with faith, determination, and a positive mindset.

With such resolute practice, the practitioner gradually advances toward spiritual freedom and lasting inner peace.
commentary_summary: Krishna defines Yoga as the state of freedom from suffering and teaches that it must be practiced with determination and an undiscouraged mind.
theme: Yoga is the path that frees the soul from suffering and must be practiced with determination

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: सङ्कल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषत: | मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्तत: ||24||
transliteration: saṅkalpa-prabhavān kāmāns tyaktvā sarvān aśheṣhataḥ | manasaivendriya-grāmaṁ viniyamya samantataḥ ||
translation: Completely renouncing all desires arising from worldly thoughts, one should control the senses from all directions with the mind.
commentary_full:
In this verse, Shree Krishna begins explaining the practical method of meditation. The first step in meditation is withdrawing the mind from worldly attachments. Desires arise from thoughts about objects, people, and experiences of the world. These thoughts gradually develop into intentions and cravings, which disturb the mind and prevent concentration.

Krishna explains that such desires originate from mental resolutions or repeated thoughts about sensory pleasures. Therefore, the practitioner must consciously abandon these desires and prevent them from dominating the mind.

The senses naturally move outward toward objects of enjoyment, constantly stimulating the mind. Through discipline and awareness, the practitioner must restrain the senses using the power of the mind. This process gradually weakens the influence of worldly attachments and prepares the mind for meditation.

By withdrawing the senses and reducing material desires, the mind becomes calmer and more receptive to spiritual focus. This is the first essential stage in developing deep meditation.
commentary_summary: Krishna instructs the seeker to renounce desires arising from worldly thoughts and restrain the senses through disciplined control of the mind.
theme: Renouncing worldly desires and controlling the senses prepares the mind for meditation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: शनै: शनैरुपरमेद्बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया | आत्मसंस्थं मन: कृत्वा न किञ्चिदपि चिन्तयेत् ||25||
transliteration: śhanaiḥ śhanair uparamed buddhyā dhṛiti-gṛihītayā | ātma-sansthaṁ manaḥ kṛitvā na kiñchid api chintayet ||
translation: Gradually, step by step, with firm determination guided by the intellect, one should bring the mind to rest in God and think of nothing else.
commentary_full:
After explaining the need to withdraw the mind from worldly desires, Shree Krishna now describes the second part of meditation: fixing the mind on God. This process does not happen instantly but requires gradual and persistent effort.

Krishna emphasizes that the practitioner should proceed slowly and steadily. The restless mind cannot be controlled all at once; it must be trained step by step through continuous practice and determination.

The intellect plays an important role in this discipline. When guided by wisdom and conviction, the intellect helps the practitioner recognize the temporary nature of worldly pleasures and the higher value of spiritual realization. This understanding strengthens determination and supports the effort to control the mind.

Through repeated practice, the mind gradually becomes accustomed to turning inward and focusing on the divine. Eventually, it becomes steady and remains absorbed in spiritual awareness rather than wandering toward worldly distractions.

Thus, meditation is a gradual journey of training the mind—removing it from worldly attachments and steadily fixing it on the divine reality.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that through gradual effort and determined intellect, the mind should be steadily trained to rest in God alone.
theme: Meditation requires gradual discipline and steady effort to fix the mind on the divine

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी विगतकल्मष: | सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते || 28||
transliteration: yuñjann evaṁ sadātmānaṁ yogī vigata-kalmaṣhaḥ sukhena brahma-sansparśham atyantaṁ sukham aśhnute
translation: The self-controlled yogi, thus uniting the self with God, becomes free from material contamination, and being in constant touch with the Supreme, achieves the highest state of perfect happiness.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna describes the result of continuous spiritual practice and meditation. When a yogi repeatedly disciplines the mind and unites the self with God, the impurities and sinful tendencies that cloud the consciousness gradually disappear. As these impurities fade, the mind becomes pure and capable of experiencing deeper spiritual awareness.

The yogi then experiences brahma-sansparsha, which means direct contact or communion with the Supreme. This connection with God brings an extraordinary kind of happiness that is beyond worldly pleasures. Unlike material happiness, which is temporary and dependent on external objects, this bliss arises from the soul’s direct connection with the divine.

The scriptures describe four types of happiness experienced by living beings. Tamasic happiness comes from ignorance and harmful indulgences such as intoxication, violence, and excessive sleep. Rajasic happiness arises from sensory enjoyment and worldly achievements. Sattvic happiness is experienced through knowledge, virtue, and self-realization. However, beyond all these is nirguna happiness—the divine bliss experienced when the soul becomes united with God.

Krishna explains that the yogi who purifies the mind and establishes a steady connection with God experiences this highest and infinite bliss. This happiness is permanent, pure, and incomparable to any worldly pleasure.
commentary_summary: A yogi who purifies the mind and remains united with God experiences the highest divine bliss beyond all material happiness.
theme: Union with God brings the highest and eternal spiritual happiness

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: प्राप्य पुण्यकृतां लोकानुषित्वा शाश्वती: समा: | शुचीनां श्रीमतां गेहे योगभ्रष्टोऽभिजायते || 41||
transliteration: prāpya puṇya-kṛitāṁ lokān uṣhitvā śhāśhvatīḥ samāḥ śhuchīnāṁ śhrīmatāṁ gehe yoga-bhraṣhṭo ’bhijāyate
translation: The unsuccessful yogis, after attaining the abodes of the virtuous and dwelling there for many years, are reborn on earth in a family of pious and prosperous people.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that no sincere spiritual effort is ever wasted. When a seeker practices Yog but fails to attain complete perfection in one lifetime, their spiritual progress is preserved. Such a person, known as a yoga-bhrashta (one who has fallen from Yog), does not meet destruction or loss.

After death, these individuals first attain the celestial realms reserved for those who have performed virtuous deeds. They dwell there for a long period and enjoy the results of their past spiritual and moral actions. Eventually, they are reborn on earth in favorable circumstances that support further spiritual progress.

Krishna states that such souls are often born in families that are both virtuous and prosperous. A pious family provides an environment of moral discipline, spiritual values, and good character. A prosperous family frees the individual from excessive struggle for survival, allowing more time and opportunity for spiritual practice.

Thus, the spiritual impressions gathered in previous lives influence the conditions of future birth. The favorable environment helps the seeker resume the spiritual journey from where it was previously left off.
commentary_summary: A yogi who fails to attain perfection is first rewarded in higher realms and later reborn in a pious and prosperous family to continue the spiritual journey.
theme: Incomplete spiritual efforts are preserved and lead to favorable rebirth for continued progress

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit: अथवा योगिनामेव कुले भवति धीमताम् | एतद्धि दुर्लभतरं लोके जन्म यदीदृशम् || 42||
transliteration: atha vā yoginām eva kule bhavati dhīmatām etad dhi durlabhataraṁ loke janma yad īdṛiśham
translation: Or such a seeker may be born into a family of wise yogis. Such a birth is very rare and difficult to obtain in this world.
commentary_full:
Krishna describes an even more fortunate rebirth for advanced spiritual seekers. If a yogi had progressed significantly in spiritual practice and developed strong detachment from worldly pleasures, they may not need to pass through celestial realms. Instead, they are directly born into a family of spiritually enlightened yogis.

Such a birth is considered extremely rare and valuable. In these families, spiritual knowledge and practices are naturally part of daily life. From childhood, the individual receives guidance in meditation, devotion, and self-discipline. This environment allows them to quickly reconnect with the spiritual path and continue their progress toward God-realization.

The verse also highlights the broader principle of karma and continuity of spiritual effort. The circumstances of birth are not random but are shaped by past actions and spiritual development. The accumulated impressions from previous lives guide the soul toward environments that support further growth.

Therefore, Krishna reassures that sincere spiritual practice never goes to waste. Every effort contributes to future advancement, ultimately leading the soul closer to liberation and union with God.
commentary_summary: Advanced yogis may be reborn into spiritually wise families, providing an ideal environment to continue their journey toward God-realization.
theme: Highly advanced seekers are reborn in spiritually elevated families to continue their path to realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
इदं तु ते गुह्यतमं प्रवक्ष्याम्यनसूयवे |
ज्ञानं विज्ञानसहितं यज्ज्ञात्वा मोक्ष्यसेऽशुभात् || 1||
transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha |
idaṁ tu te guhyatamaṁ pravakṣhyāmyanasūyave |
jñānaṁ vijñāna-sahitaṁ yaj jñātvā mokṣhyase ’śhubhāt ||
translation: The Supreme Lord said: O Arjun, because you are not envious of Me, I shall impart to you this most confidential knowledge and wisdom, knowing which you shall be freed from the miseries of material existence.
commentary_full: Krishna begins by stating the qualification required to receive this supreme knowledge: freedom from envy. Divine knowledge cannot enter a heart clouded by pride or hostility toward God. The Lord is about to glorify Himself extensively, and only a receptive, humble, and non-envious listener can benefit from it. This chapter reveals the most confidential truth — pure devotion to God — which surpasses mere intellectual understanding and leads to liberation from material suffering.
commentary_summary: Divine knowledge is revealed only to the non-envious and leads to liberation.
theme: Qualification for receiving supreme knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
राजविद्या राजगुह्यं पवित्रमिदमुत्तमम् |
प्रत्यक्षावगमं धर्म्यं सुसुखं कर्तुमव्ययम् || 2||
transliteration:
rāja-vidyā rāja-guhyaṁ pavitram idam uttamam |
pratyakṣhāvagamaṁ dharmyaṁ su-sukhaṁ kartum avyayam ||
translation: This knowledge is the king of sciences and the most profound secret. It is pure, directly realizable, righteous, easy to practice, and everlasting in effect.
commentary_full: Krishna calls this wisdom the king of knowledge because it reigns supreme over all sciences. It is the greatest secret because divine love requires free will; God does not force revelation upon anyone. This knowledge purifies the heart by destroying sin, its seeds, and ignorance itself. Though it begins with faith, it culminates in direct realization of God. Unlike ritualistic practices for material gain, devotion is simple, natural, and eternal in its results.
commentary_summary: Bhakti is the supreme, pure, directly realizable, and eternal science.
theme: Supremacy of devotional knowledge

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अश्रद्दधाना: पुरुषा धर्मस्यास्य परन्तप |
अप्राप्य मां निवर्तन्ते मृत्युसंसारवर्त्मनि || 3||
transliteration:
aśhraddadhānāḥ puruṣhā dharmasyāsya parantapa |
aprāpya māṁ nivartante mṛityu-samsāra-vartmani ||
translation: Those who lack faith in this path of devotion cannot attain Me, O Arjun. They return to the cycle of birth and death.
commentary_full: Faith is the starting point of spiritual progress. Just as material endeavors require trust in unseen processes, devotion requires initial faith before direct realization occurs. Without faith, one never begins the journey and thus remains bound in samsara. Krishna emphasizes that disbelief is not neutral — it results in continued bondage within material existence.
commentary_summary: Without faith, the soul remains trapped in birth and death.
theme: Necessity of faith in spiritual life

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मया ततमिदं सर्वं जगदव्यक्तमूर्तिना |
मत्स्थानि सर्वभूतानि न चाहं तेष्ववस्थित: || 4||
transliteration:
mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagad avyakta-mūrtinā |
mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni na chāhaṁ teṣhvavasthitaḥ ||
translation: This entire universe is pervaded by Me in My unmanifest form. All beings dwell in Me, yet I do not dwell in them.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals His all-pervading nature. The universe exists within Him because it is sustained by His energies. However, He remains independent and unaffected by the limitations of creation. Just as waves exist in the ocean but do not contain the entirety of the ocean, all beings exist within God, yet God transcends them.
commentary_summary: God pervades all creation yet remains transcendent.
theme: Immanence and transcendence of God

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
न च मत्स्थानि भूतानि पश्य मे योगमैश्वरम् |
भूतभृन्न च भूतस्थो ममात्मा भूतभावन: || 5||
transliteration:
na cha mat-sthāni bhūtāni paśhya me yogam aiśhwaram |
bhūta-bhṛin na cha bhūta-stho mamātmā bhūta-bhāvanaḥ ||
translation: And yet, beings do not dwell in Me. Behold My divine mystery! Though I sustain all beings and am their source, I remain unaffected by them.
commentary_full: Krishna deepens the paradox: although all beings exist in Him, He remains completely independent and untouched. This is the power of His divine Yogmaya. He sustains creation yet is never conditioned by it. The infinite cannot be confined within the finite. His transcendence remains intact despite His immanence.
commentary_summary: God sustains all yet remains untouched by creation.
theme: Divine paradox of sustenance and detachment

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यथाकाशस्थितो नित्यं वायु: सर्वत्रगो महान् |
तथा सर्वाणि भूतानि मत्स्थानीत्युपधारय || 6||
transliteration:
yathākāśha-sthito nityaṁ vāyuḥ sarvatra-go mahān |
tathā sarvāṇi bhūtāni mat-sthānītyupadhāraya ||
translation: Just as the mighty wind, blowing everywhere, always rests in the sky, likewise know that all living beings rest in Me.
commentary_full: Krishna clarifies how all beings exist in Him by offering a tangible analogy. The wind moves powerfully and independently, yet it cannot exist separate from the sky. Similarly, souls wander through time and various bodies, yet they never exist outside God. He is not physically holding the universe like a pillar; rather, everything exists within His sustaining energy and will.
commentary_summary: All beings exist within God just as wind exists within the sky.
theme: Dependence of creation on the Divine

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सर्वभूतानि कौन्तेय प्रकृतिं यान्ति मामिकाम् |
कल्पक्षये पुनस्तानि कल्पादौ विसृजाम्यहम् || 7||
प्रकृतिं स्वामवष्टभ्य विसृजामि पुन: पुन: |
भूतग्राममिमं कृत्स्नमवशं प्रकृतेर्वशात् || 8||
transliteration:
sarva-bhūtāni kaunteya prakṛitiṁ yānti māmikām |
kalpa-kṣhaye punas tāni kalpādau visṛijāmyaham ||
prakṛitiṁ svām avaṣhṭabhya visṛijāmi punaḥ punaḥ |
bhūta-grāmam imaṁ kṛitsnam avaśhaṁ prakṛiter vaśhāt ||
translation: At the end of a kalpa, all living beings merge into My primordial material energy. At the beginning of the next creation, I manifest them again, repeatedly bringing forth these forms according to their natures.
commentary_full: Creation operates in vast cosmic cycles. At dissolution, all beings withdraw into God’s material energy, retaining only their causal impressions. When creation begins again, they re-emerge according to their karmic tendencies. Krishna presides over this cyclical manifestation without being altered by it. The variety of life forms arises from the interplay of prakriti and the stored tendencies of souls.
commentary_summary: Creation and dissolution occur cyclically under God’s supervision.
theme: Cyclical creation under divine oversight

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
न च मां तानि कर्माणि निबध्नन्ति धनञ्जय |
उदासीनवदासीनमसक्तं तेषु कर्मसु || 9||
transliteration:
na cha māṁ tāni karmāṇi nibadhnanti dhanañjaya |
udāsīna-vad āsīnam asaktaṁ teṣhu karmasu ||
translation: O Arjun, these actions do not bind Me. I remain like a neutral observer, detached from these activities.
commentary_full: Although creation unfolds by His will, Krishna remains unaffected and detached. Material energy is inert and acts only under divine sanction. Just as a tool functions in the hands of a craftsman without affecting him, creation operates under God’s glance without binding Him. His transcendental blissful nature remains untouched by worldly transformations.
commentary_summary: God remains detached and unbound by creation.
theme: Divine detachment from material action

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मयाध्यक्षेण प्रकृति: सूयते सचराचरम् |
हेतुनानेन कौन्तेय जगद्विपरिवर्तते || 10||
transliteration:
mayādhyakṣheṇa prakṛitiḥ sūyate sa-charācharam |
hetunānena kaunteya jagad viparivartate ||
translation: Under My supervision, material nature brings forth all moving and non-moving beings. Thus the world undergoes its cycles of change.
commentary_full: Krishna clarifies that material nature acts under His direction. Just as a government functions through appointed officials while the authority rests with the head of state, creation unfolds through prakriti and cosmic administrators under divine sanction. God is therefore the ultimate cause, though not directly entangled in the mechanics of manifestation.
commentary_summary: Material nature works under God’s supervision.
theme: God as the supreme overseer

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अवजानन्ति मां मूढा मानुषीं तनुमाश्रितम् |
परं भावमजानन्तो मम भूतमहेश्वरम् || 11||
transliteration:
avajānanti māṁ mūḍhā mānuṣhīṁ tanum āśhritam |
paraṁ bhāvam ajānanto mama bhūta-maheśhvaram ||
translation: When I descend in My personal form, the deluded disregard Me. They do not understand My supreme divine nature as the Lord of all beings.
commentary_full: Krishna addresses the inability of materially conditioned souls to recognize divinity when it appears in human form. Considering God incapable of assuming form contradicts His omnipotence. The Lord’s form is not material but sat-chit-ānanda—eternal, full of knowledge, and bliss. However, perception of His divinity depends on the purity of one’s consciousness. Those influenced by the modes of nature interpret Him according to their conditioning, while only spiritually awakened souls recognize His true nature.
commentary_summary: Deluded minds fail to recognize the divine nature of God’s personal form.
theme: Failure to recognize divine incarnation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मोघाशा मोघकर्माणो मोघज्ञाना विचेतस: |
राक्षसीमासुरीं चैव प्रकृतिं मोहिनीं श्रिता: || 12||
transliteration:
moghāśhā mogha-karmāṇo mogha-jñānā vichetasaḥ |
rākṣhasīm āsurīṁ chaiva prakṛitiṁ mohinīṁ śhritāḥ ||
translation: Deluded by material nature, such persons adopt demoniac views. Their hopes are vain, their actions fruitless, and their knowledge bewildered.
commentary_full: Those who deny or distort the divinity of the Supreme become absorbed in atheistic and materialistic ideologies. Their intellectual pursuits and actions lack ultimate value because they are disconnected from the eternal truth. Since devotion to the personal God is rejected and realization of the formless Absolute remains difficult, they remain deprived of spiritual welfare and continue in illusion.
commentary_summary: Atheistic views lead to wasted effort and spiritual confusion.
theme: Consequences of denying divine reality

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
महात्मानस्तु मां पार्थ दैवीं प्रकृतिमाश्रिता: |
भजन्त्यनन्यमनसो ज्ञात्वा भूतादिमव्ययम् || 13||
transliteration:
mahātmānas tu māṁ pārtha daivīṁ prakṛitim āśhritāḥ |
bhajantyananya-manaso jñātvā bhūtādim avyayam ||
translation: But the great souls, taking shelter of My divine energy, worship Me with undivided minds, knowing Me as the eternal origin of all creation.
commentary_full: In contrast to the deluded, the mahātmas awaken from material ignorance and take refuge in divine energy. Recognizing Krishna as the imperishable source of all existence, they engage in exclusive devotion. Freed from worldly illusion, they align their consciousness entirely toward Him, sustained by divine grace and Yogmaya.
commentary_summary: Great souls, sheltered by divine energy, engage in exclusive devotion.
theme: Characteristics of enlightened devotees

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सततं कीर्तयन्तो मां यतन्तश्च दृढव्रता: |
नमस्यन्तश्च मां भक्त्या नित्ययुक्ता उपासते || 14||
transliteration:
satataṁ kīrtayanto māṁ yatantaśh cha dṛiḍha-vratāḥ |
namasyantaśh cha māṁ bhaktyā nitya-yuktā upāsate ||
translation: Always chanting My glories, striving with firm resolve, bowing down before Me in devotion, they worship Me constantly.
commentary_full: Krishna describes the dynamic life of devotion. Devotees constantly engage in kirtan—hearing, chanting, and remembering His names and glories. Through determined practice and humility, they remain internally united with Him. Kirtan purifies the mind, anchors attention, and transforms consciousness, making devotion both practical and powerful.
commentary_summary: Devotees remain constantly engaged in devoted remembrance and praise.
theme: Practice of constant devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ज्ञानयज्ञेन चाप्यन्ये यजन्तो मामुपासते |
एकत्वेन पृथक्त्वेन बहुधा विश्वतोमुखम् || 15||
transliteration:
jñāna-yajñena chāpyanye yajanto mām upāsate |
ekatvena pṛithaktvena bahudhā viśhvato-mukham ||
translation: Others worship Me through the sacrifice of knowledge. Some perceive Me as the undifferentiated Absolute, others as distinct from themselves, and still others worship Me in My universal cosmic form.
commentary_full: Spiritual aspirants approach the Divine through varied philosophical paths. Jñāna yogis contemplate identity with the formless Absolute, others relate to God as distinct from themselves, and some worship the cosmic manifestation as divine. Though these paths differ in understanding and completeness, they ultimately direct their reverence toward the same Supreme Reality.
commentary_summary: Different spiritual paths approach the same Supreme through varied conceptions.
theme: Multiple approaches to the Divine

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अहं क्रतुरहं यज्ञ: स्वधाहमहमौषधम् |
मन्त्रोऽहमहमेवाज्यमहमग्निरहं हुतम् || 16||
पिताहमस्य जगतो माता धाता पितामह: |
वेद्यं पवित्रमोङ्कार ऋक्साम यजुरेव च || 17||
transliteration:
ahaṁ kratur ahaṁ yajñaḥ svadhāham aham auṣhadham |
mantro ’ham aham evājyam aham agnir ahaṁ hutam ||
pitāham asya jagato mātā dhātā pitāmahaḥ |
vedyaṁ pavitram oṁkāra ṛik sāma yajur eva cha ||
translation: I am the Vedic ritual, the sacrifice, and the offering to the ancestors. I am the medicinal herb, the sacred mantra, the clarified butter, the fire, and the act of offering. I am the Father, Mother, Sustainer, and Grandsire of the universe. I am the purifier, the sacred syllable Om, and the Ṛig, Sāma, and Yajur Vedas.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals the all-encompassing nature of His existence. Every sacred ritual, every element of sacrifice, and even the knowledge contained in the Vedas are manifestations of His divine energy. As Father and Mother, He is both the source and the womb of creation. As Sustainer, He nourishes all existence. By declaring Himself the Vedas and Om, He establishes that sacred knowledge itself is an expression of His being. Nothing in the realm of worship exists independently of Him.
commentary_summary: All rituals, knowledge, and relationships originate from and rest in God.
theme: God as the essence of all sacred acts and relationships

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
गतिर्भर्ता प्रभु: साक्षी निवास: शरणं सुहृत् |
प्रभव: प्रलय: स्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् || 18||
transliteration:
gatir bhartā prabhuḥ sākṣhī nivāsaḥ śharaṇaṁ suhṛit |
prabhavaḥ pralayaḥ sthānaṁ nidhānaṁ bījam avyayam ||
translation: I am the Supreme Goal, the Sustainer, the Master, the Witness, the Abode, the Shelter, and the Friend. I am the Origin, Dissolution, Foundation, Repository, and the Eternal Seed.
commentary_full: Krishna shifts attention from worldly attachments to the eternal relationship between the soul and God. All temporary relationships dissolve with time, but the Lord accompanies the soul through every birth as witness and well-wisher. He is both the origin and the ultimate destination. Just as waves arise from and return to the ocean, souls emerge from and return to Him. True fulfillment arises when the soul redirects its attachment from transient relations to the eternal Divine.
commentary_summary: God alone is the soul’s eternal refuge and relationship.
theme: God as the eternal relative and ultimate refuge

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
तपाम्यहमहं वर्षं निगृह्णम्युत्सृजामि च |
अमृतं चैव मृत्युश्च सदसच्चाहमर्जुन || 19||
transliteration:
tapāmyaham ahaṁ varṣhaṁ nigṛihṇāmyutsṛijāmi cha |
amṛitaṁ chaiva mṛityuśh cha sad asach chāham arjuna ||
translation: I give heat as the sun and send forth or withhold rain. I am immortality and death. I am both spirit and matter, O Arjun.
commentary_full: Krishna emphasizes His immanence in natural forces and existential realities. The cycles of nature—heat, rain, life, and death—operate under His sovereignty. Spirit and matter are not independent principles; both exist within His being. Thus, every aspect of existence, whether perceived as positive or negative, eternal or temporary, rests in the Supreme. Worship, therefore, involves recognizing His presence in all phenomena.
commentary_summary: All forces of nature and existence operate under the Divine.
theme: God as the force behind all natural and existential realities

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
त्रैविद्या मां सोमपा: पूतपापा
यज्ञैरिष्ट्वा स्वर्गतिं प्रार्थयन्ते |
ते पुण्यमासाद्य सुरेन्द्रलोक
मश्नन्ति दिव्यान्दिवि देवभोगान् || 20||
transliteration:
trai-vidyā māṁ soma-pāḥ pūta-pāpā |
yajñair iṣhṭvā svar-gatiṁ prārthayante |
te puṇyam āsādya surendra-lokam |
aśhnanti divyān divi deva-bhogān ||
translation: Those versed in the Vedas, purified by sacrifices and drinking the Soma, seek heaven. By their merits, they reach the celestial realm of Indra and enjoy divine pleasures.
commentary_full: Krishna now distinguishes ritualistic worship from pure devotion. Followers of karm-kāṇḍa perform sacrifices for celestial rewards. Though their actions are pious and elevate them to heavenly realms, these pleasures remain temporary and within the material cycle. Such worship acknowledges divine authority but seeks material gain rather than eternal union. Therefore, it does not grant liberation from birth and death.
commentary_summary: Ritualistic worship leads to temporary heavenly enjoyment, not liberation.
theme: Limitations of ritualistic, reward-seeking worship

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ते तं भुक्त्वा स्वर्गलोकं विशालं
क्षीणे पुण्ये मर्त्यलोकं विशन्ति |
एवं त्रयीधर्ममनुप्रपन्ना
गतागतं कामकामा लभन्ते || 21||
transliteration:
te taṁ bhuktvā swarga-lokaṁ viśhālaṁ
kṣhīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśhanti |
evaṁ trayī-dharmam anuprapannā
gatāgataṁ kāma-kāmā labhante ||
translation: After enjoying the vast pleasures of heaven, when their merits are exhausted, they return to the mortal world. Thus, those who follow Vedic rituals seeking enjoyment repeatedly come and go.
commentary_full: Krishna highlights the temporary nature of heavenly pleasures. Even celestial enjoyment is finite because it depends on accumulated merit. Once exhausted, the soul returns to earthly existence. The cycle of ascent and descent continues for those driven by desire. Only human birth provides the unique opportunity for God-realization, which transcends this oscillation between higher and lower realms.
commentary_summary: Heavenly pleasures are temporary and do not free the soul from rebirth.
theme: Limitations of celestial enjoyment

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अनन्याश्चिन्तयन्तो मां ये जना: पर्युपासते |
तेषां नित्याभियुक्तानां योगक्षेमं वहाम्यहम् || 22||
transliteration:
ananyāśh chintayanto māṁ ye janāḥ paryupāsate |
teṣhāṁ nityābhiyuktānāṁ yoga-kṣhemaṁ vahāmyaham ||
translation: Those who think of Me alone and worship Me with exclusive devotion—I carry what they lack and preserve what they have.
commentary_full: Krishna gives a profound assurance to exclusive devotees. Yoga refers to providing what is lacking; kṣhema refers to preserving what is already attained. When surrender is complete, God personally assumes responsibility for the devotee’s spiritual welfare. Partial surrender yields partial grace, but full reliance invites full divine protection and support.
commentary_summary: God personally protects and sustains those exclusively devoted to Him.
theme: Divine protection of surrendered souls

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
येऽप्यन्यदेवता भक्ता यजन्ते श्रद्धयान्विता: |
तेऽपि मामेव कौन्तेय यजन्त्यविधिपूर्वकम् || 23||
transliteration:
ye ’pyanya-devatā-bhaktā yajante śhraddhayānvitāḥ |
te ’pi mām eva kaunteya yajantyavidhi-pūrvakam ||
translation: Even those who faithfully worship other deities actually worship Me, O Arjun, though in an improper manner.
commentary_full: All powers possessed by celestial beings originate from the Supreme. Thus, worship directed toward them ultimately reaches Him. However, such worship remains indirect and incomplete because it seeks limited material benefits rather than eternal realization. Just as watering leaves instead of the root fails to nourish a tree properly, indirect worship does not grant ultimate liberation.
commentary_summary: Worship of other deities reaches God indirectly but lacks completeness.
theme: Indirect worship versus direct devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अहं हि सर्वयज्ञानां भोक्ता च प्रभुरेव च |
न तु मामभिजानन्ति तत्त्वेनातश्च्यवन्ति ते || 24||
transliteration:
ahaṁ hi sarva-yajñānāṁ bhoktā cha prabhureva cha |
na tu mām abhijānanti tattvenātaśh chyavanti te ||
translation: I alone am the enjoyer and Lord of all sacrifices. But those who do not recognize My true nature fall back into rebirth.
commentary_full: Krishna clarifies that He is the ultimate recipient and sovereign of all sacrificial acts. Celestial beings may administer blessings, but the Supreme alone is the source and final enjoyer. Failure to recognize His supremacy limits spiritual progress, causing souls to remain within samsara. Direct devotion to Him alone leads beyond mortality.
commentary_summary: Recognizing God as the supreme enjoyer is essential for liberation.
theme: Supremacy of the Supreme Lord in all worship

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यान्ति देवव्रता देवान्पितॄ न्यान्ति पितृव्रता: |
भूतानि यान्ति भूतेज्या यान्ति मद्याजिनोऽपि माम् ||25||
transliteration:
yānti deva-vratā devān pitṝīn yānti pitṛi-vratāḥ |
bhūtāni yānti bhūtejyā yānti mad-yājino ’pi mām ||
translation: Worshippers of the gods go to the gods; worshippers of ancestors go to the ancestors; worshippers of spirits go to such beings; but My devotees come to Me.
commentary_full: Destination follows devotion. One attains the realm of the object of worship. Celestial worship grants celestial realms; ancestor worship leads to ancestral spheres; lower worship yields lower states. Only devotion directed to the Supreme leads beyond the cycle of rebirth into the eternal divine abode. Spiritual aspiration determines spiritual destination.
commentary_summary: One reaches the realm of the entity one worships.
theme: Spiritual destination according to object of worship

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
पत्रं पुष्पं फलं तोयं यो मे भक्त्या प्रयच्छति |
तदहं भक्त्युपहृतमश्नामि प्रयतात्मन: || 26||
transliteration:
patraṁ puṣhpaṁ phalaṁ toyaṁ yo me bhaktyā prayachchhati |
tadahaṁ bhaktyupahṛitam aśhnāmi prayatātmanaḥ ||
translation: Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—I joyfully accept that loving offering from one whose heart is pure.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals the extraordinary accessibility of divine worship. Unlike ritualistic systems that demand elaborate procedures, the Supreme values love over material worth. Even the simplest offering—a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water—becomes spiritually exalted when infused with devotion. The repetition of the word 'bhaktyā' emphasizes that love is the essential ingredient. God does not measure offerings by external value but by inner sincerity. When the heart is pure and the intention selfless, even the humblest gift is accepted with delight. This verse beautifully expresses divine compassion and the intimate reciprocity between God and devotee.
commentary_summary: God values devotion, not the material value of the offering.
theme: The simplicity and accessibility of loving devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यत्करोषि यदश्नासि यज्जुहोषि ददासि यत् |
यत्तपस्यसि कौन्तेय तत्कुरुष्व मदर्पणम् || 27||
transliteration:
yat karoṣhi yad aśhnāsi yaj juhoṣhi dadāsi yat |
yat tapasyasi kaunteya tat kuruṣhva mad-arpaṇam ||
translation: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give in charity, and whatever austerity you perform—O son of Kunti—do it as an offering unto Me.
commentary_full: Krishna universalizes devotion. Spiritual life is not confined to ritual spaces but extends to every action. By consciously dedicating daily duties, food, charity, and discipline to the Divine, ordinary life becomes sacred. This transformation lies not in external ritual alone but in inner intention—performing each act for God’s pleasure. Such conscious offering converts material activity into spiritual service.
commentary_summary: Dedicate every action to God and transform life into devotion.
theme: Sanctifying all actions through dedication to God

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
शुभाशुभफलैरेवं मोक्ष्यसे कर्मबन्धनै: |
संन्यासयोगयुक्तात्मा विमुक्तो मामुपैष्यसि || 28||
transliteration:
śhubhāśhubha-phalair evaṁ mokṣhyase karma-bandhanaiḥ |
sannyāsa-yoga-yuktātmā vimukto mām upaiṣhyasi ||
translation: Thus you shall be freed from the bondage of good and bad results of actions. With your mind united in renunciation, you will be liberated and come to Me.
commentary_full: Both virtuous and sinful actions bind the soul within karma, as each produces consequences. Even good deeds compel rebirth to experience their rewards. By renouncing selfish intent and dedicating actions to God, karmic reactions dissolve. This is sannyāsa-yoga—not abandonment of action, but renunciation of egoistic ownership. Such alignment liberates the soul even while living, culminating in union with the Divine.
commentary_summary: Offering actions to God frees one from karmic bondage.
theme: Freedom from karma through selfless dedication

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
समोऽहं सर्वभूतेषु न मे द्वेष्योऽस्ति न प्रिय: |
ये भजन्ति तु मां भक्त्या मयि ते तेषु चाप्यहम् || 29||
transliteration:
samo ’haṁ sarva-bhūteṣhu na me dveṣhyo ’sti na priyaḥ |
ye bhajanti tu māṁ bhaktyā mayi te teṣhu chāpyaham ||
translation: I am equal to all beings; I neither hate nor favor anyone. But those who worship Me with devotion dwell in Me, and I dwell in them.
commentary_full: Krishna affirms divine impartiality. Grace is universal, like rain falling equally on all land. Yet results differ based on receptivity. Devotees, by opening their hearts in loving surrender, become fit vessels for divine presence. Thus, while God remains equal to all, the intimacy of relationship depends upon the devotee’s surrender. Love invites reciprocal closeness without contradicting divine justice.
commentary_summary: God is impartial, but devotion creates intimate reciprocity.
theme: Divine impartiality and reciprocal devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अपि चेत्सुदुराचारो भजते मामनन्यभाक् |
साधुरेव स मन्तव्य: सम्यग्व्यवसितो हि स: || 30||
transliteration:
api chet su-durāchāro bhajate mām ananya-bhāk |
sādhur eva sa mantavyaḥ samyag vyavasito hi saḥ ||
translation: Even if a person of extremely sinful conduct worships Me with exclusive devotion, that person is to be regarded as righteous, for they have made the proper resolve.
commentary_full: Krishna reveals the transformative power of exclusive devotion. Past misconduct does not permanently define a person when genuine surrender arises. The decisive factor is inner resolve—ananya-bhāk—single-pointed devotion without divided loyalty. Once the heart turns fully toward God, the spiritual trajectory shifts immediately. Bhakti does not merely modify behavior; it reorients identity. Thus, one who has firmly resolved to worship the Supreme is to be seen according to present spiritual direction, not past errors. Divine grace recognizes intention and sincere commitment over historical flaws.
commentary_summary: Exclusive devotion transforms even the gravest sinner into a righteous soul.
theme: The reformative power of wholehearted devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
क्षिप्रं भवति धर्मात्मा शश्वच्छान्तिं निगच्छति |
कौन्तेय प्रतिजानीहि न मे भक्त: प्रणश्यति || 31||
transliteration:
kṣhipraṁ bhavati dharmātmā śhaśhvach-chhāntiṁ nigachchhati |
kaunteya pratijānīhi na me bhaktaḥ praṇaśhyati ||
translation: Quickly they become righteous and attain lasting peace. O son of Kunti, declare boldly that My devotee never perishes.
commentary_full: Krishna affirms that sincere devotion rapidly purifies the heart. Spiritual transformation is not gradual alone—it can be swift when surrender is wholehearted. Divine virtues naturally manifest when the mind becomes attached to the all-pure Supreme. God then makes a powerful assurance: no devotee is ever lost. Even if external circumstances appear adverse, divine grace safeguards their ultimate welfare. This declaration emphasizes both the certainty of spiritual progress and the unfailing protection extended to those who take refuge in Him.
commentary_summary: Devotion swiftly purifies, and God guarantees the protection of His devotees.
theme: The certainty of redemption and divine protection

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मां हि पार्थ व्यपाश्रित्य येऽपि स्यु: पापयोनय: |
स्त्रियो वैश्यास्तथा शूद्रास्तेऽपि यान्ति परां गतिम् || 32||
transliteration:
māṁ hi pārtha vyapāśhritya ye ’pi syuḥ pāpa-yonayaḥ |
striyo vaiśhyās tathā śhūdrās te ’pi yānti parāṁ gatim ||
translation: Those who take refuge in Me, O Parth—even if born in circumstances considered low—women, merchants, and laborers—also attain the supreme destination.
commentary_full: Krishna universalizes eligibility for liberation. Spiritual realization is not restricted by birth, social status, gender, or prior circumstances. While other spiritual paths impose rigid qualifications, bhakti is open to all who sincerely take shelter of the Divine. Devotion transcends social distinctions because all souls are equally parts of God. Thus, refuge in Him overrides worldly limitations and grants access to the highest spiritual goal.
commentary_summary: Devotion transcends social distinctions and is open to all.
theme: Universality of the path of devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
किं पुनर्ब्राह्मणा: पुण्या भक्ता राजर्षयस्तथा |
अनित्यमसुखं लोकमिमं प्राप्य भजस्व माम् || 33||
transliteration:
kiṁ punar brāhmaṇāḥ puṇyā bhaktā rājarṣhayas tathā |
anityam asukhaṁ lokam imaṁ prāpya bhajasva mām ||
translation: What then to speak of the righteous sages and saintly kings? Having come into this transient and joyless world, engage in devotion to Me.
commentary_full: If even those born in unfavorable conditions can attain the supreme destination through devotion, then those endowed with virtue and opportunity have even greater reason to embrace it. Krishna reminds Arjun of the fleeting and unsatisfactory nature of worldly existence. Recognizing life’s impermanence should inspire earnest spiritual effort. Privilege and favorable circumstances are meaningful only when directed toward devotion and God-realization.
commentary_summary: Recognizing life’s impermanence, one should engage wholeheartedly in devotion.
theme: Use human birth for spiritual realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मन्मना भव मद्भक्तो मद्याजी मां नमस्कुरु |
मामेवैष्यसि युक्त्वैवमात्मानं मत्परायण: || 34||
transliteration:
man-manā bhava mad-bhakto mad-yājī māṁ namaskuru |
mām evaiṣhyasi yuktvaivam ātmānaṁ mat-parāyaṇaḥ ||
translation: Fix your mind on Me, become My devotee, worship Me, and offer obeisance to Me. Thus uniting yourself with Me and dedicating yourself completely, you shall surely come to Me.
commentary_full: Krishna concludes the chapter with a direct, personal call to devotion. Bhakti involves mental absorption, loving dedication, worshipful action, and humble surrender. The instruction is practical and relational—think of Me, love Me, bow to Me. When the entire personality—mind, body, and intention—is aligned toward the Divine, union becomes inevitable. This verse encapsulates the essence of bhakti-yoga: wholehearted dedication leading to assured communion with God.
commentary_summary: Wholehearted devotion guarantees union with God.
theme: Complete dedication as the culmination of devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
भूय एव महाबाहो शृणु मे परमं वच: |
यत्तेऽहं प्रीयमाणाय वक्ष्यामि हितकाम्यया || 1||
transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha |
bhūya eva mahā-bāho śhṛiṇu me paramaṁ vachaḥ |
yatte ’haṁ prīyamāṇāya vakṣhyāmi hita-kāmyayā ||
translation: The Lord said: Listen again to My supreme words, O mighty-armed one. Because you are dear to Me, I shall speak for your welfare.
commentary_full: Krishna resumes instruction out of affection for Arjun. Spiritual knowledge here is not merely philosophical discourse but a loving revelation. The term 'prīyamāṇāya' signifies intimacy—divine truths are disclosed where there is devotion and trust. Chapter 10 unfolds as a revelation of divine glories meant to deepen devotion, not merely satisfy intellectual curiosity.
commentary_summary: Divine knowledge is revealed out of love for the devotee’s welfare.
theme: Loving revelation of divine glories

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
न मे विदु: सुरगणा: प्रभवं न महर्षय: |
अहमादिर्हि देवानां महर्षीणां च सर्वश: || 2||
transliteration:
na me viduḥ sura-gaṇāḥ prabhavaṁ na maharṣhayaḥ |
aham ādir hi devānāṁ maharṣhīṇāṁ cha sarvaśhaḥ ||
translation: Neither the celestial gods nor the great sages know My origin, for I am the source of all the gods and sages.
commentary_full: Krishna establishes His transcendence. Even exalted beings such as devas and sages cannot comprehend His origin because He precedes them. The effect cannot fully grasp the cause. The Supreme exists prior to and independent of creation. Thus, divine nature cannot be deduced merely through speculation; it must be revealed by the Supreme Himself.
commentary_summary: God is the origin of even the gods and sages, beyond their comprehension.
theme: Supremacy and transcendence of the Divine

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यो मामजमनादिं च वेत्ति लोकमहेश्वरम् |
असम्मूढ: स मर्त्येषु सर्वपापै: प्रमुच्यते || 3||
transliteration:
yo māmajam anādiṁ cha vetti loka-maheśhvaram |
asammūḍhaḥ sa martyeṣhu sarva-pāpaiḥ pramuchyate ||
translation: One who knows Me as unborn, beginningless, and the Supreme Lord of all worlds is undeluded among mortals and is freed from all sins.
commentary_full: True knowledge of the Supreme dispels ignorance. Recognizing God as unborn and the ultimate Lord corrects the fundamental misconception that He is subject to material limitations. Such realization frees one from delusion and dissolves karmic bondage. Knowledge here is not theoretical—it transforms consciousness and purifies existence.
commentary_summary: Realizing God’s supreme and beginningless nature frees one from delusion and sin.
theme: Liberating knowledge of the Supreme

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
बुद्धिर्ज्ञानमसम्मोह: क्षमा सत्यं दम: शम: |
सुखं दु:खं भवोऽभावो भयं चाभयमेव च || 4||
अहिंसा समता तुष्टिस्तपो दानं यशोऽयश: |
भवन्ति भावा भूतानां मत्त एव पृथग्विधा: || 5||
transliteration:
buddhir jñānam asammohaḥ kṣhamā satyaṁ damaḥ śhamaḥ |
sukhaṁ duḥkhaṁ bhavo ’bhāvo bhayaṁ chābhayameva cha ||
ahinsā samatā tuṣhṭis tapo dānaṁ yaśho ’yaśhaḥ |
bhavanti bhāvā bhūtānāṁ matta eva pṛithag-vidhāḥ ||
translation: From Me alone arise intellect, knowledge, clarity, forgiveness, truthfulness, control of senses and mind, joy and sorrow, birth and death, fear and fearlessness, non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy.
commentary_full: Krishna declares Himself the ultimate source of all psychological, moral, and existential qualities. Human temperaments and experiences—whether perceived as positive or negative—originate in the divine energy. Just as electricity manifests differently depending on the instrument, divine energy expresses uniquely according to individual disposition and karma. This affirms both God’s sovereignty and the interdependence of all qualities upon Him.
commentary_summary: All human qualities and experiences originate from the Divine source.
theme: God as the source of all qualities and experiences

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
महर्षय: सप्त पूर्वे चत्वारो मनवस्तथा |
मद्भावा मानसा जाता येषां लोक इमा: प्रजा: || 6||
transliteration:
maharṣhayaḥ sapta pūrve chatvāro manavas tathā |
mad-bhāvā mānasā jātā yeṣhāṁ loka imāḥ prajāḥ ||
translation: The seven great Sages, the four great Saints before them, and the fourteen Manus, are all born from My mind. From them, all the people in the world have descended.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that even the greatest sages, saints, and Manus originate from Him. Through them, the entire human lineage and cosmic order unfold. This establishes that all creation, hierarchy, and life ultimately stem from the divine will and consciousness of God.
commentary_summary: All great sages and the lineage of humanity originate from the Divine, establishing God as the ultimate source of creation.
theme: Divine origin of creation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
एतां विभूतिं योगं च मम यो वेत्ति तत्त्वत: |
सोऽविकम्पेन योगेन युज्यते नात्र संशय: || 7||
transliteration:
etāṁ vibhūtiṁ yogaṁ cha mama yo vetti tattvataḥ |
so ’vikampena yogena yujyate nātra sanśhayaḥ ||
translation: Those who know in truth My glories and divine powers become united with Me through unwavering Bhakti Yog. Of this there is no doubt.
commentary_full: Krishna explains that understanding His divine powers and glories deepens devotion. True knowledge of God strengthens faith and leads to unwavering bhakti. As awareness of His greatness grows, love and connection with Him naturally intensify.
commentary_summary: True understanding of God’s divine powers strengthens devotion and leads to unwavering spiritual connection.
theme: Knowledge leading to devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
