सर्वत्रगमचिन्त्यञ्च कूटस्थमचलन्ध्रुवम् ||3||
सन्नियम्येन्द्रियग्रामं सर्वत्र समबुद्धय: |
ते प्राप्नुवन्ति मामेव सर्वभूतहिते रता: ||4||
transliteration: ye tv akṣharam anirdeśhyam avyaktaṁ paryupāsate | sarvatra-gam achintyañcha kūṭa-stham achalandhruvam || sanniyamyendriya-grāmaṁ sarvatra sama-buddhayaḥ | te prāpnuvanti mām eva sarva-bhūta-hite ratāḥ ||
translation: But those who worship the formless aspect of the Absolute Truth—the imperishable, the indefinable, the unmanifest, the all-pervading, the unthinkable, the unchanging, the eternal, and the immoveable—by restraining their senses and being even-minded everywhere, such persons, engaged in the welfare of all beings, also attain Me.
commentary_full:
After declaring devotion to His personal form as the highest path, Shree Krishna carefully clarifies that worship of the formless Brahman is not rejected. Those who contemplate and worship the imperishable, indefinable, unmanifest, and all-pervading Absolute also reach the Supreme. Their realization corresponds to the aspect of God they seek to approach.

Living beings possess diverse temperaments and inclinations, and the Supreme Lord, who has created this diversity, also manifests Himself in multiple aspects to accommodate them. For the sake of human understanding, the Vedic sages have categorized these manifestations as Brahman, Paramātmā, and Bhagavān. Each represents a valid approach to realizing the same Supreme Truth, though differing in intimacy and experiential depth.

The worshippers of the formless Brahman discipline their senses, cultivate equanimity toward all beings, and dedicate themselves to universal welfare. Such spiritual aspirants transcend selfish desires and personal attachments, developing a broad vision rooted in compassion and inner balance. Their spiritual practice is austere and demanding, requiring intense self-control and unwavering steadiness of mind.

Shree Krishna reaffirms the principle He stated earlier—that He reciprocates with seekers according to the manner in which they approach Him. Since these worshippers seek union with the attributeless, all-pervading Absolute, the Supreme reveals Himself to them as Brahman. Thus, even those devoted to the formless path ultimately attain God, though in a manifestation aligned with their chosen mode of worship.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna explains that devotees who worship the formless, imperishable Brahman with sense control, equanimity, and concern for all beings also attain the Supreme, as God reciprocates according to one’s chosen path.
theme: Attainment of the Supreme through worship of the formless Absolute

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
क्लेशोऽधिकतरस्तेषामव्यक्तासक्तचेतसाम् |
अव्यक्ता हि गतिर्दु:खं देहवद्भिरवाप्यते ||5||
transliteration: kleśho ’dhikataras teṣhām avyaktāsakta-chetasām | avyaktā hi gatir duḥkhaṁ dehavadbhir avāpyate ||
translation: For those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest, the path of realization is full of tribulations. Worship of the unmanifest is exceedingly difficult for embodied beings.
commentary_full:
After acknowledging that worshippers of the formless Absolute also attain Him, Shree Krishna reiterates His preference for devotion to the personal form by highlighting the practical difficulty of the impersonal path. He explains that for those whose minds are attached to the unmanifest Brahman, spiritual progress is fraught with hardship and inner struggle.

Human beings are embodied souls who have interacted with the world of forms throughout countless lifetimes. Naturally, the mind finds it easier to focus on and develop attachment toward a personal form that possesses attributes, beauty, and divine pastimes. When a tangible form of God is available for meditation, the mind can more readily concentrate and deepen its loving connection. In contrast, the formless Brahman offers no concrete object for the mind or senses to relate to, making sustained contemplation extremely challenging.

Another reason for the difficulty of the impersonal path lies in the absence of divine grace. This contrast is illustrated through the analogy of the baby monkey and the baby kitten. The baby monkey must cling to its mother by its own effort, whereas the kitten is effortlessly carried by its mother. Similarly, seekers of the formless Brahman must rely entirely on their own spiritual effort, since Brahman, being nirguṇa (without qualities), nirviśheṣh (without attributes), and nirākār (without form), does not actively bestow grace.

On the other hand, the personal form of God is an ocean of compassion and mercy. Devotees who worship Bhagavān receive divine assistance in their spiritual practice, which greatly eases their progress. Therefore, while realization of the unmanifest is possible, Shree Krishna emphasizes that it is a far more arduous path for embodied beings compared to the path of loving devotion.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna explains that attachment to the unmanifest Brahman makes spiritual realization extremely difficult for embodied souls, as the impersonal path lacks tangible focus and divine grace, making devotion to the personal form easier and more supportive.
theme: Difficulty of realizing the unmanifest compared to devotion to the personal form of God

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ये तु सर्वाणि कर्माणि मयि संन्न्यस्य मत्परा: |
अनन्येनैव योगेन मां ध्यायन्त उपासते ||6||
तेषामहं समुद्धर्ता मृत्युसंसारसागरात् |
भवामि नचिरात्पार्थ मय्यावेशितचेतसाम् ||7||
transliteration: ye tu sarvāṇi karmāṇi mayi sannyasya mat-parāḥ | ananyenaiva yogena māṁ dhyāyanta upāsate || teṣhām ahaṁ samuddhartā mṛityu-saṁsāra-sāgarāt | bhavāmi na chirāt pārtha mayy āveśhita-chetasām ||
translation: But those who dedicate all their actions to Me, regarding Me as the Supreme goal, worshiping Me and meditating on Me with exclusive devotion, O Parth, I swiftly deliver them from the ocean of birth and death, for their consciousness is united with Me.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna emphasizes the special grace bestowed upon devotees who practice exclusive devotion to His personal form. Such devotees surrender all their actions to God, perform their duties for His pleasure, and regard Him alone as their ultimate goal. Because their worship is undivided and wholehearted, their minds and senses naturally become absorbed in Him.

With the personal form of God as the focus of devotion, devotees easily engage every aspect of their being in spiritual practice. They chant and hear the divine names, behold His form, remember His pastimes and virtues, dedicate their actions to His service, and contemplate His glories with their intellect. Through this comprehensive engagement, their consciousness quickly becomes united with God.

In response to this uninterrupted devotion, God Himself takes responsibility for their spiritual welfare. He swiftly bestows His grace, removes obstacles from their path, and dispels their ignorance with divine knowledge. Unlike paths that rely primarily on personal effort, bhakti invokes God’s active intervention.

Thus, Shree Krishna declares that He personally becomes the deliverer of such devotees, rescuing them from the ocean of birth and death. This assurance highlights the compassion of the personal God and affirms that loving devotion leads not only to realization but also to divine protection and swift liberation.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna assures that devotees who surrender all actions to Him and worship with exclusive devotion are quickly liberated, as He personally delivers them from the cycle of birth and death through His grace.
theme: Divine assurance and swift liberation through exclusive devotion to the personal form of God

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
मय्येव मन आधत्स्व मयि बुद्धिं निवेशय |
निवसिष्यसि मय्येव अत ऊर्ध्वं न संशय: ||8||
transliteration: mayy eva mana ādhatsva mayi buddhiṁ niveśhaya | nivasiṣhyasi mayy eva ata ūrdhvaṁ na sanśhayaḥ ||
translation: Fix your mind on Me alone and surrender your intellect to Me. Thereupon, you will always live in Me. Of this, there is no doubt.
commentary_full:
After establishing the superiority of devotion to His personal form, Shree Krishna now instructs Arjun on the practical method of worship. He emphasizes two essential steps: fixing the mind upon God and surrendering the intellect to Him. The mind is responsible for generating desires, attractions, and aversions, while the intellect analyzes, discriminates, and makes decisions.

The Vedic scriptures repeatedly stress that bondage and liberation are determined by the state of the mind. If the mind is attached to the world, the soul remains bound; if it becomes absorbed in God, liberation follows. Mere external acts of devotion are insufficient unless the mind is engaged, because sensory activities have no value without mental involvement. Even when the senses are inactive, as in dreams, the mind independently experiences perceptions, demonstrating its central role in spiritual life.

However, the mind can be firmly fixed on God only when the intellect is surrendered. In worldly matters, when we face situations beyond our understanding, we naturally rely on experts such as doctors or lawyers, trusting their superior knowledge. Similarly, the intellect under material illusion is riddled with defects and misconceptions, having been conditioned by countless lifetimes of erroneous thinking.

Because the conditioned intellect is prone to reversal of truth, spiritual progress cannot be achieved by following it blindly. Therefore, surrendering the intellect to God is essential. This surrender means aligning one’s thinking with divine knowledge received through scriptures and the guidance of a bona fide Guru. When both the mind and intellect are offered to God in this way, the devotee comes to dwell in constant union with Him, free from doubt and firmly established on the spiritual path.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna teaches that true devotion requires fixing the mind on God and surrendering the intellect to divine guidance, ensuring constant union with Him and freedom from doubt.
theme: Fixing the mind and surrendering the intellect as the foundation of devotion

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अथ चित्तं समाधातुं न शक्नोषि मयि स्थिरम् |
अभ्यासयोगेन ततो मामिच्छाप्तुं धनञ्जय ||9||
transliteration: atha chittaṁ samādhātuṁ na śhaknoṣhi mayi sthiram | abhyāsa-yogena tato mām ichchhāptuṁ dhanañjaya ||
translation: If you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, O Arjun, then practice remembering Me with devotion while constantly restraining the mind from worldly affairs.
commentary_full:
Fixing the mind completely upon Shree Krishna is the highest perfection of sādhanā, or spiritual practice. However, at the beginning of the spiritual journey, such steadiness is rarely possible. Recognizing this human limitation, Shree Krishna compassionately offers an alternative path.

He advises that when the mind cannot remain steadily absorbed in God, one should repeatedly practice bringing it back with devotion. This disciplined repetition is known as abhyāsa yog, the path of union with God through constant practice. Each time the mind wanders toward worldly objects, the devotee should gently redirect it toward remembrance of God’s Names, Forms, Virtues, Pastimes, Abodes, and divine Associates.

Through such repeated effort, the restless mind gradually becomes trained and purified. Over time, remembrance becomes natural rather than forced, allowing the seeker to progress steadily toward unwavering devotion and inner union with God.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna teaches that when steady meditation is difficult, one should repeatedly practice remembering Him with devotion, gradually training the mind through abhyāsa yog.
theme: Progress toward God through repeated devotional practice

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अभ्यासेऽप्यसमर्थोऽसि मत्कर्मपरमो भव |
मदर्थमपि कर्माणि कुर्वन्सिद्धिमवाप्स्यसि ||10||
transliteration: abhyāse ’py asamartho ’si mat-karma-paramo bhava | mad-artham api karmāṇi kurvan siddhim avāpsyasi ||
translation: If you cannot practice remembering Me with devotion, then just try to work for Me. Thus performing devotional service to Me, you shall achieve the stage of perfection.
commentary_full:
The instruction to constantly remember God is often easier said than practiced. The mind, shaped by material energy, naturally flows toward worldly objects, and redirecting it toward God demands sustained effort. Even sincere seekers may find that while engaged in daily responsibilities, remembrance of God slips away. Recognizing this difficulty, Shree Krishna offers a compassionate and practical alternative.

He explains that those who struggle with continuous remembrance should focus on working for Him. Whatever actions one performs—whether professional duties, household responsibilities, or bodily maintenance—should be done with the intention of pleasing God. The external activity may remain the same, but the inner consciousness must shift from self-centered motivation to divine dedication.

By performing all actions for God’s sake, selfish tendencies gradually diminish and devotion naturally deepens. Such selfless action purifies the mind, stabilizes thought, and prepares the heart for constant remembrance. In this way, karma offered to God becomes a powerful means of spiritual progress, ultimately leading the seeker toward love for God and inner perfection.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna teaches that when remembrance is difficult, one should dedicate all actions to God, transforming daily work into devotion and steadily progressing toward spiritual perfection.
theme: Attaining spiritual perfection through selfless work offered to God

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अथैतदप्यशक्तोऽसि कर्तुं मद्योगमाश्रित: |
सर्वकर्मफलत्यागं तत: कुरु यतात्मवान् ||11||
transliteration: athaitad apy aśhakto ’si kartuṁ mad-yogam āśhritaḥ | sarva-karma-phala-tyāgaṁ tataḥ kuru yatātmavān ||
translation: If you are unable to even work for Me in devotion, then try to renounce the fruits of your actions and be situated in the self.
commentary_full:
Beginning from verse 12.8, Shree Krishna has been gradually presenting practical paths suited to seekers of different spiritual capacities. Having spoken about fixing the mind on God, practicing remembrance, and working for His pleasure, He now offers a fourth and more accessible alternative for those who find even devotional work difficult.

Some people may not yet feel a deep conviction about their relationship with God or may not have made God-realization the central goal of their lives. For such individuals, working explicitly for God’s pleasure may seem beyond their present capability. Recognizing this limitation, Shree Krishna advises them to continue performing their usual duties, but with one crucial change—renounce attachment to the fruits of actions.

Detachment from results purifies the mind by gradually freeing it from the influence of passion and ignorance, and elevating it toward goodness. As the mind becomes purer and calmer, the intellect gains clarity and strength. This inner purification prepares the seeker for higher spiritual practices and deeper understanding. Thus, renunciation of the fruits of action serves as a foundational step that leads one steadily toward devotion and self-realization.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna teaches that when devotion and dedicated work feel difficult, renouncing attachment to the results of one’s actions purifies the mind and prepares the seeker for higher spiritual growth.
theme: Progress toward spirituality through renunciation of the fruits of action

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
श्रेयो हि ज्ञानमभ्यासाज्ज्ञानाद्ध्यानं विशिष्यते |
ध्यानात्कर्मफलत्यागस्त्यागाच्छान्तिरनन्तरम् ||12||
transliteration: śhreyo hi jñānam abhyāsāj jñānād dhyānaṁ viśhiṣhyate | dhyānāt karma-phala-tyāgas tyāgāch chhāntir anantaram ||
translation: Better than mechanical practice is knowledge; better than knowledge is meditation. Better than meditation is renunciation of the fruits of actions, for peace immediately follows such renunciation.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna here presents a clear hierarchy of spiritual practices, guiding seekers step by step according to their inner maturity. Many people begin their spiritual journey with mechanical or ritualistic practice, performing religious duties without engaging the mind or heart. While such practice is not useless, it remains external and limited in its ability to transform consciousness.

Above mechanical practice is spiritual knowledge, which awakens understanding about the true goal of life—God-realization rather than material achievement. Knowledge inspires a seeker to look beyond rituals and begin the process of inner purification. However, knowledge alone cannot fully cleanse the heart if it remains merely intellectual.

Therefore, Shree Krishna states that meditation is superior to knowledge. Through meditation, the mind is actively trained to withdraw from worldly distractions and focus inwardly, fostering detachment from sensory pleasures. As detachment develops, the seeker becomes capable of renouncing attachment to the fruits of actions.

Renunciation of results is declared the highest among these practices because it directly leads to peace. When one no longer depends on outcomes for happiness, the mind becomes calm and free from anxiety. This inner peace arises immediately, making karma-phala-tyāga a powerful and practical means for spiritual progress.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna outlines a progression from ritual practice to knowledge, meditation, and finally renunciation of results, emphasizing that detachment from the fruits of action brings immediate peace.
theme: Gradual refinement of spiritual practice leading to peace through renunciation

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अद्वेष्टा सर्वभूतानां मैत्र: करुण एव च |
निर्ममो निरहङ्कार: समदु:खसुख: क्षमी ||13||
सन्तुष्ट: सततं योगी यतात्मा दृढनिश्चय: |
मय्यर्पितमनोबुद्धिर्यो मद्भक्त: स मे प्रिय: ||14||
transliteration: adveṣhṭā sarva-bhūtānāṁ maitraḥ karuṇa eva cha | nirmamo nirahankāraḥ sama-duḥkha-sukhaḥ kṣhamī || santuṣhṭaḥ satataṁ yogī yatātmā dṛiḍha-niśhchayaḥ | mayy arpita-mano-buddhir yo mad-bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ ||
translation: Those devotees are very dear to Me who are free from malice toward all living beings, who are friendly and compassionate. They are free from attachment to possessions and ego, equipoised in happiness and distress, forgiving, ever content, steadily united with Me in devotion, self-controlled, of firm resolve, and dedicated to Me in mind and intellect.
commentary_full:
After establishing devotion to His personal form as the highest path, Shree Krishna now describes the inner qualities of devotees who are especially dear to Him. These qualities are not superficial behaviors but natural expressions of a heart purified by bhakti.

Devotees are free from malice toward all living beings because they perceive every soul as a part of God. Harboring hatred or envy toward others would contradict their vision of spiritual unity. Thus, even when others act with hostility, devotees remain free from ill will.

Friendliness and compassion arise naturally from devotion, as the sense of separateness diminishes. Seeing all beings as children of the same Divine Father, devotees develop empathy and actively wish for the welfare of others.

They are free from possessiveness and ego because pride and attachment obstruct devotion. By recognizing themselves as servants of God rather than proprietors, they relinquish false identification with the body and its belongings.

Devotees remain equipoised in happiness and distress, accepting both as outcomes arranged by God. Knowing that effort lies in their hands while results rest with the Divine, they maintain inner balance in all situations.

Forgiveness is another hallmark of devotion. Rather than nurturing resentment, devotees leave judgment and recompense to God, protecting their own spiritual growth from being damaged by negativity.

They are content because their happiness no longer depends on material accumulation. With desires reduced and faith strengthened, they accept whatever comes by God’s will with satisfaction.

Steadily united with God, such devotees are true yogis. Their consciousness remains continuously absorbed in Him, not intermittently but with constancy and depth. Through this absorption, they gain mastery over the mind and senses.

Their determination is firm because their intellect is anchored in scriptural knowledge and guided by the Guru. No external influence can shake their conviction. With mind and intellect fully offered to God, every aspect of their being naturally aligns in His service. Shree Krishna declares that devotees endowed with these qualities are exceedingly dear to Him.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna describes the qualities of devotees dear to Him, highlighting compassion, humility, equanimity, forgiveness, contentment, steady devotion, self-control, and complete dedication of mind and intellect.
theme: Qualities of a devotee who is dear to the Supreme Lord

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यस्मान्नोद्विजते लोको लोकान्नोद्विजते च य: |
हर्षामर्षभयोद्वेगैर्मुक्तो य: स च मे प्रिय: ||15||
transliteration: yasmān nodvijate loko lokān nodvijate cha yaḥ | harṣhāmarṣha-bhayodvegair mukto yaḥ sa cha me priyaḥ ||
translation: Those devotees of Mine are very dear to Me who are not a source of disturbance to the world, and who are not disturbed by others, who are free from pleasure, pain, fear, and anxiety.
commentary_full:
The soul is pure by nature, but its divine qualities remain concealed due to the impurities of the mind. When devotion cleanses the mind, the innate virtues of the soul manifest effortlessly. The Shreemad Bhagavatam explains that all noble qualities naturally reside in those who are devoted to God, while those devoid of devotion remain driven by restless mental desires.

Shree Krishna highlights that His devotees are not a cause of distress to anyone. Devotion softens the heart and makes one gentle and considerate in thought, word, and action. Seeing God dwelling within every being, devotees cannot even conceive of harming others.

At the same time, devotees are not disturbed by others. Though they never hurt anyone, they may still face hostility or opposition. History bears witness to saints who endured suffering with compassion and forgiveness. Their inner stability allows them to remain unaffected by external provocations.

Such devotees are equipoised in pleasure and pain. Guided by scriptural wisdom, they recognize joy and sorrow as temporary phases of life, like changing seasons. Viewing both as expressions of God’s will, they use every circumstance to deepen their devotion.

They are also free from fear and anxiety. Fear arises from attachment and the dread of loss. Since devotees are detached from material dependencies and aligned with the divine will, fear and anxiety no longer bind them. In this state of surrender and inner harmony, they experience deep peace. Shree Krishna declares that devotees endowed with these qualities are exceedingly dear to Him.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna describes devotees who neither disturb others nor are disturbed themselves, who remain balanced in joy and sorrow, and who are free from fear and anxiety, declaring such devotees to be very dear to Him.
theme: Inner peace and emotional balance as qualities of a beloved devotee

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अनपेक्ष: शुचिर्दक्ष उदासीनो गतव्यथ: |
सर्वारम्भपरित्यागी यो मद्भक्त: स मे प्रिय: ||16||
transliteration: anapekṣhaḥ śhuchir dakṣha udāsīno gata-vyathaḥ | sarvārambha-parityāgī yo mad-bhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ ||
translation: Those devotees of Mine are very dear to Me who are indifferent to worldly gains, externally and internally pure, skillful, free from cares, untroubled, and who renounce selfish motives in all undertakings.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna continues describing the refined inner qualities that blossom naturally in a devoted soul. Such devotees are indifferent to worldly gains. Just as one who possesses immense wealth is not disturbed by small losses or gains, devotees who are rich in divine love regard material achievements as insignificant. Their highest priority is loving service to God, which makes them unconcerned with worldly profit.

They are externally and internally pure. Constant absorption in the all-pure Lord cleanses their minds of lust, anger, greed, envy, and ego. This inner purity naturally expresses itself outwardly as cleanliness in conduct, body, and surroundings.

Devotees are skillful in action. Seeing every task as an opportunity to serve God, they perform their duties with sincerity, care, and excellence. This devotional attitude enhances their competence and efficiency.

They are without cares and untroubled. Firm faith in God’s protection frees them from anxiety. Surrendering the results of their actions to the Supreme, they focus on sincere effort alone. Success or failure does not disturb them, as they accept every outcome as the will of God.

Such devotees renounce selfishness in all undertakings. Their spirit of service elevates them above personal gain and narrow self-interest. Shree Krishna affirms that devotees who live with this purity, skill, detachment, and surrender are exceedingly dear to Him.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna explains that devotees who are pure, skillful, free from anxiety, detached from worldly gain, and devoid of selfish motives in their actions are especially dear to Him.
theme: Selfless action and inner purity as marks of a beloved devotee

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यो न हृष्यति न द्वेष्टि न शोचति न काङ् क्षति |
शुभाशुभपरित्यागी भक्तिमान्य: स मे प्रिय: || 17||
transliteration: yo na hṛiṣhyati na dveṣhṭi na śhochati na kāṅkṣhati | śhubhāśhubha-parityāgī bhaktimān yaḥ sa me priyaḥ ||
translation: Those who neither rejoice in mundane pleasures nor despair in worldly sorrows, who neither lament for any loss nor hanker for any gain, who renounce both good and evil deeds, such persons who are full of devotion are very dear to Me.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna describes the inner state of a perfected devotee who has risen above emotional dualities. Such devotees do not become elated by worldly pleasures nor disturbed by material sorrows because their happiness is rooted in divine love rather than external circumstances.

They neither grieve over losses nor crave gains, as their fulfillment lies in devotion to God. Their mind remains steady, unaffected by success or failure, gain or loss. This emotional balance arises from deep spiritual wisdom and detachment.

Renunciation of both good and evil actions refers to giving up selfishly motivated deeds as well as ritualistic actions performed for personal rewards. When actions are performed solely as an offering to God, they no longer bind the soul. Such actions become akarma.

Being filled with devotion, these devotees experience ever-increasing divine love. Their hearts overflow with bhakti, making them exceedingly dear to Shree Krishna.
commentary_summary: Devotees who remain balanced in joy and sorrow, free from attachment to gain or loss, and act with pure devotion are deeply cherished by the Lord.
theme: Transcendence of emotional dualities through pure devotion

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सम: शत्रौ च मित्रे च तथा मानापमानयो: |
शीतोष्णसुखदु:खेषु सम: सङ्गविवर्जित: || 18||
तुल्यनिन्दास्तुतिर्मौनी सन्तुष्टो येन केनचित् |
अनिकेत: स्थिरमतिर्भक्तिमान्मे प्रियो नर: || 19||
transliteration: samaḥ śhatrau cha mitre cha tathā mānāpamānayoḥ | śhītoṣhṇa-sukha-duḥkheṣhu samaḥ saṅga-vivarjitaḥ || tulya-nindā-stutir maunī santuṣhṭo yena kenachit | aniketaḥ sthira-matir bhaktimān me priyo naraḥ ||
translation: Those who are alike to friend and foe, equipoised in honor and dishonor, cold and heat, joy and sorrow, and are free from all unfavorable association; those who take praise and reproach alike, who are given to silent contemplation, content with what comes their way, without attachment to the place of residence, whose intellect is firmly fixed in Me, and who are full of devotion to Me, such persons are very dear to Me.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna describes several refined qualities that naturally manifest in advanced devotees. Such devotees remain equal toward friends and enemies, having transcended personal likes and dislikes. They are unaffected by honor or dishonor, understanding both to be temporary and external to the soul. Similarly, they remain balanced in cold and heat, joy and sorrow, recognizing these dualities as passing conditions of material existence.

Free from unfavorable association, devotees avoid influences that pull the mind toward worldly attachments and instead seek company that nurtures devotion. Praise and criticism do not disturb them, as their motivation is internal and rooted in service to God rather than social validation. Their inclination toward silence does not indicate withdrawal from life, but rather a preference for contemplation and divine remembrance over idle talk.

Contentment with whatever comes their way reflects their trust in divine providence. Without attachment to any fixed residence, they recognize the temporary nature of worldly shelters. Their intellect remains firmly fixed in God, sustained by unwavering faith and devotion. Shree Krishna declares that such steadfast, detached, and devoted souls are exceedingly dear to Him.
commentary_summary: Devotees who remain balanced in all dualities, detached from worldly attachments, content, contemplative, and firmly devoted to God are deeply dear to the Lord.
theme: Steady devotion expressed through equanimity and detachment from worldly dualities

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ये तु धर्म्यामृतमिदं यथोक्तं पर्युपासते |
श्रद्दधाना मत्परमा भक्तास्तेऽतीव मे प्रिया: || 20||
transliteration: ye tu dharmyāmṛitam idaṁ yathoktaṁ paryupāsate | śhraddadhānā mat-paramā bhaktās te ’tīva me priyāḥ ||
translation: Those who honor this nectar of wisdom declared here, have faith in Me, and are devoted and intent on Me as the supreme goal, they are exceedingly dear to Me.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna concludes the Bhakti Yog chapter by affirming the supreme value of devotion. He refers to His teachings as dharmya-amṛitam, the nectar of divine wisdom that uplifts the soul and leads it toward eternal fulfillment. Those who follow this path exactly as instructed, without distortion or doubt, are praised as ideal devotees.

Such devotees practice bhakti with faith, trusting completely in the words of the Lord. They accept Him as the highest goal of life, placing Him above all material aspirations and personal desires. Their devotion is not casual or occasional, but steady, sincere, and guided by the principles explained throughout the chapter.

By summarizing the qualities, practices, and mindset of true devotees, Shree Krishna reaffirms that bhakti is the highest spiritual path. Those who walk this path with faith, dedication, and adherence to divine teachings become exceedingly dear to Him, attaining His grace and ultimate spiritual fulfillment.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna concludes that devotees who faithfully follow His teachings, accept Him as the supreme goal, and practice devotion with sincerity are exceedingly dear to Him.
theme: Supremacy of bhakti as the highest spiritual path

speaker: Arjun
text_sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच |
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव क्षेत्रं क्षेत्रज्ञमेव च |
एतद्वेदितुमिच्छामि ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं च केशव || 1||
transliteration: arjuna uvācha | prakṛitiṁ puruṣhaṁ chaiva kṣhetraṁ kṣhetra-jñam eva cha | etad veditum ichchhāmi jñānaṁ jñeyaṁ cha keśhava ||
translation: Arjun said, “O Keshav, I wish to understand what are prakṛiti and puruṣh, and what are kṣhetra and kṣhetrajña? I also wish to know what is true knowledge, and what is the goal of this knowledge?”
commentary_full:
At the opening of the thirteenth chapter, Arjun raises a set of profound philosophical questions that form the foundation of spiritual inquiry. He asks about prakṛiti (material nature) and puruṣh (the conscious enjoyer), which together explain the interaction between matter and consciousness. He further inquires about kṣhetra, the field of activities—primarily the body—and kṣhetrajña, the knower of that field, the conscious self.

By asking about knowledge (jñāna) and the object of knowledge (jñeya), Arjun seeks clarity on what constitutes true wisdom and the ultimate aim of spiritual realization. These questions indicate a shift from practical devotion toward deeper metaphysical understanding.

Shree Krishna’s forthcoming answers will explain the distinction between the body and the soul, the role of material nature, and the Supreme Lord as the ultimate knower of all fields. Thus, this verse sets the stage for the detailed exposition of knowledge, discernment, and liberation that follows in Chapter 13.
commentary_summary: Arjun seeks to understand the nature of matter, consciousness, the body, the soul, true knowledge, and its ultimate goal, setting the foundation for Krishna’s teachings in Chapter 13.
theme: Inquiry into matter, consciousness, and true knowledge

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
श्रीभगवानुवाच |
इदं शरीरं कौन्तेय क्षेत्रमित्यभिधीयते |
एतद्यो वेत्ति तं प्राहु: क्षेत्रज्ञ इति तद्विद: || 2||
transliteration: śhrī-bhagavān uvācha | idaṁ śharīraṁ kaunteya kṣhetram ity abhidhīyate | etad yo vetti taṁ prāhuḥ kṣhetra-jña iti tad-vidaḥ ||
translation: The Supreme Divine Lord said: O Arjun, this body is termed as kṣhetra (the field of activities), and the one who knows this body is called kṣhetrajña (the knower of the field) by the sages who discern the truth about both.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna begins His response by clearly distinguishing between the body and the conscious self. He explains that the physical body, along with the mind and intellect, is called kṣhetra—the field of activities—because it is the medium through which all actions and experiences take place. Just as a field is the ground where cultivation occurs, the body is the ground where life’s activities are carried out.

The soul, however, is distinct from this field. Though it does not directly see, hear, touch, or act, it experiences everything through the body-mind-intellect mechanism. Because the soul is aware of the body and its changes, it is called kṣhetrajña, the knower of the field. This awareness proves that the soul is separate from the body, just as a witness is separate from what is being observed.

This understanding has been articulated by enlightened sages who realized their true identity beyond the body. By establishing this fundamental distinction, Shree Krishna lays the foundation for spiritual knowledge—recognizing oneself not as the body, but as the conscious knower dwelling within it.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna explains that the body is the field of activities, while the soul is the knower of that field, establishing the essential distinction between matter and consciousness.
theme: Distinction between the body as the field and the soul as its knower

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
क्षेत्रज्ञं चापि मां विद्धि सर्वक्षेत्रेषु भारत |
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोर्ज्ञानं यत्तज्ज्ञानं मतं मम || 3||
transliteration: kṣhetra-jñaṁ chāpi māṁ viddhi sarva-kṣhetreṣhu bhārata | kṣhetra-kṣhetrajñayor jñānaṁ yat taj jñānaṁ mataṁ mama ||
translation: O scion of Bharat, know Me also to be the knower of all the individual fields of activity. The understanding of the field and the knower of the field, this I consider to be true knowledge.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna now expands the concept of kṣhetrajña by revealing His own position as the Supreme Knower. While the individual soul is the knower of only its own body, even that knowledge is partial and limited. In contrast, God exists as the Supreme Soul within the hearts of all living beings and is the knower of every field of activity. His knowledge is complete, perfect, and unobstructed.

By stating this, Shree Krishna establishes a clear distinction between three realities: the body as the field of activities, the individual soul as the limited knower of one field, and the Supreme Lord as the all-pervading knower of all fields. This understanding prevents confusion between the soul and God, while simultaneously affirming God’s immanence within all beings.

Shree Krishna then defines true knowledge. According to Him, genuine knowledge is not mere intellectual achievement or accumulation of information, but the correct understanding of the body, the soul, the Supreme Soul, and the distinctions among them. Without this realization, even the most learned individuals remain ignorant from a spiritual standpoint. Thus, this verse sets the philosophical foundation for self-realization and God-realization.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna explains that He is the Supreme Knower of all fields, and true knowledge lies in understanding the distinction between the body, the individual soul, and the Supreme Soul.
theme: True knowledge as understanding the body, the soul, and the Supreme Knower

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
तत्क्षेत्रं यच्च यादृक्च यद्विकारि यतश्च यत् |
स च यो यत्प्रभावश्च तत्समासेन मे शृणु || 4||
transliteration: tat kṣhetraṁ yach cha yādṛik cha yad-vikāri yataśh cha yat | sa cha yo yat-prabhāvaśh cha tat samāsena me śhṛiṇu ||
translation: Listen as I explain to you briefly what that field is, what its nature is, how it undergoes change, from what it is created, who the knower of the field is, and what his powers are.
commentary_full:
Having identified the field (kṣhetra) and the knower of the field (kṣhetrajña), Shree Krishna now prepares Arjun for a systematic explanation of both. He assures Arjun that He will explain the nature of the body, its constitution, and the transformations it undergoes. This includes how the body evolves, changes, and eventually perishes.

Shree Krishna also indicates that He will explain the origin of the field—namely, material nature—and clarify who the knower of the field is, along with the extent of his powers. This distinction is essential for developing true spiritual understanding, as it prevents confusion between the body, the individual soul, and the Supreme Soul.

By stating that He will present this knowledge in summary form, Shree Krishna emphasizes clarity and practicality. The purpose is not mere theoretical discussion, but enabling the seeker to discern the temporary from the eternal. This verse thus serves as an introduction to the detailed analysis of the kṣhetra and kṣhetrajña that follows in the subsequent verses.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna introduces His explanation of the body, its nature and changes, its origin, and the powers of the knower of the field, setting the foundation for deeper spiritual discrimination.
theme: Introduction to the analysis of the field and the knower of the field

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ऋषिभिर्बहुधा गीतं छन्दोभिर्विविधै: पृथक् |
ब्रह्मसूत्रपदैश्चैव हेतुमद्भिर्विनिश्चितै: || 5 ||
transliteration: ṛiṣhibhir bahudhā gītaṁ chhandobhir vividhaiḥ pṛithak | brahma-sūtra-padaiśh chaiva hetumadbhir viniśhchitaiḥ ||
translation: Great sages have sung the truth about the field and the knower of the field in manifold ways. It has been stated in various Vedic hymns, and especially revealed in the Brahma Sūtra, with sound logic and conclusive evidence.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna emphasizes that the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field is not speculative, but firmly established through multiple authoritative sources. Great sages have explained this truth in diverse ways to suit different levels of understanding, and it is recorded in various Vedic hymns. The Vedas are eternal knowledge revealed by God at the beginning of creation and are accepted as infallible authority in spiritual matters.

To further establish this knowledge with logical precision, Sage Ved Vyās composed the Brahma Sūtra, also known as Vedānt Darśhan, which systematically presents the conclusions of Vedic wisdom. The Brahma Sūtra uses sound reasoning and conclusive logic to clarify the distinction between the soul, the body, and the Supreme Reality.

By citing the sages, the Vedas, and the Brahma Sūtra, Shree Krishna assures Arjun that the teachings He is presenting are validated by both scriptural authority and rational analysis. This reinforces the reliability of the knowledge being imparted and encourages the seeker to accept it with confidence.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna affirms that the knowledge of the field and its knower is well-established in the Vedas and Brahma Sūtra, having been explained by sages with sound logic and authoritative evidence.
theme: Scriptural authority and logical validation of spiritual knowledge

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
महाभूतान्यङ्ककारो बुद्धिरव्यक्त मेव च |
इन्द्रियाणि दशैकं च पञ्च चेन्द्रियगोचरा: || 6||
transliteration: mahā-bhūtāny ahaṅkāro buddhir avyaktam eva cha | indriyāṇi daśhaikaṁ cha pañcha chendriya-gocharāḥ ||
translation: The field of activities is composed of the five great elements, the ego, the intellect, the unmanifest primordial matter, the eleven senses, and the five objects of the senses.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna now enumerates the components of the kṣhetra, or the field of activities, in a systematic manner. The five great elements—earth, water, fire, air, and space—form the gross physical basis of the body. Beyond these are the subtle components: the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), and the unmanifest material nature (avyakta), which is the primordial source of matter.

He further includes the eleven senses, comprising the five knowledge-acquiring senses, the five working senses, and the mind. The mind is counted as a sense because it coordinates sensory input and directs action. Additionally, the five sense objects—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—are included since they exist in subtle form within the mind and influence the soul’s experience of the material world.

By listing these elements, Shree Krishna clarifies that the body is not a single entity but a complex assemblage of material components. This understanding helps the seeker distinguish between the changing field (body and mind) and the unchanging knower of the field (the soul), which is essential for genuine spiritual realization.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna lists the material components that constitute the body and mind, defining the field of activities and preparing the seeker to distinguish it from the soul.
theme: Constitution of the field of activities

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
इच्छा द्वेष: सुखं दु:खं सङ्घातश्चेतना धृति: |
एतत्क्षेत्रं समासेन सविकारमुदाहृतम् || 7||
transliteration: ichchhā dveṣhaḥ sukhaṁ duḥkhaṁ saṅghātaśh chetanā dhṛitiḥ | etat kṣhetraṁ samāsena sa-vikāram udāhṛitam ||
translation: Desire and aversion, happiness and misery, the body, consciousness, and the will—all these comprise the field and its modifications.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna further elaborates on the kṣhetra by describing its functional attributes and the changes it undergoes. Desire and aversion arise from the interaction of the mind and intellect with the objects of the senses, motivating action and avoidance. Happiness and misery are the mental experiences resulting from favorable and unfavorable circumstances, respectively.

The term saṅghāta refers to the assembled body, a composite of material elements that undergo constant transformation. Consciousness appears to pervade the body due to the presence of the soul, just as fire lends heat to iron placed within it. Although consciousness belongs to the soul, it is perceived as a characteristic of the field while the soul resides in the body.

Dhṛiti, or willpower, sustains effort and determination, enabling purposeful action through the body and mind. All these aspects together constitute the field of activities along with its modifications. By identifying them as part of the kṣhetra, Shree Krishna helps the seeker recognize that these experiences and attributes are not the soul itself, but belong to the material domain.
commentary_summary: Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body, consciousness, and will are identified as attributes and modifications of the field of activities.
theme: Attributes and modifications of the field of activities

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अमानित्वमदम्भित्वमहिंसा क्षान्तिरार्जवम् |
आचार्योपासनं शौचं स्थैर्यमात्मविनिग्रह: || 8||
इन्द्रियार्थेषु वैराग्यमनहङ्कार एव च |
जन्ममृत्युजराव्याधिदु:खदोषानुदर्शनम् || 9||
असक्तिरनभिष्वङ्ग: पुत्रदारगृहादिषु |
नित्यं च समचित्तत्वमिष्टानिष्टोपपत्तिषु || 10||
मयि चानन्ययोगेन भक्तिरव्यभिचारिणी |
विविक्तदेशसेवित्वमरतिर्जनसंसदि || 11||
अध्यात्मज्ञाननित्यत्वं तत्वज्ञानार्थदर्शनम् |
एतज्ज्ञानमिति प्रोक्तमज्ञानं यदतोऽन्यथा || 12||
transliteration: amānitvam adambhitvam ahinsā kṣhāntir ārjavam | āchāryopāsanaṁ śhauchaṁ sthairyam ātma-vinigrahaḥ || indriyārtheṣhu vairāgyam anahankāra eva cha | janma-mṛityu-jarā-vyādhi-duḥkha-doṣhānudarśhanam || asaktir anabhiṣhvaṅgaḥ putra-dāra-gṛihādiṣhu | nityaṁ cha sama-chittatvam iṣhṭāniṣhṭopapattiṣhu || mayi chānanya-yogena bhaktir avyabhichāriṇī | vivikta-deśha-sevitvam aratir jana-sansadi || adhyātma-jñāna-nityatvaṁ tattva-jñānārtha-darśhanam | etaj jñānam iti proktam ajñānaṁ yad ato ’nyathā ||
translation: Humbleness; freedom from hypocrisy; non-violence; forgiveness; simplicity; service of the Guru; cleanliness of body and mind; steadfastness; self-control; dispassion toward sense objects; absence of ego; reflection on the miseries of birth, death, old age, and disease; non-attachment; absence of clinging to family and home; even-mindedness in desirable and undesirable situations; constant and exclusive devotion to Me; preference for solitude; aversion to mundane society; constancy in spiritual knowledge; and philosophical pursuit of the Absolute Truth—all these are declared to be knowledge. That which is contrary to this is ignorance.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna defines true knowledge not as intellectual accumulation, but as the cultivation of virtues that purify the heart and refine perception. These qualities transform the field of activities into a suitable instrument for realizing the self and the Supreme. Humility, simplicity, forgiveness, and non-violence dissolve ego-based consciousness, while devotion, self-control, and detachment redirect the mind toward God.

The emphasis on remembering the sufferings inherent in birth, old age, disease, and death strengthens dispassion and clarity of purpose. Even-mindedness amid success and failure stabilizes the intellect, while solitude and detachment from mundane society aid inward contemplation. Constancy in spiritual knowledge ensures that wisdom is lived, not merely understood.

Shree Krishna concludes by declaring that all these qualities together constitute knowledge itself. Anything that opposes or neglects these virtues, regardless of intellectual brilliance, is to be understood as ignorance, as it perpetuates identification with the body and the material field.
commentary_summary: Shree Krishna lists the virtues and attitudes that constitute true spiritual knowledge and declares all opposing tendencies to be ignorance.
theme: Definition of true knowledge through spiritual virtues

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ज्ञेयं यत्तत्प्रवक्ष्यामि यज्ज्ञात्वामृतमश्रुते |
अनादिमत्परं ब्रह्म न सत्तन्नासदुच्यते || 13||
transliteration: jñeyaṁ yat tat pravakṣhyāmi yaj jñātvāmṛitam aśhnute | anādi mat-paraṁ brahma na sat tan nāsad uchyate ||
translation: I shall now reveal to you that which ought to be known, and by knowing which, one attains immortality. It is the beginningless Brahman, which lies beyond existence and non-existence.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna now explains the object of true knowledge—jñeya—by knowing which one attains immortality. This knowledge does not pertain to material learning, but to the realization of Brahman, the Supreme Reality. Krishna describes Brahman as beginningless, indicating that it is beyond time and causation.

He further states that Brahman transcends the dual categories of existence and non-existence. These terms apply only within the relative material world, where things come into being and are destroyed. Brahman, however, is absolute and eternal, and thus cannot be adequately described by such relative concepts.

In its formless and attributeless aspect, Brahman is worshiped by the jñānīs. In its personal aspect, it is worshiped as Bhagavān by the bhaktas. When residing within the body as the inner witness, it is known as Paramātmā. These are not different realities, but three manifestations of the same Supreme Truth. Shree Krishna later clarifies that He Himself is the foundation of the formless Brahman, establishing the unity between the personal and impersonal aspects of the Divine.
commentary_summary: Krishna reveals Brahman as the ultimate object of knowledge—beginningless, eternal, and beyond existence and non-existence—whose realization leads to immortality.
theme: Revelation of Brahman as the ultimate object of knowledge

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सर्वत: पाणिपादं तत्सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखम् |
सर्वत: श्रुतिमल्लोके सर्वमावृत्य तिष्ठति || 14||
transliteration: sarvataḥ pāṇi-pādaṁ tat sarvato ’kṣhi-śhiro-mukham | sarvataḥ śhrutimal loke sarvam āvṛitya tiṣhṭhati ||
translation: Everywhere are His hands and feet, eyes, heads, and faces. His ears too are in all places, for He pervades everything in the universe.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains the all-pervading nature of the Supreme Being by describing Him as possessing hands, feet, eyes, heads, faces, and ears everywhere. This does not imply a material form like that of living beings, but rather indicates God’s infinite presence and awareness.

Often, people argue that God cannot possess limbs or senses. However, placing such limitations on God arises from a narrow, material understanding. God is omnipotent and unrestricted, capable of manifesting in ways that transcend human logic. His limbs and senses are divine and unlimited, unlike the material and localized senses of humans.

While human senses operate in a single location, God’s senses are omnipresent. Hence, He sees everything, hears every prayer, and witnesses all actions across the universe simultaneously. As stated in the Chhāndogya Upaniṣhad, “sarvaṁ khalvidaṁ brahma” — everything is Brahman. Because of this all-pervasiveness, God accepts offerings made anywhere, hears the prayers of countless devotees at once, and remains the eternal witness of all events in the three worlds.
commentary_summary: Krishna reveals that God’s divine senses and limbs pervade the entire universe, emphasizing His omnipresence, omniscience, and unlimited nature.
theme: Omnipresence and limitless nature of the Supreme Reality

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
सर्वेन्द्रियगुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितम् |
असक्तं सर्वभृच्चैव निर्गुणं गुणभोक्तृ च || 15||
transliteration: sarvendriya-guṇābhāsaṁ sarvendriya-vivarjitam | asaktaṁ sarva-bhṛich chaiva nirguṇaṁ guṇa-bhoktṛi cha ||
translation: Though He perceives all sense-objects, yet He is devoid of the senses. He is unattached to everything, and yet He is the sustainer of all. Although He is without attributes, yet He is the enjoyer of the three modes of material nature.
commentary_full:
After describing God as possessing senses everywhere, Shree Krishna now presents the complementary truth—that God is devoid of senses. To the material intellect, this appears contradictory, but God transcends mundane logic. The Supreme Lord simultaneously possesses innumerable mutually contradictory attributes.

The phrase sarvendriya vivarjitam indicates that God does not possess material senses like living beings. However, sarvendriya-guṇābhāsaṁ signifies that He performs all the functions of the senses and perceives all sense-objects through His divine, all-pervading awareness. Thus, while He lacks material organs, His divine faculties operate everywhere.

This paradox is affirmed in the Śhwetāśhvatar Upaniṣhad, which states that although God has no material hands, feet, eyes, or ears, He grasps, moves, sees, and hears everything. Shree Krishna further explains that God is the sustainer of all creation, maintaining the universe through His expansion as Lord Vishnu, while remaining completely unattached and self-satisfied.

Although God is nirguṇa—beyond the three modes of material nature—He is also the enjoyer of the guṇas because material nature works under His control for His pleasure. The guṇas are material and subordinate, whereas God is divine and eternally transcendental.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that God transcends material senses and qualities, yet perceives, sustains, and enjoys creation through His divine, all-pervading nature.
theme: Transcendence of God beyond material senses and qualities

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
बहिरन्तश्च भूतानामचरं चरमेव च |
सूक्ष्मत्वात्तदविज्ञेयं दूरस्थं चान्तिके च तत् || 16||
transliteration: bahir antaśh cha bhūtānām acharaṁ charam eva cha | sūkṣhmatvāt tad avijñeyaṁ dūra-sthaṁ chāntike cha tat ||
translation: He exists outside and inside all living beings, those that are moving and not moving. He is subtle, and hence, He is incomprehensible. He is very far, but He is also very near.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna describes the Supreme Reality as simultaneously existing both within and outside all living beings, whether moving or non-moving. This emphasizes God’s all-pervading nature, transcending physical boundaries and limitations.

He further states that God is acharaṁ and charam—both immovable and movable—indicating that while God Himself is changeless and eternal, He is also present within the dynamic processes of creation. Due to His extreme subtlety, He cannot be comprehended by the material senses, mind, or intellect.

This apparent paradox is echoed in the Īśhopaniṣhad, which declares that the Supreme does not walk, yet He walks; He is far away, yet He is very near; He is within everything, yet outside everything. Shree Krishna earlier explained that knowing God is true knowledge, but here He clarifies that such knowledge is not attainable through intellectual effort alone.

God is incomprehensible to material perception because the intellect itself is a product of material energy, whereas God is divine. However, when God bestows His grace upon a soul, He becomes knowable through spiritual realization rather than sensory or intellectual means.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that God pervades everything, is both near and far, moving and unmoving, and remains beyond material comprehension due to His divine subtlety.
theme: All-pervasiveness and incomprehensibility of the Supreme Reality

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अविभक्तं च भूतेषु विभक्तमिव च स्थितम् |
भूतभर्तृ च तज्ज्ञेयं ग्रसिष्णु प्रभविष्णु च || 17||
transliteration: avibhaktaṁ cha bhūteṣhu vibhaktam iva cha sthitam | bhūta-bhartṛi cha taj jñeyaṁ grasiṣhṇu prabhaviṣhṇu cha ||
translation: He is indivisible, yet He appears to be divided amongst living beings. Know the Supreme Entity to be the Sustainer, Annihilator, and Creator of all beings.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that although the Supreme Being appears divided among countless living beings and objects, He remains eternally indivisible. All manifest and unmanifest entities are expansions of His energies, and thus nothing exists independently of Him.

Just as space seems divided by the objects it contains yet remains one, and just as the reflection of the sun appears fragmented in multiple bodies of water while the sun itself remains whole, God appears divided without ever losing His unity. This apparent division is a function of perception, not reality.

Because all of creation arises from God, is sustained by Him, and ultimately dissolves back into Him, He is simultaneously the Creator, the Maintainer, and the Annihilator of all beings. Like waves arising from and merging back into the ocean, the universe emanates from God and returns to Him, while He Himself remains unchanged and complete.
commentary_summary: Krishna reveals that God is indivisible yet appears divided in creation, and He alone is the Creator, Sustainer, and Annihilator of all beings.
theme: Unity of the Supreme Reality amidst apparent multiplicity

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ज्योतिषामपि तज्ज्योतिस्तमस: परमुच्यते |
ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं ज्ञानगम्यं हृदि सर्वस्य विष्ठितम् || 18||
transliteration: jyotiṣhām api taj jyotis tamasaḥ param uchyate | jñānaṁ jñeyaṁ jñāna-gamyaṁ hṛidi sarvasya viṣhṭhitam ||
translation: He is the source of light in all luminaries, and is entirely beyond the darkness of ignorance. He is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the goal of knowledge. He dwells within the hearts of all living beings.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna establishes the absolute supremacy of God by describing Him as the source of all illumination. Although there are many luminous objects such as the sun, moon, stars, fire, and jewels, none of them possess independent power to illuminate. Their ability to give light is derived from God alone.

The Kaṭhopaniṣhad affirms that it is by God’s radiance that everything shines, and even the sun and moon borrow their luminosity from Him. While material sources of light may lose their brilliance over time, God’s luminosity is eternal and inexhaustible.

Krishna further explains that God transcends the darkness of ignorance and is Himself knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the ultimate goal of knowledge. Just as He is the source of physical light, He is also the source of spiritual illumination. Residing in the hearts of all living beings as the indwelling witness, He guides them toward realization through true knowledge.
commentary_summary: Krishna reveals God as the eternal source of all light and knowledge, transcending ignorance and residing within the hearts of all beings.
theme: God as the source of light, knowledge, and inner realization

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
इति क्षेत्रं तथा ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं चोक्तं समासत: |
मद्भक्त एतद्विज्ञाय मद्भावायोपपद्यते || 19||
transliteration: iti kṣhetraṁ tathā jñānaṁ jñeyaṁ choktaṁ samāsataḥ | mad-bhakta etad vijñāya mad-bhāvāyopapadyate ||
translation: I have thus revealed to you the nature of the field, the meaning of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. Only My devotees can understand this in reality, and by doing so, they attain My divine nature.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna concludes His exposition on the field (kṣhetra), knowledge (jñāna), and the object of knowledge (jñeya) by revealing the fruit of understanding this wisdom. He emphasizes that true comprehension of this knowledge is not merely intellectual, but devotional in nature.

Krishna declares that only His devotees can truly grasp this teaching. Paths such as karm, jñāna, or aṣhṭāṅg yog, when practiced without bhakti, remain incomplete and cannot lead to genuine realization of God. Bhakti is the essential force that gives life and meaning to all spiritual disciplines.

Devotion not only enables the devotee to know God, but also transforms the devotee by bestowing divine qualities. Hence, Krishna states that His devotees attain His very nature. This truth is repeatedly affirmed across the Vedic scriptures, which declare that bhakti alone leads to God, reveals Him, and places Him within the reach of the loving heart.

The Bhagavad Gita consistently reinforces this message—that loving devotion is the sole means of truly knowing the Supreme. Through bhakti, the soul transcends bondage and enters into divine communion with God, attaining His eternal nature.
commentary_summary: Krishna teaches that true understanding of knowledge arises through devotion, and through bhakti, the devotee attains God’s divine nature.
theme: Devotion as the path to true knowledge and divine realization

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
प्रकृतिं पुरुषं चैव विद्ध्यनादी उभावपि |
विकारांश्च गुणांश्चैव विद्धि प्रकृतिसम्भवान् || 20||
transliteration: prakṛitiṁ puruṣhaṁ chaiva viddhy anādī ubhāv api | vikārānśh cha guṇānśh chaiva viddhi prakṛiti-sambhavān ||
translation: Know that prakṛiti (material nature) and puruṣh (the individual souls) are both beginningless. Also know that all transformations of the body and the three modes of nature are produced by material energy.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that both prakṛiti (material nature) and puruṣh (the individual soul) are beginningless. Material nature, also known as Māyā, is an eternal energy of God and has existed as long as God Himself has existed. Similarly, the soul is eternal and is referred to here as puruṣh, while God is known as Param Puruṣh, the Supreme Living Entity.

The soul is an expansion of God’s jīva-śhakti, or conscious energy, which is sentient, divine, and immutable. Unlike the body, the soul does not undergo transformation and remains unchanged through different lifetimes and the various stages within a single lifetime.

In contrast, all bodily transformations arise from material nature. These include the six stages of bodily change—existence in the womb, birth, growth, reproduction, decline, and death. Material energy also produces the three guṇas—sattva, rajas, and tamas—and their innumerable combinations, which govern all material experiences and changes in the physical world.
commentary_summary: Krishna explains that both material nature and the soul are eternal, while all bodily changes and the three modes of nature arise from prakṛiti.
theme: Eternal nature of the soul and material energy

speaker: Shri Krishna
text_sanskrit:
कार्यकारणकर्तृत्वे हेतु: प्रकृतिरुच्यते |
पुरुष: सुखदु:खानां भोक्तृत्वे हेतुरुच्यते || 21||
transliteration: kārya-kāraṇa-kartṛitve hetuḥ prakṛitir uchyate | puruṣhaḥ sukha-duḥkhānāṁ bhoktṛitve hetur uchyate ||
translation: In the matter of creation, the material energy is responsible for cause and effect; in the matter of experiencing happiness and distress, the individual soul is declared responsible.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains the distinct roles of material nature and the soul. Material energy (prakṛiti), under divine direction, is responsible for all creation, including the vast variety of bodies and life forms. The Vedas describe 8.4 million species, all of which are transformations of prakṛiti. Thus, material nature governs cause-and-effect relationships in the physical world.

The soul, however, becomes responsible for experiencing happiness and distress because it identifies itself with the body, mind, and intellect obtained through past karmas. When the senses interact with sense objects, pleasurable or painful sensations arise in the mind. Since the soul associates with the mind, it experiences these sensations indirectly.

This condition is compared to a dream state: although the experiences are illusory, they feel real until one awakens. Similarly, due to identification with the material body, the soul undergoes pleasure and pain according to its karmic actions, and is therefore said to be responsible for its experiences.
commentary_summary: Material nature creates bodies and governs cause and effect, while the soul is responsible for experiencing pleasure and pain due to its identification with the body.
theme: Division of responsibility between material nature and the soul

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
य एवं वेत्ति पुरुषं प्रकृतिं च गुणै: सह |
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि न स भूयोऽभिजायते || 24||
transliteration: ya evaṁ vetti puruṣhaṁ prakṛitiṁ cha guṇaiḥ saha | sarvathā vartamāno ’pi na sa bhūyo ’bhijāyate ||
translation: Those who understand the truth about the Supreme Soul, the individual soul, material nature, and the interaction of the three modes of nature will not take birth here again. They will be liberated regardless of their present condition.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that ignorance is the root cause of the soul’s bondage in the material world. Forgetting its spiritual identity as a fragment of God, the soul becomes absorbed in material consciousness and repeatedly takes birth. True knowledge dispels this ignorance and leads to liberation.

The Śhwetāśhvatar Upaniṣhad describes three eternal realities: material nature, which is ever-changing; the individual souls, which are unchangeable; and the Supreme Lord, who governs both. Ignorance of these truths binds the soul, while proper understanding frees it from the chains of Maya.

The knowledge spoken of here is not mere intellectual learning, but realized wisdom. Such realization begins with receiving authentic knowledge from the Guru and the scriptures and is perfected through sincere spiritual practice. One who truly understands the distinction and relationship between puruṣh, prakṛiti, and the guṇas transcends material entanglement and is no longer forced to take birth, irrespective of their current external circumstances.
commentary_summary: Realized knowledge of the soul, material nature, and the Supreme Lord frees a person from ignorance and bondage, leading to liberation and freedom from rebirth.
theme: Liberation through realized knowledge of reality

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
ध्यानेनात्मनि पश्यन्ति केचिदात्मानमात्मना |
अन्ये साङ् ख्येन योगेन कर्मयोगेन चापरे || 25||
transliteration: dhyānenātmani paśhyanti kechid ātmānam ātmanā | anye sānkhyena yogena karma-yogena chāpare ||
translation: Some try to perceive the Supreme Soul within their hearts through meditation, and others try to do so through the cultivation of knowledge, while still others strive to attain that realization by the path of action.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that different aspirants have different inclinations toward spiritual practice. Some find joy in meditation, focusing their minds to perceive God seated within their hearts. Others are drawn to intellectual inquiry and cultivate knowledge about the soul, God, and material nature, engaging in hearing, contemplation, and deep reflection. Yet others seek realization through selfless action, using their abilities in service to God. 

The Gita emphasizes that the diversity of spiritual paths accommodates the varied nature of human beings. True fulfillment in any of these paths arises when they are combined with devotion to God, aligning meditation, knowledge, or action toward the pleasure of the Supreme. The Shreemad Bhagavatam reinforces this: “True knowledge is that which helps us develop love for God. The fulfillment of karma occurs when it is done for the pleasure of the Lord.”
commentary_summary: Different souls have unique inclinations; some attain God through meditation, some through knowledge, and others through action. True realization requires devotion to the Supreme.
theme: Multiple paths to realizing the Supreme, aligned with devotion

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अन्ये त्वेवमजानन्त: श्रुत्वान्येभ्य उपासते |
तेऽपि चातितरन्त्येव मृत्युं श्रुतिपरायणा: || 26||
transliteration: anye tv evam ajānantaḥ śhrutvānyebhya upāsate | te ’pi chātitaranty eva mṛityuṁ śhruti-parāyaṇāḥ ||
translation: There are still others who are unaware of these spiritual paths, but they hear from others and begin worshipping the Supreme Lord. By such devotion to hearing from saints, they too can gradually cross over the ocean of birth and death.
commentary_full: Some people, initially unaware of spiritual practices, come to hear about God from others. Upon hearing, they develop interest and begin devotional practices, gradually progressing toward liberation. In the Vedic tradition, śravaṇa (hearing from saints) is highly emphasized as a potent means for purification and spiritual elevation. The Shreemad Bhagavatam explains that simply hearing about the divine Names, Forms, Pastimes, and virtues from saints cleanses the heart of accumulated impurities. Hearing not only imparts knowledge but also conveys the faith and enthusiasm of the saint, which motivates aspirants to overcome material inertia and advance on the path of devotion. Thus, devotion through hearing (śruti-parāyaṇā) can lead even the initially ignorant toward liberation.
commentary_summary: Even those unaware of spiritual methods can attain liberation by hearing about God from saints, as this cultivates devotion, faith, and enthusiasm for spiritual practice.
theme: The power of hearing from saints as a path to spiritual liberation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यावत्सञ्जायते किञ्चित्सत्वं स्थावरजङ्गमम् |
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञसंयोगात्तद्विद्धि भरतर्षभ || 27||
transliteration: yāvat sañjāyate kiñchit sattvaṁ sthāvara-jaṅgamam | kṣhetra-kṣhetrajña-sanyogāt tad viddhi bharatarṣhabha ||
translation: O best of the Bharatas, whatever moving or unmoving being you see in existence, know it to be a combination of the field of activities and the knower of the field.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna explains that all beings, moving or unmoving, are composed of two fundamental aspects: the kṣhetra (field of activities, i.e., the body and mind) and the kṣhetrajña (the conscious soul that knows and experiences the field). The phrase yāvat kiñchit emphasizes that this applies to every living entity, no matter how small or large. This underscores the universality of consciousness; wherever there is life, there is the presence of the soul. 

Vedic philosophy teaches that the presence of consciousness in all forms of life, including plants and lower animals, indicates the presence of a soul. Experiments by scientists like Sir J.C. Bose in the 20th century supported this idea, showing that plants respond to stimuli and even exhibit emotional-like responses. Krishna’s teaching here highlights that all life is a combination of material energy (the field) and the conscious soul (the knower), stressing respect for all forms of life and the inherent presence of consciousness everywhere.
commentary_summary: All living beings, whether moving or stationary, are a combination of body/mind and the conscious soul. Consciousness exists universally in all life forms, emphasizing respect for all entities.
theme: Universality of consciousness in all living beings

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
समं सर्वेषु भूतेषु तिष्ठन्तं परमेश्वरम् |
विनश्यत्स्वविनश्यन्तं य: पश्यति स पश्यति || 28||
transliteration: samaṁ sarveṣhu bhūteṣhu tiṣhṭhantaṁ parameśhvaram | vinaśhyatsv avinaśhyantaṁ yaḥ paśhyati sa paśhyati ||
translation: They alone truly see, who perceive the Paramātmā (Supreme Soul) accompanying the soul in all beings, and who understand both to be imperishable in this perishable body.
commentary_full:
Shree Krishna emphasizes that true vision is not limited to perceiving the individual soul in the body. One must also recognize the presence of the Supreme Soul, the Paramātmā, within all living beings. This Supreme Soul is imperishable, eternal, and omnipresent, accompanying each individual soul through its journey across lifetimes. By understanding both the soul and God as imperishable amidst the perishable material body, a seeker attains spiritual insight. Vedic texts reinforce this concept: 

- Śhwetāśhvatar Upaniṣhad: “God is one, resides in all hearts, omnipresent, and the Supreme Soul of all souls.”
- Bhagavatam: “God is seated inside all beings as the Witness and Master.”
- Ramayan: “The Supreme Lord is eternal, beyond everything, and resides in the hearts of all living entities.”

This realization transforms the seeker’s perception, fostering reverence for all life and understanding of the eternal divine presence within everything.
commentary_summary: True vision is seeing the Supreme Soul within all beings and recognizing the imperishable nature of both the soul and God within the perishable body, fostering reverence for all life.
theme: Recognizing the Supreme Soul within all beings and the imperishable nature of soul and God

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
समं पश्यन्हि सर्वत्र समवस्थितमीश्वरम् |
न हिनस्त्यात्मनात्मानं ततो याति परां गतिम् || 29||
transliteration: samaṁ paśhyan hi sarvatra samavasthitam īśhvaram | na hinasty ātmanātmānaṁ tato yāti parāṁ gatim ||
translation: Those, who see God as the Supreme Soul equally present everywhere and in all living beings, do not degrade themselves by their mind. Thereby, they reach the supreme destination.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna emphasizes that the mind, by nature inclined toward seeking pleasures, can lead the soul into material degradation. To avoid this, one must cultivate the intellect with true knowledge. When a seeker sees God as the Supreme Soul equally present in all beings, they live in accordance with this understanding. They no longer seek personal gain or pleasure from relationships and do not harbor attachment or hatred based on others’ actions. By perceiving God in all, human-made distinctions such as nationality, caste, creed, sex, status, or color become irrelevant. This vision elevates the mind, prevents self-degradation, and leads the seeker to the supreme destination, uniting them with the eternal and imperishable.
commentary_summary: Seeing God as equally present in all beings prevents mental degradation and attachments, guiding one to the supreme goal.
theme: Recognizing God in all beings to attain supreme realization and mental elevation

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
प्रकृत्यैव च कर्माणि क्रियमाणानि सर्वश: |
य: पश्यति तथात्मानमकर्तारं स पश्यति || 30||
transliteration: prakṛityaiva cha karmāṇi kriyamāṇāni sarvaśhaḥ | yaḥ paśhyati tathātmānam akartāraṁ sa paśhyati ||
translation: They alone truly see who understand that all actions (of the body) are performed by material nature, while the embodied soul actually does nothing.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna clarifies that the ego, by identifying with the body and mind, traps the soul in the cycle of life and death. Material consciousness attributes all actions to the soul, leading one to think 'I am the doer.' The enlightened soul, however, perceives that while the body, mind, and intellect perform actions like eating, speaking, or walking, the soul itself remains actionless. Yet, it remains responsible for the results of these actions, much like a leader is responsible for the decisions of a country even without direct involvement in the acts. Spiritual aspirants are taught to act externally as if responsible for results, but internally remain aware of their true nature as the non-doer.
commentary_summary: True vision is seeing that the embodied soul does not act; all bodily actions are performed by material nature, though the soul remains responsible.
theme: Understanding the soul as the actionless witness while material nature performs all actions

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यदा भूतपृथग्भावमेकस्थमनुपश्यति |
तत एव च विस्तारं ब्रह्म सम्पद्यते तदा || 31||
transliteration: yada bhuta-prithag-bhavam eka-stham anupashyati | tata eva cha vistāram brahma sampadyate tada ||
translation: When they see the diverse variety of living beings situated in the same material nature, and understand all of them to be born from it, they attain the realization of the Brahman.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna illustrates that just as the ocean manifests as waves, froth, tides, and ripples, yet remains one ocean, so too all living beings, from the tiniest to the mightiest, are rooted in the same material nature and the same spiritual essence. The apparent distinctions are due to different bodies created by material energy, not the soul itself. Recognizing that all diversity arises from the same underlying reality—the material energy and the soul within—leads one to understand the unity behind the multiplicity. Such realization of the inherent oneness of creation is the direct perception of Brahman.
commentary_summary: Understanding the unity behind the diversity of all beings in material nature leads to the realization of Brahman.
theme: Seeing all beings as rooted in the same material nature to attain Brahman realization

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
अनादित्वान्निर्गुणत्वात्परमात्मायमव्यय: |
शरीरस्थोऽपि कौन्तेय न करोति न लिप्यते || 32||
transliteration: anāditvān nirguṇatvāt paramātmāyam avyayaḥ | śharīra-stho ’pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate ||
translation: The Supreme Soul is imperishable, without beginning, and devoid of any material qualities, O son of Kunti. Although situated within the body, It neither acts, nor is It tainted by material energy.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna explains that the Supreme Soul (Paramātmā) resides in the heart of every living being but never identifies with the body or mind. Being imperishable and without beginning, the Supreme Soul transcends all material qualities (guṇas). Although present within the physical frame, It remains untouched by karma, actions, or the cycles of birth and death, unlike the embodied soul (jīvātmā). The Supreme Soul is the eternal witness and the ultimate knower, remaining pure and unaffected by material nature.
commentary_summary: The Supreme Soul, though residing in the body, is imperishable, beginningless, free from material qualities, and untouched by actions or karma.
theme: Understanding the imperishable and unaffected nature of the Supreme Soul within the body

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यथा सर्वगतं सौक्ष्म्यादाकाशं नोपलिप्यते |
सर्वत्रावस्थितो देहे तथात्मा नोपलिप्यते || 33||
transliteration: yathā sarva-gataṁ saukṣhmyād ākāśhaṁ nopalipyate | sarvatrāvasthito dehe tathātmā nopalipyate ||
translation: Space holds everything within it, but being subtle, does not get contaminated by what it holds. Similarly, though its consciousness pervades the body, the soul is not affected by the attributes of the body.
commentary_full: Shree Krishna explains that just as space contains all objects but remains uncontaminated due to its subtlety, the soul pervades the body but is never tainted by the body’s material attributes. The soul may appear to experience sleep, fatigue, or pleasure, but these are effects of the body-mind complex, not of the soul itself. Its subtle and divine nature keeps it pure, untouched by the temporary changes and activities of the physical frame.
commentary_summary: The soul, subtler than the body, pervades it but remains pure and unaffected, just as space contains everything yet remains uncontaminated.
theme: The soul’s purity and transcendence despite pervading the material body

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
यथा प्रकाशयत्येक: कृत्स्नं लोकमिमं रवि: |
क्षेत्रं क्षेत्री तथा कृत्स्नं प्रकाशयति भारत || 34||
transliteration: yathā prakāśhayaty ekaḥ kṛitsnaṁ lokam imaṁ raviḥ | kṣhetraṁ kṣhetrī tathā kṛitsnaṁ prakāśhayati bhārata ||
translation: Just as one sun illumines the entire solar system, so does the individual soul illumine the entire body (with consciousness).
commentary_full: Although the soul is exceedingly small, it energizes the entire body with consciousness. The Muṇḍakopaniṣhad describes the soul as extremely tiny (eṣho ’ṇurātmā), while the Śhwetāśhvatar Upaniṣhad explains that dividing the tip of a hair into hundreds of parts repeatedly approximates the size of the soul. Despite its minuteness, the soul illuminates the body just as the sun, situated in one place, illumines the entire solar system. The Vedānt Darśhan states that the soul, seated in the heart, spreads its consciousness throughout the field of the body (guṇādvā lokavat).
commentary_summary: The tiny soul energizes and illumines the entire body with consciousness, just as the sun illuminates the entire solar system.
theme: The soul’s subtle yet pervasive illumination of the body

speaker: Shree Krishna
text_sanskrit:
क्षेत्रक्षेत्रज्ञयोरेवमन्तरं ज्ञानचक्षुषा |
भूतप्रकृतिमोक्षं च ये विदुर्यान्ति ते परम् || 35||
