The sarga serves as a peaceful interlude of familial bliss before the storm that is about to arrive through Manthara.
commentary_summary: Rama bids farewell to his joyful mother Kausalya and informs Sita of the coronation, as both begin fasting in prayerful preparation for the next dawn.
theme: Domestic dharma and prayerful preparation on the eve of a great auspicious event

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
ज्ञातिदासी यतो जाता कैकेय्या तु सहोषिता |
प्रासादं चन्द्रसङ्काशमारुरोह यदृच्छया || २-७-१
transliteration:
jñātidāsī yato jātā kaikeyyā tu sahoṣitā |
prāsādaṃ candrasaṅkāśam āruroha yadṛcchayā || 2-7-1
translation: Manthara, a housemaid who had resided with Kaikeyi since birth, by chance ascended the balcony of Kaikeyi's white moon-like palace.
commentary_full: This sarga introduces the dark turn of the Ayodhya Kanda. Manthara, the hunchbacked maid of Kaikeyi, ascends the palace roof and sees the city of Ayodhya brilliantly lit and decorated for Rama's coronation. She descends and finds Kaikeyi sleeping peacefully. Manthara, driven by ill will and jealousy on Kaikeyi's behalf (though Kaikeyi herself has no ill feelings toward Rama at this point), begins to poison the queen's mind. She tells Kaikeyi that Rama's coronation spells ruin for her and Bharata. Kaikeyi initially defends Rama and refuses to see any cause for worry, even offering Manthara a jewel as a reward for what she wrongly supposes is 'good news.' But Manthara persists, describing in vivid terms how Kaikeyi's influence would wane under Rama's rule and how Bharata would become a servant. The seeds of discord are sown.
commentary_summary: Manthara, the scheming maidservant, first sees Ayodhya's coronation preparations and then begins to poison Kaikeyi's mind against Rama's coronation.
theme: The entry of envy and scheming as destroyers of a perfect moment

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
सा मन्थरा दुर्मतिः पापदर्शिनी |
कैकेयीं शयनीयगतां इदं अब्रवीत् || २-८-१
transliteration:
sā mantharā durmatir pāpadarśinī |
kaikeyīṃ śayanīyagatāṃ idaṃ abravīt || 2-8-1
translation: That Manthara, of wicked mind and sinful vision, approached Kaikeyi who was resting on her bed and spoke these words.
commentary_full: Manthara intensifies her manipulation of Kaikeyi in this sarga. She elaborates on the supposed dangers to Kaikeyi's position: once Rama is king, Kaikeyi would be reduced to a servant of Kausalya; Bharata, sent away to his maternal uncle's home, would be politically marginalized; and the entire kingdom would be consolidated under Rama and Kausalya's control. She advises Kaikeyi to invoke the two boons that Dasaratha had granted her long ago — when she had saved his life in the battle of the gods and demons. Kaikeyi, gradually swayed, asks Manthara to explain how she should use these boons. Manthara prescribes a specific plan: use one boon to send Rama to the forest for fourteen years, and the second to install Bharata as crown prince instead. By the end of this sarga, Kaikeyi is fully convinced of Manthara's plan and sets off to the kopa-griha (chamber of anger) to force Dasaratha's hand.
commentary_summary: Manthara convinces Kaikeyi to use her two old boons to exile Rama for fourteen years and crown Bharata instead, sending Kaikeyi to the chamber of anger.
theme: How manipulation and greed transform a good queen into an instrument of destruction

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
सा विहाय शयनं राज्ञो भूमौ पतितमूर्धजा |
कैकेयी दुःखसंतप्ता तस्थौ विगतभूषणा || २-९-१
transliteration:
sā vihāya śayanaṃ rājño bhūmau patitamūrdhajā |
kaikeyī duḥkhasaṃtaptā tasthau vigatabhūṣaṇā || 2-9-1
translation: Kaikeyi, tormented with grief, abandoned her royal bed, her hair disheveled and ornaments cast aside, and lay on the bare floor.
commentary_full: Kaikeyi enters the kopa-griha (the chamber of wrath, a traditional queen's space for expressing grievance), casts off her royal ornaments and fine garments, and lies on the floor with disheveled hair, mimicking the posture of deep distress and anger. Dasaratha, completing his evening rounds, goes to Kaikeyi's apartments expecting his usual pleasant reception from his most beloved queen. Instead, he finds her apartments empty and servants pointing him toward the kopa-griha. The king is deeply alarmed. He enters the chamber of wrath and sees Kaikeyi lying on the floor like a fallen apsara, her beauty dimmed by her affected grief. He tries to comfort her with tender words, asking what has caused her sorrow and promising to fulfill any wish she desires. This sarga is a pivotal psychological portrait — Kaikeyi's performance of grief as a weapon of manipulation against a loving but weak husband.
commentary_summary: Kaikeyi enters the chamber of anger, lying disheveled on the floor, and Dasaratha — alarmed and desperate — promises to fulfill whatever wish she desires.
theme: Love as vulnerability — how Dasaratha's blind love for Kaikeyi becomes his fatal weakness

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
ततः कैकेयी प्रसन्नमुखी कृताञ्जलिः |
वरं ययाचे दशरथं तं च राजानमब्रवीत् || २-१०-१
transliteration:
tataḥ kaikeyī prasannamukhī kṛtāñjaliḥ |
varaṃ yayāce daśarathaṃ taṃ ca rājānam abravīt || 2-10-1
translation: Then Kaikeyi, with a brightened face and joined palms, formally made her demands, asking Dasaratha for her two boons.
commentary_full: Having extracted Dasaratha's promise to grant her two boons (ratified by repeated oaths on Rama's name, his life, and all he holds dear), Kaikeyi now formally presents her demands. The first boon: let Bharata be anointed as Yuvaraja. The second boon: let Rama be sent to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, wearing bark-cloth and matted hair like an ascetic. Dasaratha is utterly shattered. He first pleads, then begs, then swoons. He appeals to her conscience, reminding her of Rama's goodness and their happy life together. He offers her anything else — wealth, kingdoms, other sons' exile — anything but this. But Kaikeyi is unmovable. The sarga captures Dasaratha's psychological collapse — the king who could defeat armies in battle is helpless before a woman's calculated cruelty, trapped by his own words and love.
commentary_summary: Kaikeyi demands her two boons: Bharata's coronation and Rama's fourteen-year exile to the forest — and Dasaratha collapses in utter devastation.
theme: The moment dharma is struck down by personal desire and broken oaths

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
रजनीं तां महाराजः शोकोपहतचेतनः |
स्तम्भयित्वा महाबाहुर्विलपन् समनुस्मरन् || २-११-१
transliteration:
rajanīṃ tāṃ mahārājaḥ śokopahatacelanaḥ |
stambhayitvā mahābāhur vilapan samanusmaran || 2-11-1
translation: The great king, his mind paralyzed with grief, spent that night in lamentation, helplessly remembering his beloved Rama.
commentary_full: Dasaratha spends a night of unspeakable anguish, prostrated by grief, swinging between pleading with Kaikeyi and lamenting his own helplessness. He curses the moment he gave her the boons. He recalls the incident from his past — how he had accidentally killed the young ascetic Shravana Kumar with a misdirected arrow in the dark, and how the blind parents of that boy had cursed him: 'You too, O king, shall die in grief for your son.' Dasaratha recognizes that the curse is now coming to fruition. This sarga introduces the concept of karma and the irreversibility of past deeds — even for a king who has lived righteously, past actions must yield their consequences. The sarga is a meditation on the helplessness of even the most powerful before the law of karma.
commentary_summary: Dasaratha spends a grief-stricken night and recalls the curse of Shravana Kumar's blind parents — foreseeing it is now coming to fulfillment.
theme: The ripening of past karma — even a righteous king cannot escape the consequences of his actions

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
रात्रौ तस्यां व्यतीतायां प्रभातायां च शर्वर्याम् |
वसिष्ठः प्रययावाशु राजद्वारमुपस्थितम् || २-१२-१
transliteration:
rātrau tasyāṃ vyatītāyāṃ prabhātāyāṃ ca śarvaryām |
vasiṣṭhaḥ prayayāvāśu rājadvāram upasthitam || 2-12-1
translation: When that night had passed and dawn arrived, Vasishtha swiftly made his way to the king's doorway.
commentary_full: Dawn arrives — the auspicious day of Pushyami, designated for Rama's coronation. Sage Vasishtha and the other priests arrive at the palace, ready to perform the sacred rites. The city of Ayodhya is dressed in festive splendor. But inside the palace, the situation is catastrophically different. Vasishtha tries to gain access to the king and is told that Dasaratha is indisposed. Kaikeyi, fully in command now, comes forward. The contrast between the festival-ready city outside and the grief within the palace walls is heartbreaking. Vasishtha is eventually led to Kaikeyi, who discloses the situation. This sarga depicts the terrible disjunction between the world's innocent joy and the hidden tragedy unfolding within the palace — a classic device of the epic, amplifying tragedy through contrast.
commentary_summary: Dawn of the coronation day arrives with Ayodhya in festive splendor, but Vasishtha finds the palace plunged in hidden grief — Kaikeyi reveals what has transpired.
theme: The cruel contrast between public festivity and private catastrophe

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
स राममानय्य तु भार्गवेण |
उवाच वाक्यं मधुरं महात्मा |
तातेति सम्बोध्य महानुभावः || २-१३-१
transliteration:
sa rāmam ānāyya tu bhārgaveṇa |
uvāca vākyaṃ madhuraṃ mahātmā |
tāteti sambodhya mahānubhāvaḥ || 2-13-1
translation: Summoning Rama through a messenger, the great-souled Vasishtha addressed him affectionately with the word 'Tata' (dear son).
commentary_full: Vasishtha summons Rama, who has spent the night in fasting and prayer and arrives fresh and composed for the expected coronation. Vasishtha's heart is heavy, but he keeps his composure. However, it is Kaikeyi who takes over the proceedings. In this sarga, Kaikeyi herself delivers the devastating news to Rama directly — with no softening, no remorse, and no hesitation. She presents the demands as if they are entirely normal: Dasaratha has given her two boons, and she has asked for Bharata's coronation and Rama's exile. She tells Rama bluntly to go to the forest in bark clothes and matted hair for fourteen years. Rama's response is the soul of this sarga — completely unshaken, without a shadow of anger, resentment, or regret. He accepts the news with perfect equanimity, almost with joy, saying his only concern is that his father has not spoken to him directly.
commentary_summary: Kaikeyi delivers the devastating news directly to Rama — exile for fourteen years and Bharata's coronation — and Rama accepts it with complete, serene equanimity.
theme: Rama's supreme equanimity as the embodiment of dharmic acceptance

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
तमुवाच ततः कैकेयी प्राञ्जलिं स्थितमग्रतः |
रामं सूर्योपमं देवी भर्तुः प्रियहितैषिणी || २-१४-१
transliteration:
tam uvāca tataḥ kaikeyī prāñjaliṃ sthitam agrataḥ |
rāmaṃ sūryopamaṃ devī bhartuḥ priyahitaiṣiṇī || 2-14-1
translation: Then Kaikeyi, claiming to be acting in her husband's interests, spoke to Rama who stood before her with joined palms — Rama who was as radiant as the sun.
commentary_full: This sarga depicts Kaikeyi formally explaining to Rama the terms of the two boons and instructing him to immediately remove his royal robes and ornaments and put on bark-cloth and matted locks. She also reveals that Dasaratha is too grief-stricken to speak directly to him. Rama's response is again extraordinary: he does not need his father to speak to him. A father's wish, however conveyed, is a command. He immediately sends for Sita, and before that, he expresses only one desire — to visit his mother Kausalya and bid her farewell. Kaikeyi, wary of any delay, urges haste. Lakshmana, who has been present throughout, is consumed with rage. He rails against Kaikeyi's injustice and offers to kill anyone who opposes Rama. But Rama calms him with gentle words, explaining that he gladly accepts the forest and asks only for their mother's forbearance.
commentary_summary: Kaikeyi demands Rama immediately change into bark-cloth; Rama calmly complies, asking only to bid farewell to his mother, while Lakshmana seethes with righteous fury.
theme: Dharma over ego — Rama's willing acceptance versus Lakshmana's righteous indignation

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
कौसल्यायास्तु भवनं राघवः प्राविशत् तदा |
मातरमभिवाद्याशु विलपन्तीमकारयत् || २-१५-१
transliteration:
kausalyāyāstu bhavanaṃ rāghavaḥ prāviśat tadā |
mātaram abhivādyāśu vilapantīm akārayat || 2-15-1
translation: Rama entered Kausalya's apartments, quickly paid his obeisance to his mother who was lamenting bitterly, and stood before her.
commentary_full: Rama enters Kausalya's apartments to bid her farewell before departing for the forest. Kausalya had been performing rituals and prayers for his coronation when she heard the terrible news. She is shattered. She laments bitterly, asking how the gods could allow such injustice, how a good woman like herself could suffer such a fate. She expresses anguish at being surpassed by Kaikeyi in the king's affections, at spending years of faithful devotion only to have them come to nothing. She also asks Rama to take her with him to the forest. Rama gently but firmly explains that his duty is to obey his father and that her duty is to remain and serve Dasaratha during his sorrow. He consoles her with philosophical insights — that all sorrow passes, that time is the healer, and that he will return after fourteen years. The sarga is a deeply emotional portrayal of a mother's helpless grief.
commentary_summary: Rama visits Kausalya to bid farewell before exile; she is devastated, implores him to take her along, but Rama gently explains her duty is to remain and serve Dasaratha.
theme: A mother's heartbreak and a son's steadfast adherence to dharma

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
सीतापि तु तदा श्रुत्वा भर्तुः प्रस्थानमुत्तमम् |
आनन्देन महाभागा समाविष्टा मनस्विनी || २-१६-१
transliteration:
sītāpi tu tadā śrutvā bhartuḥ prasthānam uttamam |
ānandena mahābhāgā samāviṣṭā manasvinī || 2-16-1
translation: Sita, the noble and devoted wife, hearing of her husband's departure for the forest, was filled with a strange sense of joy — for she would go wherever he went.
commentary_full: Rama goes to Sita to break the news of his exile and to instruct her to remain safely in the palace during his absence. However, Sita's response is the very definition of a devoted wife in the Vedic tradition. Far from being frightened or resentful, she responds with quiet joy — because her place is always at her husband's side. She recites the classical teaching that a wife's dharma is to be with her husband and that a forest with Rama is sweeter than a palace without him. She firmly states that she will accompany him into exile. Rama tries to dissuade her, describing the terrors of the forest: wild animals, poisonous plants, extreme temperatures, hardships of forest life. But Sita counters each argument with wisdom and devotion. Her speech in this sarga is one of the most celebrated portraits of pativrata (wifely) dharma in all of Sanskrit literature.
commentary_summary: Sita insists on accompanying Rama into exile, declaring that a wife's place is always at her husband's side — a celebrated portrait of devoted dharma.
theme: Sita's unshakeable devotion — the forest with Rama is heaven, the palace without him is exile

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
लक्ष्मणस्तु तदा श्रुत्वा रामस्य गमनं वनम् |
भ्रातुः प्रियहिते युक्तः सम्मतं दर्शयत् सुहृत् || २-१७-१
transliteration:
lakṣmaṇastu tadā śrutvā rāmasya gamanaṃ vanam |
bhrātuḥ priyahite yuktaḥ sammataṃ darśayat suhṛt || 2-17-1
translation: Lakshmana, hearing of Rama's departure for the forest and being devoted to his brother's happiness, expressed his own wish to accompany him.
commentary_full: Lakshmana, who has been burning with rage since Kaikeyi's demands, now approaches Rama and formally seeks his permission to accompany him into exile. He argues passionately and at length. He says Rama's going to the forest is an act of injustice, and that righteousness demands he disobey a command given under coercion. He offers to fight all who oppose Rama and to seize the kingdom by force. But Rama, with characteristic patience, corrects him: the king's command, even if influenced by a woman, is legitimate and must be obeyed. The son who obeys his father attains the highest merit. Rama then grants Lakshmana permission to accompany him, recognizing both the depth of his brother's devotion and the practical reality that Sita will need protection. Lakshmana immediately begins preparations — gathering weapons, bows, and provisions for the forest journey.
commentary_summary: Lakshmana passionately demands to accompany Rama, arguing against the injustice; Rama gently corrects him and finally grants him permission to join the forest exile.
theme: Brotherhood as dharma — Lakshmana's inseparable bond with Rama

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
स दद‍र्श आसने रामः निषण्णं पितरं शुभे |
कैकेय्या सहितं दीनं मुखेन परिशुष्यता || २-१८-१
transliteration:
sa dadarśa āsane rāmaḥ niṣaṇṇaṃ pitaraṃ śubhe |
kaikeyā sahitaṃ dīnaṃ mukhena pariśuṣyatā || 2-18-1
translation: Rama saw his father seated on his royal throne beside Kaikeyi — his face completely parched, his spirit utterly miserable.
commentary_full: Rama goes to take formal leave of his father before departing. He finds Dasaratha in a catastrophic state — collapsed in grief, barely able to speak, able only to whisper 'Rama!' before dissolving in tears. Kaikeyi, cold and composed, is seated beside him. She fills the gap the speechless king cannot fill, bluntly stating her demands one more time — that Rama go to the forest in bark-cloth. Rama, completely composed, accepts everything and formally pays his respects to his father and to Kaikeyi with equal reverence — addressing even the woman who has wronged him with the respect due to a mother. This is perhaps the most emotionally devastating scene in the sarga: the sight of a great king unmanned by grief, a scheming queen unmoved by compassion, and a perfect son maintaining his dignity through it all. Dasaratha, unable to even look at Rama, is the image of a man destroyed by his own weakness.
commentary_summary: Rama comes to take formal leave, finds his father collapsed in grief and speechless; Kaikeyi coldly repeats her demands, and Rama accepts all with perfect composure.
theme: The perfect son — Rama's unshakeable dignity in the face of unbearable injustice

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
तदप्रियमरित्रघ्नः वचनं मरणोपमम् |
श्रुत्वा न विव्यथे रामः कैकेयीं चेदमब्रवीत् || २-१९-१
transliteration:
tad apriyam amitraghnaḥ vacanaṃ maraṇopamam |
śrutvā na vivyathe rāmaḥ kaikeyīṃ cedam abravīt || 2-19-1
translation: Rama, the annihilator of enemies, hearing those harsh words deadly as a death sentence, was unruffled, and spoke these words to Kaikeyi.
commentary_full: Rama formally accepts the exile from Kaikeyi herself. He asks only one poignant question: 'Why has my father not spoken to me directly? A father's command needs no intermediary.' He expresses no anger, no bitterness, no sense of injustice. His only stated concern is for his father's grief, which he tries to minimize by immediately announcing his readiness to leave today itself. He asks Kaikeyi to ensure that his mother Kausalya is treated well and that Bharata conducts himself virtuously as king. He also requests that messengers be sent to Bharata immediately. Throughout, Rama's speech is measured, compassionate, and entirely devoid of self-pity. Kaikeyi, hearing Rama's willing acceptance, is delighted and urges him to depart without delay. This sarga is one of the finest portraits of dharmic acceptance in world literature.
commentary_summary: Rama accepts exile with perfect grace, asks only why his father couldn't speak to him directly, expresses only concern for others' welfare, and prepares to leave at once.
theme: The highest dharma — accepting injustice gracefully for the sake of a father's word

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
रामस्तु भृशमायस्तो निह्श्वसन्निव कुञ्जरः |
जगाम सहितो भ्रात्रा मातुरन्तःपुरं वशी || २-२०-८
transliteration:
rāmastu bhṛśam āyasto niḥśvasan iva kuñjaraḥ |
jagāma sahito bhrātrā mātur antaḥpuraṃ vaśī || 2-20-8
translation: Rama, greatly burdened, sighing like a great elephant, subdued his senses and went with Lakshmana to his mother's palace.
commentary_full: This sarga portrays the emotional whirlwind that sweeps through the palace when the news of Rama's exile begins to spread. Kausalya and the other queens weep loudly. The king's consorts, like cows who have lost their calves, lament and curse Kaikeyi. Dasaratha, hearing the terrible sounds of grief from the women's quarters, clings to his seat, overcome by grief for his son. Rama, though himself burdened as a great elephant, subdues his own sorrow and goes to bid farewell to Kausalya with Lakshmana. The city of Ayodhya, which was decorated with festive joy only the night before, is now plunged into a grief so deep it resembles the darkness after the sun has set. The contrast is complete and devastating. This sarga begins the great lamentation that will characterize much of the early Ayodhya Kanda.
commentary_summary: News of Rama's exile spreads through the palace — the queens weep, Dasaratha collapses in grief, and Ayodhya's festive joy turns to inconsolable sorrow.
theme: A city's joy instantly transformed into grief — the ripple effects of one woman's greed

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
कौसल्या तु सुदुःखार्ता पुत्रशोकेन मोहिता |
रामं परिष्वज्य बाष्पकण्ठी रुरोद ह || २-२१-१
transliteration:
kausalyā tu suduḥkhārtā putraśokena mohitā |
rāmaṃ pariṣvajya bāṣpakaṇṭhī ruroda ha || 2-21-1
translation: Kausalya, overwhelmed with immense grief and bewildered by sorrow for her son, embraced Rama and wept with a tear-choked voice.
commentary_full: This sarga is dominated by Kausalya's heartbreaking lamentation. She embraces Rama, weeping bitterly, and asks how she is supposed to bear fourteen years of separation from him. She expresses her desolate situation: her husband is enslaved by Kaikeyi's will, she herself has no power, and now her son — her only support — is going away. She recounts all her prayers, fasts, and devotions over the years, which seemed to have counted for nothing. She blames herself, wondering what sin she committed in a past life to deserve this fate. Rama, with great tenderness, reminds her of her dharma as a queen — she must remain and serve the king during his period of grief. He promises that fourteen years will pass quickly and he will return. He takes formal leave, circumambulating her, and the image of him leaving while she stands watching is one of the most emotionally devastating moments in the epic.
commentary_summary: Kausalya's lamentation — embracing Rama in tears, questioning the cruelty of fate — is followed by Rama's gentle reminder of her dharmic duty to remain and serve the king.
theme: A mother's helpless grief and the weight of dharma that prevents her from following her son

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
विसृष्टो मातरं रामो गत्वा स्वां भार्यामब्रवीत् |
सीते दुःखमनुप्राप्तं श्रृणु यद्वक्ष्यामि ते मया || २-२२-१
transliteration:
visṛṣṭo mātaraṃ rāmo gatvā svāṃ bhāryām abravīt |
sīte duḥkham anuprāptaṃ śṛṇu yad vakṣyāmi te mayā || 2-22-1
translation: Taking leave of his mother, Rama went to Sita and said: 'O Sita, listen to the misfortune that has come upon me, and what I am about to tell you.'
commentary_full: Rama formally tries once more to persuade Sita not to accompany him to the forest. He describes in vivid detail the hardships of forest life — the wild animals, extreme temperatures, thorny paths, the diet of roots and fruits, sleeping on the hard ground. He tells her that a palace without him is far safer than a forest with him. But Sita's response, delivered in this sarga, is the famous and celebrated passage on wifely dharma that has echoed through Indian culture for millennia. She says that a wife who does not follow her husband in difficulty is no wife at all. She declares that wherever Rama goes, that is her home; whatever hardship he faces, she will face it gladly. She dismisses the forests and wild animals as irrelevant — her only protection and her only joy is her husband's presence. Rama is moved but not entirely convinced. He asks her again. Sita's resolve is unshakeable.
commentary_summary: Rama tries once more to dissuade Sita from the forest; Sita's response is the celebrated declaration that a devoted wife follows her husband through any hardship.
theme: Sita's pativrata devotion — love that transcends comfort, safety, and royal luxury

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
एवमुक्त्वा तु वैदेही रामस्याग्निं प्रदक्षिणम् |
चकार सा सुकेशान्तान्माल्यानि विविधानि च || २-२३-१
transliteration:
evam uktvā tu vaidehī rāmasyāgniṃ pradakṣiṇam |
cakāra sā sukeśāntān mālyāni vividhāni ca || 2-23-1
translation: Having spoken thus, Sita circumambulated the sacred fire and also Rama with her beautiful hair adorned with garlands of various flowers.
commentary_full: Having made her decision irrevocably clear, Sita begins preparing for the forest. She discards her royal ornaments and jewels and asks Rama what she should wear for the journey. He gives her the bark-cloth and she changes without hesitation. This sarga contains a poignant scene where Sita, accustomed to royal robes all her life, struggles to tie the bark-cloth properly. Rama helps her. The sight of Janaka's daughter, Dasaratha's daughter-in-law — the most pampered princess in the realm — now wearing rough forest attire is deeply moving. The queens weep. Vasishtha rebukes Kaikeyi for making a princess endure this. Kaikeyi is unmoved. Lakshmana also formally takes leave of his mother Sumitra, who blesses him and tells him to treat the forest as Ayodhya and Rama as his father — one of the most touching parting blessings in the entire epic.
commentary_summary: Sita changes into bark-cloth without hesitation; Sumitra blesses Lakshmana with the remarkable words: 'Treat the forest as Ayodhya and Rama as your father.'
theme: Voluntary sacrifice of royal luxury as an act of love and dharma

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
राज्ञश्च दशरथस्याज्ञा श्रुत्वा लोकानुशासिनः |
संसृज्य गुरवे रामो ददौ सर्वस्वमेव च || २-२४-१
transliteration:
rājñaśca daśarathasyājñā śrutvā lokānuśāsinaḥ |
saṃsṛjya gurave rāmo dadau sarvasvam eva ca || 2-24-1
translation: Hearing the king's commands, Rama distributed all his possessions to Vasishtha and other brahmanas and to the poor.
commentary_full: Before departing, Rama distributes all his personal wealth. He gives away his treasures — gold, jewels, horses, elephants, and land — to Vasishtha and the brahmanas, to the poor, and to those in need. He sends special gifts to particular devotees. He also privately meets his loyal friend and devotee Suvarna and gives him his charioteer's family special blessings. This distribution is deeply symbolic: a king departing for the forest has no use for royal wealth, and giving it away is an act of ultimate renunciation. When Sita tries to give away her own jewelry to a brahmin scholar named Trijata, she finds that her hands, unaccustomed to such giving, cannot manage the clasps — Rama helps her. This small domestic detail among massive acts of charity reveals the human warmth in these divine figures. The sarga ends with all preparations complete for the departure.
commentary_summary: Rama distributes all his wealth to brahmanas and the poor before departing — a symbolic act of complete renunciation before entering the forest.
theme: Renunciation as the first act of the forest life — giving away all worldly attachments

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
ततो रामः परिवृत्य पितरं वचनं महत् |
प्रोवाच प्रयतो देवीः कौसल्यां प्रमुखे स्थिताम् || २-२५-१
transliteration:
tato rāmaḥ parivṛtya pitaraṃ vacanaṃ mahat |
provāca prayato devīḥ kausalyāṃ pramukhe sthitām || 2-25-1
translation: Then Rama turned to speak final words to his father, addressing first Kausalya who stood before him, with purity of mind.
commentary_full: Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana formally depart from the royal palace. Sumantra, the charioteer, brings their chariot. Dasaratha, utterly broken, tries to come down from his throne to follow Rama. The doorkeepers restrain him. As the chariot moves through the city streets, the entire population of Ayodhya follows in grief. Old men, women, children, merchants, scholars — all pour out of their homes and follow the chariot, weeping and crying out Rama's name. They curse Kaikeyi. They question the justice of the gods. Some hold onto the chariot wheels trying to stop it. Some run alongside. The scene of an entire city following their beloved prince into exile is one of the most powerful crowd scenes in world literature — it dramatizes, through sheer numbers of grief, just how much Rama meant to his people.
commentary_summary: As Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana depart by chariot, the entire population of Ayodhya follows in grief — an entire city's love made visible in its sorrow.
theme: A whole city's love expressed through grief — the depth of Rama's bond with his people

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
अथाब्रवीत् सुमन्त्रस्तु दशरथं महीपतिम् |
यान्तं रामं प्रेक्ष्य शोकेन मुह्यन्तम् अकरोत् स्मृतिम् || २-२६-१
transliteration:
athābravīt sumantras tu daśarathaṃ mahīpatim |
yāntaṃ rāmaṃ prekṣya śokena muhyantam akarot smṛtim || 2-26-1
translation: Sumantra then spoke to king Dasaratha, who was on the verge of losing consciousness with grief while watching Rama depart.
commentary_full: The chariot bearing Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana departs into the distance. Dasaratha, standing at the gate of the city, watches until the dust of the chariot's wheels fades beyond the horizon. He cannot bear to withdraw his eyes. He stands fixed, watching the emptying road. Even the dust raised by the chariot wheels is precious to him. Sumantra, caught between loyalty to Dasaratha and his driver's duty to take Rama away, does his best to comfort the king. The city folk who had followed Rama eventually turn back, exhausted. They return to an Ayodhya that already feels like a different city. Dasaratha is finally led back inside. The city that had been illuminated and festooned for a coronation is now dark with grief. Ayodhya feels like a body from which the soul has departed — and indeed it has.
commentary_summary: Dasaratha watches until Rama's chariot-dust disappears, unable to turn away; Ayodhya, emptied of its beloved prince, feels like a body from which the soul has departed.
theme: Ayodhya without Rama — the desolation of a kingdom whose heart has departed

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
अथ रामस्तमासाद्य तमसाकूलमव्ययम् |
तीरे वासमकरोत् तस्याः सह सीतेन लक्ष्मणेन च || २-२७-१
transliteration:
atha rāmas tam āsādya tamasākūlam avyayam |
tīre vāsam akarot tasyāḥ saha sītena lakṣmaṇena ca || 2-27-1
translation: Then Rama, reaching the eternal and sacred Tamasa river, made camp on its banks for the night along with Sita and Lakshmana.
commentary_full: Rama's chariot travels all day and reaches the bank of the river Tamasa by evening. He decides to camp here for the night. The citizens of Ayodhya who had followed the chariot camp at a distance, still unwilling to turn back. In the deep of night, Rama takes a momentous decision: he instructs Sumantra to drive the chariot away in a different direction before dawn, so that the citizens, when they wake up, will follow the chariot tracks and not find Rama. He does not want the people of Ayodhya to suffer by following him into the forest. This act — deceiving his own devoted citizens for their own welfare — is presented as an act of compassionate dharma. At first light, Sumantra does as instructed. When the citizens wake and discover they cannot follow Rama, they are devastated. Some turn toward Ayodhya in grief; others stand lost, not knowing which way to go.
commentary_summary: Camping at the Tamasa river, Rama compassionately tricks his devoted citizens into losing his trail so they won't suffer by following him into the forest.
theme: Compassionate deception — protecting those who love you by leading them away from suffering

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
तेषां तत् करुणं दृष्ट्वा रामः परमधार्मिकः |
दद‍र्श गङ्गामासाद्य श्रृङ्गवेरपुरं ततः || २-२८-१
transliteration:
teṣāṃ tat karuṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā rāmaḥ paramadhārmikaḥ |
dadarśa gaṅgām āsādya śṛṅgaverapuraṃ tataḥ || 2-28-1
translation: Seeing the pitiful state of those citizens, the greatly righteous Rama proceeded onward and reached the town of Shringaverapura on the banks of the Ganga.
commentary_full: Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana continue their journey and arrive at Shringaverapura, on the banks of the sacred Ganga. This is the kingdom of Guha, the tribal chief and devoted friend of Rama. Guha comes out to receive Rama with great honor and hospitality, offering food, comfortable accommodation, and all royal amenities. He urges Rama to accept all comforts, at least for this one night. Rama accepts food for the horses but declines the other amenities — he has already committed to the ascetic life and will eat only forest fare. He rests under a tree. Guha, who cannot sleep for grief and anxiety, keeps watch through the night, walking around Rama's resting place. This sarga introduces Guha as an ideal devotee — a tribal king who loves Rama not because of his royal status but because of who he is. His sleepless vigil of love is one of the most touching portraits of devotion in the epic.
commentary_summary: Rama reaches Shringaverapura where his devoted tribal friend Guha receives him with honor; Guha keeps a sleepless vigil of love while Rama rests under a tree.
theme: Pure devotion beyond social rank — Guha's selfless love for Rama

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
गुहश्च राघवं दृष्ट्वा तापसं प्रियदर्शनम् |
सत्कारेण महार्हेण सर्वान् परिजनान् सह || २-२९-१
transliteration:
guhaśca rāghavaṃ dṛṣṭvā tāpasaṃ priyadarśanam |
satkāreṇa mahārheṇa sarvān parijanān saha || 2-29-1
translation: Guha, seeing the auspicious-looking Raghava now dressed as an ascetic, received him with great honor along with all his attendants.
commentary_full: In the morning, after the brief rest, Lakshmana proceeds to the river Ganga to make arrangements to cross it. He speaks to Guha and tries to understand the route forward. Sumantra, the charioteer, is deeply grieved — he has been Dasaratha's trusted charioteer for decades, and the thought of returning to Ayodhya without Rama is unbearable to him. He begs Rama to allow him to serve even in the forest. Rama gently but firmly declines, explaining that Sumantra's presence in Ayodhya will actually comfort his grieving father by serving as a connection to his son. Rama instructs Sumantra to give specific messages to Dasaratha, to Kausalya, and to all the queens. His farewell instructions are models of thoughtful consideration for each person — he thinks of everyone else even in his own moment of departure. Sumantra weeps bitterly as Rama prepares to cross the Ganga.
commentary_summary: Rama bids farewell to Sumantra, asking him to return to Ayodhya to comfort Dasaratha; Rama's farewell instructions reveal his deep consideration for each person he is leaving behind.
theme: Leaving with love — Rama's farewell instructions show his care for every person he leaves behind

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit:
किं हि कृत्वा विषण्णस्त्वं कुतो वा भयमस्ति ते |
यत् परित्यक्तुकामस्त्वं मामनन्यपरायणाम् || २-३०-५
transliteration:
kiṃ hi kṛtvā viṣaṇṇas tvaṃ kuto vā bhayam asti te |
yat parityaktukāmas tvaṃ māṃ ananyaparāyaṇām || 2-30-5
translation: Sita asked Rama: 'For what reason are you cast down? Whence is this fear in you, that you are willing to desert me — for whom there is no other recourse?'
commentary_full: As the trio prepares to cross the Ganga, Sita comes forward to offer her own prayers and vows to the sacred river goddess. She prays that Rama may complete his vow and return safely, that Lakshmana may remain protected, and that they may all return safely to Ayodhya after the fourteen years. This sarga includes Sita's moving comparison of herself to Savitri — the legendary wife who followed her husband even to the realm of death. She reminds Rama of this comparison when he once again tries to gently suggest she stay behind: 'Know me to be as dependent on your will as Savitri was on Satyavan.' The three cross the Ganga with Guha's assistance and enter the far bank. Guha, his heart heavy with grief, watches them disappear into the forest. The sarga marks the moment of no return — once across the great river, the world of Ayodhya is truly left behind.
commentary_summary: Sita prays to the Ganga goddess for their safe return; comparing herself to Savitri, she joins Rama and Lakshmana in crossing the great river, leaving Ayodhya's world behind.
theme: Crossing the Ganga — the final and irreversible departure from the world of Ayodhya

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: तपःस्वाध्यायनिरतं तपस्वी वाग्विदां वरम् | नारदं परिपप्रच्छ वाल्मीकिर्मुनिपुङ्गवम् ||
transliteration: tapaḥ-svādhyāya-nirataṁ tapasvī vāg-vidāṁ varam | nāradaṁ paripapraccha vālmīkir muni-puṅgavam ||
translation: The ascetic Valmiki inquired of Narada, who was deeply engaged in austerity and Vedic study, the foremost among eloquent speakers and eminent among sages.
commentary_full: This opening verse of the Valmiki Ramayana marks the beginning of a sacred dialogue between Sage Valmiki and Sage Narada. Valmiki, described as a tapasvī (ascetic), approaches Narada with reverence. Narada is portrayed as deeply engaged in tapas (austerity) and svadhyaya (study of the Vedas), and as the श्रेष्ठ among speakers (vāg-vidām varam), highlighting his wisdom and eloquence. He is also called 'muni-pungava', meaning the foremost among sages. The verse signifies the beginning of an inquiry into the ideal human being. Additionally, it is traditionally noted that the epic begins with the auspicious syllable 'ta', which is considered to remove obstacles (vighna-naashaka) and grant well-being (saukhyadaayaka), indicating a spiritually blessed commencement of the Ramayana.
commentary_summary: Valmiki approaches Narada, the foremost sage, to seek knowledge. The Ramayana begins with an auspicious and spiritually significant inquiry.
theme: The auspicious beginning of the Ramayana and the inquiry into supreme wisdom

speaker: Valmiki
text_sanskrit: को न्वस्मिन् साम्प्रतं लोके गुणवान् कश्च वीर्यवान् | धर्मज्ञश्च कृतज्ञश्च सत्यवाक्यो दृढव्रतः ||
transliteration: ko nvasmin sāmprataṁ loke guṇavān kaśca vīryavān | dharmajñaśca kṛtajñaśca satyavākyo dṛḍhavrataḥ ||
translation: Who indeed, in this present world, is virtuous and valiant, knowledgeable in dharma, grateful for good deeds done to him, truthful in speech, and firm in his resolve?
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Valmiki begins his inquiry to Narada by describing the qualities of the ideal human being he seeks to know. The question is not about an ordinary person, but someone who embodies a perfect combination of moral and heroic virtues. The term 'guṇavān' signifies one endowed with noble qualities, while 'vīryavān' indicates strength and valor. 'Dharmajña' refers to one who understands and follows righteousness, and 'kṛtajña' highlights gratitude and the ability to remember good deeds. 'Satyavākya' emphasizes truthfulness in speech, a cornerstone of ethical living, and 'dṛḍhavrata' denotes unwavering determination and commitment to one's principles. This verse sets the foundation for the Ramayana’s central theme—the search for the ideal person who harmonizes strength, virtue, and righteousness in life.
commentary_summary: Valmiki asks who in the world embodies ideal virtues like strength, righteousness, gratitude, truthfulness, and determination.
theme: The search for the ideal human possessing perfect moral and heroic qualities

speaker: Valmiki
text_sanskrit: चारित्रेण च को युक्तः सर्वभूतेषु को हितः | विद्वान् कः कः समर्थश्च कश्चैकप्रियदर्शनः ||
transliteration: cāritreṇa ca ko yuktaḥ sarvabhūteṣu ko hitaḥ | vidvān kaḥ kaḥ samarthaśca kaścaika-priyadarśanaḥ ||
translation: Who is endowed with noble character, who works for the welfare of all beings, who is knowledgeable and capable, and who is uniquely pleasant in appearance?
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Valmiki continues describing the qualities of the ideal person he seeks to know. The term 'cāritreṇa yuktaḥ' emphasizes one whose conduct is righteous and aligned with noble values, shaped by good lineage, proper education, and adherence to Vedic principles. 'Sarvabhūteṣu hitaḥ' highlights universal compassion—the person must care for the welfare of all beings, irrespective of status, treating both the noble and the humble with kindness and fairness. The word 'vidvān' signifies deep knowledge—not merely theoretical, but practical wisdom applied in real-life actions. 'Samarthaḥ' denotes capability and efficiency in executing duties responsibly. Lastly, 'eka-priyadarśanaḥ' suggests a uniquely pleasing personality—not just physical beauty, but a presence that feels ever-refreshing and graceful, embodying charm and dignity. True beauty, as implied, lies in a constantly renewing pleasantness (kṣaṇe kṣaṇe yat navatām upaiti), reflecting inner virtue outwardly. Thus, this verse expands the vision of the ideal human as one who combines character, compassion, wisdom, capability, and graceful presence.
commentary_summary: Valmiki seeks a person of noble character, universal compassion, practical wisdom, capability, and uniquely pleasing presence.
theme: The ideal human as a blend of character, compassion, wisdom, and graceful presence

speaker: Valmiki
text_sanskrit: आत्मवान् को जितक्रोधो द्युतिमान् कोऽनसूयकः | कस्य बिभ्यति देवाश्च जातरोषस्य संयुगे ||
transliteration: ātmavān ko jitakrodho dyutimān ko'nasūyakaḥ | kasya bibhyati devāśca jātaroshasya saṁyuge ||
translation: Who is self-composed, who has conquered anger, who is radiant and free from jealousy, and whose wrath in battle even the gods fear?
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Valmiki further refines his search for the ideal human by focusing on inner discipline and divine-like strength. The term 'ātmavān' signifies one who is self-controlled and firmly established in inner awareness. 'Jitakrodhaḥ' highlights mastery over anger—not the absence of anger, but the ability to restrain and channel it appropriately. 'Dyutimān' denotes brilliance, both in physical radiance and spiritual aura. 'Anasūyakaḥ' refers to one who is free from envy or jealousy, indicating purity of heart and noble intent. The latter part of the verse elevates this ideal further—'kasya bibhyati devāḥ'—even the gods fear such a person when he is righteously angered in battle. This suggests that while the individual is gentle and composed by nature, when provoked in the cause of dharma, his शक्ति becomes formidable and unstoppable. Thus, the verse portrays a perfect balance between inner calmness and outer strength, emphasizing that true greatness lies in controlled power guided by righteousness.
commentary_summary: Valmiki seeks one who is self-controlled, free from anger and jealousy, radiant, and so powerful that even the gods fear his righteous wrath.
theme: The ideal human as one who balances inner discipline with immense righteous power

speaker: Valmiki
text_sanskrit: एतदिच्छाम्यहं श्रोतुं परं कौतूहलं हि मे | महर्षे त्वं समर्थोऽसि ज्ञातुमेवंविधं नरम् ||
transliteration: etadicchāmyahaṁ śrotuṁ paraṁ kautūhalaṁ hi me | maharṣe tvaṁ samartho'si jñātumevaṁvidhaṁ naram ||
translation: I wish to hear all this from you, O great sage, for my curiosity is immense. You are capable of knowing such a person.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Valmiki expresses his deep eagerness to learn about the ideal person possessing all the previously described virtues. Addressing Narada as 'Maharshi', he acknowledges Narada’s supreme wisdom and omniscience. Valmiki’s curiosity (kautūhalam) is not casual but profound, reflecting a sincere quest for truth and perfection. He seeks not just knowledge, but a living example of a person embodying divine qualities. This inquiry sets the stage for the revelation of Lord Rama as the ideal human. Interestingly, both Valmiki and Narada are already aware of Rama and his deeds, yet this question is posed deliberately. If Narada had directly declared Rama as Lord Vishnu, the purpose of composing the Ramayana as a human narrative would be diminished. Instead, the epic unfolds as the story of an exemplary human life. The sixteen qualities listed across the previous verses—such as virtue, valor, righteousness, gratitude, truthfulness, character, compassion, wisdom, capability, pleasantness, self-control, mastery over anger, brilliance, non-jealousy, and divine prowess—are symbolically compared to the sixteen phases (kalas) of the full moon. Valmiki envisions his hero, Rama, as पूर्णचन्द्र समान—complete, radiant, and universally pleasing. Thus, this verse emphasizes both the depth of Valmiki’s inquiry and the poetic foundation for portraying Rama as the embodiment of ideal human excellence.
commentary_summary: Valmiki expresses deep curiosity and asks Narada to reveal the ideal person, setting the stage for Rama as the embodiment of sixteen divine qualities.
theme: The eager quest for the ideal human and the foundation for portraying Rama as the embodiment of perfect virtues

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: श्रुत्वा चैतत्त्रिलोकज्ञो वाल्मीकेर्नारदो वचः | श्रूयतामिति चामन्त्र्य प्रहृष्टो वाक्यमब्रवीत् ||
transliteration: śrutvā caitat trilokajño vālmīker nārado vacaḥ | śrūyatāmiti cāmantrya prahṛṣṭo vākyam abravīt ||
translation: Hearing these words of Valmiki, Narada—the knower of the three worlds—joyfully said, 'Listen,' and inviting him to attend, spoke the following words.
commentary_full: This verse marks the transition from inquiry to revelation. After hearing Valmiki’s profound questions, Sage Narada—described as 'trilokajña', the knower of all three worlds (Bhūloka, Bhuvarloka, and Suvarloka)—responds with delight. His joy (prahṛṣṭaḥ) reflects both appreciation for the depth of Valmiki’s inquiry and readiness to reveal the answer. By saying 'śrūyatām' (let it be heard), Narada invites attentive listening, indicating that what follows is of great significance. As an omniscient sage who understands events across all realms, Narada is uniquely qualified to answer Valmiki’s question about the ideal human. This moment sets the stage for Narada’s narration of Lord Rama’s qualities and life, thus initiating the core story of the Ramayana. The verse emphasizes the importance of a worthy teacher and a sincere seeker in the transmission of sacred knowledge.
commentary_summary: Narada, the knower of the three worlds, joyfully invites Valmiki to listen and begins revealing the answer to his inquiry.
theme: The transition from inquiry to revelation through the dialogue of a sincere seeker and an omniscient sage

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: बहवो दुर्लभाश्चैव ये त्वया कीर्तिता गुणाः | मुने वक्ष्याम्यहं बुद्ध्वा तैर्युक्तः श्रूयतां नरः ||
transliteration: bahavo durlabhāścaiva ye tvayā kīrtitā guṇāḥ | mune vakṣyāmyahaṁ buddhvā tairyuktaḥ śrūyatāṁ naraḥ ||
translation: O Sage, the qualities you have described are many and indeed rare. Having understood such a man endowed with these virtues, I shall describe him—listen.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada responds to Valmiki’s inquiry by acknowledging the extraordinary nature of the qualities described. He states that these virtues are not only many but also 'durlabhāḥ'—extremely rare and difficult to find in a single individual. Addressing Valmiki as 'Mune', Narada prepares to reveal the identity of such a person. The phrase 'buddhvā' indicates that Narada speaks with complete knowledge and realization, traditionally understood as knowledge received from Brahma. Thus, Narada becomes the medium through which divine knowledge is transmitted. His invitation 'śrūyatām' emphasizes attentive listening, signaling the importance of what follows. This verse highlights a divine alignment—Brahma’s will, Narada’s narration, and Valmiki’s inquiry—all converging to bring forth the Ramayana. It also reinforces the idea that the ideal human, embodying all these virtues, is an exceptional and almost unattainable figure, soon to be revealed as Lord Rama.
commentary_summary: Narada says the qualities described are rare and prepares to reveal the ideal person, marking the beginning of Rama’s introduction.
theme: The rarity of perfect virtues and the divine revelation of the ideal human

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकुवंशप्रभवो रामो नाम जनैः श्रुतः | नियतात्मा महावीर्यो द्युतिमान् धृतिमान् वशी ||
transliteration: ikṣvāku-vaṁśa-prabhavo rāmo nāma janaiḥ śrutaḥ | niyatātmā mahāvīryo dyutimān dhṛtimān vaśī ||
translation: Born in the Ikshvaku dynasty, he is known among people as Rama. He is self-controlled, highly valorous, radiant, steadfast, and a master of his senses.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada begins answering Valmiki’s inquiry by introducing Lord Rama as the embodiment of all the virtues previously described. Rama is said to be born in the illustrious Ikshvaku dynasty, a lineage known for righteousness and noble kingship. The name 'Rama' is already renowned among people, indicating his widespread fame and virtue. The qualities listed—'niyatātmā' (self-controlled), 'mahāvīryaḥ' (immensely valorous), 'dyutimān' (radiant), 'dhṛtimān' (steadfast), and 'vaśī' (one who has mastery over his senses)—are not merely human virtues but are deeply rooted in Vedantic philosophy. These attributes are often associated with the Supreme Being (Brahman) as described in the Upanishads. For instance, 'niyatātmā' reflects the immutable and pure Self, free from all defects; 'mahāvīryaḥ' indicates infinite शक्ति and capability; 'dyutimān' symbolizes self-luminous consciousness; 'dhṛtimān' represents inner bliss and contentment; and 'vaśī' signifies supreme control over all existence. Thus, Rama is portrayed not just as an ideal human king but as a manifestation of the Absolute, embodying both human excellence and divine essence. This verse establishes Rama as the perfect synthesis of dharma, strength, wisdom, and spiritual completeness.
commentary_summary: Narada introduces Rama of the Ikshvaku dynasty as the ideal person, embodying self-control, valor, radiance, steadfastness, and mastery over senses, reflecting both human and divine qualities.
theme: The introduction of Rama as the embodiment of ideal human virtues and divine qualities

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: बुद्धिमान्नीतिमान्वाग्ग्मी श्रीमान् शत्रुनिबर्हणः | विपुलांसो महाबाहुः कम्बुग्रीवो महाहनुः ||
transliteration: buddhimān nītimān vāgmī śrīmān śatrunibarhaṇaḥ | vipulāṁso mahābāhuḥ kambugrīvo mahāhanuḥ ||
translation: He is intelligent, righteous, eloquent, and glorious, a destroyer of enemies. He has broad shoulders, long arms, a conch-shaped neck, and prominent cheeks.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada continues describing the qualities of Lord Rama, combining both intellectual virtues and ideal physical attributes. Rama is 'buddhimān' (wise), possessing deep understanding and discernment, and 'nītimān' (righteous), upholding moral principles and governance. As 'vāgmī', he is eloquent, capable of expressing truth with clarity and grace. The term 'śrīmān' signifies prosperity, auspiciousness, and divine splendor, indicating that fortune naturally resides with him. 'Śatrunibarhaṇaḥ' portrays him as a destroyer of enemies, symbolizing his role in upholding dharma by eliminating evil forces. The latter half of the verse describes Rama’s physical features as per Sāmudrika Śāstra (physiognomy). 'Vipulāṁsaḥ' (broad-shouldered) and 'mahābāhuḥ' (long-armed) indicate strength and capability. 'Kambugrīvaḥ' refers to a conch-shaped neck with three auspicious lines, symbolizing fortune and nobility. 'Mahāhanuḥ' (prominent cheeks/jaw) reflects authority and determination. These features collectively define the ideal form of a महान् ruler. Philosophically, these attributes also hint at the Supreme Being—omniscient (sarvajña), sustainer of cosmic order, and the source of prosperity and strength. Thus, Rama is depicted as the perfect blend of wisdom, righteousness, strength, and divine grace, both in character and form.
commentary_summary: Narada describes Rama as wise, righteous, eloquent, glorious, and powerful, with ideal physical features of a महान् ruler.
theme: The perfection of Rama in both intellectual virtues and ideal physical form

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: महोरस्को महेष्वासो गूढजत्रुररिन्दमः | आजानुबाहुः सुशिराः सुललाटः सुविक्रमः ||
transliteration: mahorasko maheṣvāso gūḍhajatruḥ arindamaḥ | ājānubāhuḥ suśirāḥ sulalāṭaḥ suvikramaḥ ||
translation: He is broad-chested, a wielder of a mighty bow, with strong and concealed collarbones, a subduer of enemies, with arms reaching his knees, a well-formed head, a broad forehead, and a majestic gait.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada continues to describe the majestic physical and heroic attributes of Lord Rama. 'Mahoraskaḥ' (broad-chested) signifies strength and courage, while 'maheṣvāsaḥ' indicates his ability to wield a great bow, symbolizing both martial prowess and readiness to protect dharma. 'Gūḍhajatruḥ' refers to well-built shoulders with concealed collarbones, a mark of physical perfection according to traditional physiognomy. 'Arindamaḥ' highlights his role as a conqueror of enemies—not only external foes but also internal adversaries like desire, anger, greed, pride, and delusion (ariṣaḍvarga). 'Ājānubāhuḥ' describes his long arms reaching the knees, a sign of royal and divine stature. 'Suśirāḥ' (well-shaped head) and 'sulalāṭaḥ' (broad forehead) indicate intelligence, dignity, and auspiciousness. 'Suvikramaḥ' denotes a majestic and powerful gait, often compared to that of a lion, reflecting confidence and authority. Though the mention of the bow amidst physical traits may seem abrupt, it actually complements the description—his powerful physique is capable of wielding such a mighty weapon. Thus, Rama is portrayed as the perfect warrior-king, embodying both physical excellence and inner strength, capable of conquering all forms of adversity.
commentary_summary: Narada describes Rama’s majestic physique and strength, emphasizing his power as both a warrior and conqueror of inner and outer enemies.
theme: The ideal warrior-king as a blend of physical excellence and inner strength

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: समः समविभक्ताङ्गः स्निग्धवर्णः प्रतापवान् | पीनवक्षा विशालाक्षो लक्ष्मीवान् शुभलक्षणः ||
transliteration: samaḥ samavibhaktāṅgaḥ snigdhavarṇaḥ pratāpavān | pīnavakṣā viśālākṣo lakṣmīvān śubhalakṣaṇaḥ ||
translation: He is well-proportioned in form, with symmetrically built limbs, of charming complexion, and radiant with courage. He has a strong chest, large eyes, is endowed with prosperity, and bears auspicious features.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada continues to describe the divine physical perfection of Lord Rama. 'Samaḥ' and 'samavibhaktāṅgaḥ' emphasize perfect bodily proportions and symmetry, indicating harmony and balance—qualities of an ideal being. 'Snigdhavarṇaḥ' refers to a pleasing and radiant complexion, symbolizing both physical beauty and inner purity. 'Pratāpavān' denotes brilliance and courage, reflecting both valor and a commanding presence. 'Pīnavakṣā' (broad and strong chest) and 'viśālākṣaḥ' (large, expansive eyes) are marks of strength, compassion, and nobility. The term 'lakṣmīvān' signifies one endowed with prosperity, grace, and divine fortune, often associated with the presence of Lakshmi. 'Śubhalakṣaṇaḥ' highlights the presence of auspicious bodily signs as described in traditional texts like Sāmudrika Śāstra. Up to this point, Narada elaborates on the divine form (bhagavad-vigraha) of Rama, which is perceptible and inspiring to devotees. Such a form reflects not only physical beauty but also spiritual excellence, as echoed in the Upanishadic vision of the divine person. Thus, Rama is portrayed as the embodiment of harmony, beauty, strength, and auspiciousness—both outwardly and inwardly.
commentary_summary: Narada describes Rama’s perfectly proportioned and auspicious physical form, symbolizing harmony, beauty, strength, and divine grace.
theme: The divine physical perfection and auspicious nature of the ideal being

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: धर्मज्ञः सत्यसन्धश्च प्रजानां च हिते रतः | यशस्वी ज्ञानसंपन्नः शुचिर्वश्यः समाधिमान् ||
transliteration: dharmajñaḥ satyasandhaśca prajānāṁ ca hite rataḥ | yaśasvī jñānasaṁpannaḥ śucirvaśyaḥ samādhimān ||
translation: He is knowledgeable in righteousness, devoted to truth, engaged in the welfare of his subjects, renowned, endowed with wisdom, pure in conduct, self-controlled, and deeply focused.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada highlights the ethical, intellectual, and governance qualities of Lord Rama. 'Dharmajñaḥ' signifies one who deeply understands dharma—not just in theory but in practice. 'Satyasandhaḥ' denotes unwavering commitment to truth in thought, word, and action. 'Prajānāṁ hite rataḥ' emphasizes Rama’s dedication to the welfare of his people, portraying him as an ideal ruler who prioritizes the well-being of his subjects. 'Yaśasvī' reflects his widespread fame earned through righteous deeds. 'Jñānasaṁpannaḥ' indicates profound wisdom and discernment, enabling him to make just decisions. 'Śuciḥ' refers to purity in both inner intention and outward conduct. 'Vaśyaḥ' denotes mastery over oneself, especially the senses and impulses. 'Samādhimān' highlights deep concentration and mental steadiness, reflecting a composed and focused mind. Together, these qualities present Rama as the perfect embodiment of ethical leadership, wisdom, purity, and self-discipline, making him an ideal king and human being.
commentary_summary: Narada describes Rama as righteous, truthful, devoted to his people, wise, pure, self-controlled, and mentally composed—an ideal leader.
theme: The embodiment of ideal leadership through righteousness, truth, wisdom, and self-discipline

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: प्रजापतिसमः श्रीमान् धाता रिपुनिषूदनः | रक्षिता जीवलोकस्य धर्मस्य परिरक्षिता ||
transliteration: prajāpatisamaḥ śrīmān dhātā ripuniṣūdanaḥ | rakṣitā jīvalokasya dharmasya parirakṣitā ||
translation: He is equal to Prajapati (the Lord of creatures), endowed with prosperity, the sustainer, destroyer of enemies, protector of all living beings, and the upholder of dharma.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada elevates the description of Lord Rama to a divine level, equating him with 'Prajapati'—the Lord of all beings. Here, Prajapati is understood as Lord Vishnu, the sustainer of the universe, emphasizing Rama’s divine nature. The term 'śrīmān' indicates that he is accompanied by Sri (Lakshmi), symbolizing prosperity, grace, and auspiciousness. 'Dhātā' further reinforces his role as the sustainer and supporter of the cosmos. 'Ripuniṣūdanaḥ' highlights his शक्ति in destroying evil forces and protecting righteousness. 'Rakṣitā jīvalokasya' portrays Rama as the protector of all living beings, not limited to humans but encompassing the entire creation. 'Dharmasya parirakṣitā' emphasizes his unwavering commitment to preserving and upholding dharma in its entirety. Traditional commentators like Govindaraja and Maheshvara Tirtha note that such qualities are attributes of the Supreme Being and cannot be fully found in ordinary individuals. Thus, this verse firmly establishes Rama not only as an ideal human king but as a manifestation of the divine, embodying the cosmic roles of creation, sustenance, and protection of dharma.
commentary_summary: Narada describes Rama as equal to the Supreme, a sustainer, protector of all beings, destroyer of evil, and guardian of dharma.
theme: The divine nature of Rama as the protector, sustainer, and upholder of dharma

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: रक्षिता स्वस्य धर्मस्य स्वजनस्य च रक्षिता | वेदवेदाङ्गतत्त्वज्ञो धनुर्वेदे च निष्ठितः ||
transliteration: rakṣitā svasya dharmasya svajanasya ca rakṣitā | vedavedāṅgatattvajño dhanurvede ca niṣṭhitaḥ ||
translation: He is the protector of his own righteousness and also the protector of his people. He is well-versed in the essence of the Vedas and their auxiliaries, and is proficient in the science of archery.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada highlights Lord Rama’s commitment to both personal righteousness and social responsibility. 'Rakṣitā svasya dharmasya' indicates that Rama steadfastly preserves his own dharma, never deviating from righteousness even under adversity. 'Svajanasya ca rakṣitā' shows his role as a guardian of his people, ensuring their welfare and protection. The phrase 'vedavedāṅgatattvajñaḥ' reveals his deep mastery over the Vedas and their six auxiliary disciplines (Vedāṅgas), such as phonetics (śikṣā), grammar (vyākaraṇa), prosody (chandas), etymology (nirukta), astronomy (jyotiṣa), and ritual (kalpa). This signifies not just scholarly knowledge but understanding of their essence. 'Dhanurvede ca niṣṭhitaḥ' emphasizes his expertise in Dhanurveda—the science of warfare and archery. Traditionally, Dhanurveda is not limited to simple weaponry but includes advanced knowledge of astras (divine weapons), strategies, and disciplined combat. It is considered a specialized branch of knowledge for warriors. Thus, Rama is portrayed as a perfect synthesis of spiritual wisdom and martial excellence—one who upholds dharma intellectually, ethically, and through righteous action.
commentary_summary: Rama is described as a protector of dharma and people, deeply learned in Vedas, and highly skilled in the science of warfare.
theme: The harmony of spiritual wisdom and martial skill in upholding righteousness

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: सर्वशास्त्रार्थतत्त्वज्ञः स्मृतिमान् प्रतिभानवान् | सर्वलोकप्रियः साधुरदीनात्मा विचक्षणः ||
transliteration: sarvaśāstrārthatattvajñaḥ smṛtimān pratibhānavān | sarvalokapriyaḥ sādhuradīnātmā vicakṣaṇaḥ ||
translation: He knows the true essence of all scriptures, possesses excellent memory, is brilliant, beloved by all, gentle, never dejected in spirit, and discerning in judgment.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada continues to describe the intellectual and emotional excellence of Lord Rama. 'Sarvaśāstrārthatattvajñaḥ' indicates his deep understanding of the true meaning and essence of all scriptures, not merely superficial knowledge but profound insight. 'Smṛtimān' highlights his exceptional memory, enabling him to retain and apply knowledge effectively. 'Pratibhānavān' denotes brilliance and quick intellect, reflecting his ability to respond wisely in all situations. 'Sarvalokapriyaḥ' shows that he is beloved by all beings, owing to his noble qualities and compassionate nature. 'Sādhuḥ' emphasizes his gentleness and righteousness in conduct. 'Adīnātmā' signifies emotional stability—he remains composed and undisturbed even in adversity. 'Vicakṣaṇaḥ' refers to his sharp discernment, the ability to distinguish right from wrong and act accordingly. Together, these qualities portray Rama as an ideal embodiment of wisdom, emotional strength, compassion, and clarity of judgment, making him universally admired and respected.
commentary_summary: Rama is described as wise, intelligent, beloved, gentle, emotionally stable, and discerning—an ideal of intellectual and emotional excellence.
theme: The perfection of intellect, emotional balance, and universal appeal in the ideal human

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: सर्वदाभिगतः सद्भिः समुद्र इव सिन्धुभिः | आर्यः सर्वसमश्चैव सदैव प्रियदर्शनः ||
transliteration: sarvadābhigataḥ sadbhiḥ samudra iva sindhubhiḥ | āryaḥ sarvasamaścaiva sadaiva priyadarśanaḥ ||
translation: He is always approachable by the noble, like the ocean by rivers; he is noble, treats all equally, and is ever pleasing to behold.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada beautifully illustrates Lord Rama’s accessibility, equality, and noble demeanor. 'Sarvadābhigataḥ sadbhiḥ' means that Rama is always approachable to the virtuous and pure-hearted, just as rivers naturally flow into the ocean ('samudra iva sindhubhiḥ'). This metaphor signifies that all sincere seekers inevitably find refuge in him. 'Āryaḥ' denotes nobility in character, conduct, and values. 'Sarvasamaḥ' highlights his impartiality—he treats all beings equally without discrimination based on caste, status, or background, as seen in his interactions with individuals like Guha, Shabari, and others. 'Sadaiva priyadarśanaḥ' emphasizes that he is always pleasant to behold, not just physically but through his consistent, gracious conduct toward everyone. The word 'eva' underscores the constancy of this quality—his demeanor never changes. At the same time, while he is accessible to the righteous, those with harmful intentions cannot withstand his justice. Thus, Rama is portrayed as the ultimate refuge for the good, embodying equality, compassion, and unwavering nobility.
commentary_summary: Rama is approachable to the noble, treats all equally, and is ever gracious and pleasing, serving as a refuge for all righteous beings.
theme: The universal accessibility, equality, and compassionate nature of the ideal being

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: स च सर्वगुणोपेतः कौसल्यानन्दवर्धनः | समुद्र इव गाम्भीर्ये धैर्येण हिमवानिव ||
transliteration: sa ca sarvaguṇopetaḥ kausalyānandavardhanaḥ | samudra iva gāmbhīrye dhairyeṇa himavān iva ||
translation: He is endowed with all virtues and brings joy to Kausalya; in depth he is like the ocean, and in courage he is like the Himalayas.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada beautifully summarizes Lord Rama’s completeness in both character and emotional depth. 'Sarvaguṇopetaḥ' signifies that Rama embodies all noble qualities in perfection. 'Kausalyānandavardhanaḥ' means he enhances the joy of his mother Kausalya, symbolizing not only filial devotion but also the nurturing and auspicious nature associated with the name 'Kausalya', which can imply well-being, skill, and virtue. 'Samudra iva gāmbhīrye' compares Rama’s inner depth to the ocean—profound, vast, and unfathomable. His heart contains immense treasures of virtues, accessible to sincere seekers, yet incomprehensible to those lacking purity. 'Dhairyeṇa himavān iva' likens his courage and steadfastness to the Himalayas—immovable, resilient, and majestic. Just as mountains remain unshaken by storms, Rama remains unwavering in adversity. At the same time, like snow that melts under warmth, his heart softens with compassion toward his devotees. Thus, Rama is portrayed as a perfect balance of depth and strength—profound in wisdom and emotion, yet firm and unshakable in righteousness.
commentary_summary: Rama is described as the embodiment of all virtues, deep like the ocean, and steadfast like the Himalayas, combining compassion with unshakable strength.
theme: The perfect balance of depth, compassion, and unshakable strength in the ideal being

speaker: Narada
text_sanskrit: विष्णुना सदृशो वीर्ये सोमवत्प्रियदर्शनः | कालाग्निसदृशः क्रोधे क्षमया पृथिवीसमः || धनदेन समस्त्यागे सत्ये धर्म इवापरः |
transliteration: viṣṇunā sadṛśo vīrye somavat priyadarśanaḥ | kālāgni-sadṛśaḥ krodhe kṣamayā pṛthivī-samaḥ || dhanadena samaḥ tyāge satye dharma ivāparaḥ |
translation: In valor he is like Vishnu, in appearance pleasing like the moon; in anger like the fire of dissolution, in forgiveness like the earth; in generosity equal to Kubera, and in truthfulness like Dharma itself, with none equal to him.
commentary_full: In this verse, Sage Narada presents a series of powerful comparisons to convey the extraordinary and divine nature of Lord Rama. 'Viṣṇunā sadṛśaḥ vīrye' signifies that Rama’s valor is comparable to that of Lord Vishnu, indicating supreme strength and the ability to subdue evil while remaining unaffected. 'Somavat priyadarśanaḥ' likens his pleasing appearance to the moon, symbolizing calmness, beauty, and soothing presence. 'Kālāgni-sadṛśaḥ krodhe' portrays his anger as fierce and destructive like the cosmic fire at the end of time—but this wrath arises only when dharma is threatened. 'Kṣamayā pṛthivī-samaḥ' shows his immense patience and forgiveness, like the earth which تحملs all without complaint. 'Dhanadena samaḥ tyāge' compares his generosity to Kubera, the god of wealth, highlighting his boundless giving nature. 'Satye dharma iva aparaḥ' emphasizes that in truthfulness he is like Dharma itself—absolute, unwavering, and without equal. These comparisons collectively establish Rama as the perfect embodiment of divine attributes expressed in human form. Though he is an incarnation of Vishnu, he is portrayed within the framework of human experience, making his virtues both relatable and exemplary. This verse also serves as a grand culmination of the qualities described so far, summarizing Rama as the ultimate ideal—combining strength, beauty, controlled wrath, forgiveness, generosity, and truth. It transitions the narrative from describing qualities to unfolding the events of his life, marking the movement from philosophical description to epic storytelling.
commentary_summary: Narada compares Rama to divine forces—Vishnu, the moon, fire, earth, Kubera, and Dharma—showing him as the perfect embodiment of strength, beauty, forgiveness, generosity, and truth.
theme: The divine perfection of Rama expressed through comparisons with cosmic and moral ideals

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: तमेवं गुणसम्पन्नं रामं सत्यपराक्रमम् || ज्येष्ठं श्रेष्ठगुणैर्युक्तं प्रियं दशरथस्सुतम् | प्रकृतीनां हितैर्युक्तं प्रकृतिप्रियकाम्यया || यौवराज्येन संयोक्तुमैच्छत् प्रीत्या महीपतिः |
transliteration: tamevaṁ guṇasampannaṁ rāmaṁ satyaparākramam || jyeṣṭhaṁ śreṣṭhaguṇairyuktaṁ priyaṁ daśarathas-sutam | prakṛtīnāṁ hitairyuktaṁ prakṛtipriyakāmyayā || yauvarājyena saṁyoktum aicchat prītyā mahīpatiḥ |
translation: Seeing Rama endowed with such virtues, true valor, and the best qualities, the beloved eldest son of Dasharatha, and one devoted to the welfare of the people, King Dasharatha, out of affection and for the good of his subjects, desired to install him as the heir-apparent.
commentary_full: In these verses, the narrative transitions from describing Rama’s qualities to a key turning point in the story. King Dasharatha, the ruler of Ayodhya, recognizes in Rama the perfect embodiment of all virtues—'guṇasampannaṁ' (endowed with all noble qualities) and 'satyaparākramam' (true and righteous valor). Rama is also described as 'jyeṣṭhaṁ' (the eldest son) and 'priyam' (deeply beloved), emphasizing both his rightful position and emotional closeness to the king. 'Śreṣṭhaguṇairyuktaṁ' further reinforces that Rama possesses the highest virtues, making him the ideal successor. Importantly, 'prakṛtīnāṁ hitaiḥ yuktam' shows that Rama is dedicated to the welfare of the people (prakṛti refers to the subjects or citizens of the kingdom). Dasharatha’s desire ('aicchat') to appoint Rama as the yuvarāja (heir-apparent) is not driven merely by personal affection ('prītyā') but also by a sense of responsibility toward his people ('prakṛtipriyakāmyayā'). This reflects the ideal principle of kingship in ancient India—where governance is centered on dharma and the well-being of the subjects. Thus, this moment marks the beginning of the Ayodhya narrative, where Rama’s virtues naturally lead to his selection as the future king, setting the stage for the unfolding events of the Ramayana.
commentary_summary: King Dasharatha, seeing Rama’s virtues and concern for the people, lovingly decides to make him the heir-apparent for the welfare of the kingdom.
theme: The recognition of ideal leadership and the decision to crown Rama as heir for the welfare of the kingdom

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: तस्याभिषेकसंभारान् दृष्ट्वा भार्याथ कैकयी || पुर्वं दत्तवरा देवी वरमेनमयाचत | विवासनं च रामस्य भरतस्याभिषेचनम् ||
transliteration: tasyābhiṣekasaṁbhārān dṛṣṭvā bhāryātha kaikeyī || pūrvaṁ dattavarā devī varam enam ayācata | vivāsanaṁ ca rāmasya bharatasya abhiṣecanam ||
translation: Then, seeing the preparations for Rama’s coronation, Queen Kaikeyi, recalling the boons previously granted to her, requested as her boon the exile of Rama and the coronation of Bharata.
commentary_full: In this verse, a major turning point in the Ramayana unfolds. Queen Kaikeyi, one of King Dasharatha’s wives, observes the grand preparations ('abhiṣeka-saṁbhārān') for Rama’s coronation as the heir-apparent. Influenced by her past boons ('pūrvaṁ dattavarā'), which Dasharatha had promised to fulfill at any time, she decides to claim them at this crucial moment. Instead of seeking personal gain in a conventional sense, she demands two specific boons: 'Rāmasya vivāsanam'—the exile of Rama, and 'Bharatasya abhiṣecanam'—the coronation of her own son Bharata. This decision dramatically alters the course of the epic. While outwardly it appears as an act driven by attachment and ambition, it also becomes a divine instrument for the unfolding of Rama’s destined path. The episode highlights themes of fate, duty, and the complexity of human motives. It sets the stage for Rama’s exile, which becomes central to the moral and spiritual journey depicted in the Ramayana.
commentary_summary: Kaikeyi, recalling her boons, asks for Rama’s exile and Bharata’s coronation, triggering a major turning point in the Ramayana.
theme: A निर्णायक turning point where personal desire and destiny reshape the course of the epic

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: स सत्यवचनाद् राजा धर्मपाशेन संयतः | विवासयामास सुतं रामं दशरथः प्रियम् ||
transliteration: sa satyavacanād rājā dharmapāśena saṁyataḥ | vivāsayāmāsa sutaṁ rāmaṁ daśarathaḥ priyam ||
translation: Bound by his promise of truth and by the noose of righteousness, King Dasharatha exiled his beloved son Rama.
commentary_full: In this verse, the tragic yet profound adherence to dharma is depicted through King Dasharatha’s painful decision. 'Satyavacanāt' signifies that the king is bound by his word of truth—he cannot go back on the promise he made to Kaikeyi. 'Dharmapāśena saṁyataḥ' metaphorically describes dharma as a binding force, like a noose, compelling him to act in accordance with righteousness despite immense personal suffering. Dasharatha is torn between his love for his son ('priyam sutam') and his duty as a king to uphold truth and honor his word. Ultimately, dharma prevails, and he orders the exile ('vivāsayāmāsa') of Rama. This moment is one of the most emotionally intense in the Ramayana, highlighting the supreme value placed on truth and duty in the epic. It also underscores the idea that true righteousness often demands personal sacrifice. Dasharatha’s action, though heartbreaking, preserves the moral order and sets the stage for Rama’s journey, which becomes a testament to dharma in action.
commentary_summary: Bound by truth and dharma, Dasharatha painfully exiles his beloved son Rama, showing the supreme importance of righteousness over personal attachment.
theme: The supremacy of truth and dharma over personal attachment and the sacrifice it demands

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: स जगाम वनं वीरः प्रतिज्ञामनुपालयन् | पितुर्वचननिर्देशात् कैकेय्याः प्रियकारणात् ||
transliteration: sa jagāma vanaṁ vīraḥ pratijñām anupālayaṁs | pitur vacana-nirdeśāt kaikeyyāḥ priyakāraṇāt ||
translation: That valiant Rama went to the forest, upholding the promise, obeying his father’s command, and for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyi.
commentary_full: In this verse, Lord Rama’s unwavering commitment to dharma is clearly demonstrated. Described as 'vīraḥ' (a true warrior), Rama’s heroism is not only in battle but in his moral strength. 'Pratijñām anupālayaṁs' indicates his firm resolve to uphold the promise—whether it is his own duty or his father’s pledged word. 'Pitur vacana-nirdeśāt' highlights his obedience to his father’s command, reflecting the ideal of filial duty (pitṛ-vākya-paripālanam). Additionally, 'kaikeyyāḥ priyakāraṇāt' shows his willingness to honor Kaikeyi’s wishes, despite the injustice he faces. Rama does not resist, argue, or show resentment; instead, he accepts exile with calmness and dignity. This moment exemplifies the highest standard of righteousness, where personal loss is willingly embraced to uphold truth, duty, and respect for elders. Rama’s action transforms exile into a sacred act of dharma, setting a timeless example of obedience, sacrifice, and inner strength.
commentary_summary: Rama willingly goes to the forest, upholding his father’s word and dharma with obedience, sacrifice, and calm dignity.
theme: The ideal of unwavering obedience and sacrifice in upholding dharma

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: तं व्रजन्तं प्रियो भ्राता लक्ष्मणोऽनुजगाम ह | स्नेहाद्विनयसम्पन्नः सुमित्रानन्दवर्धनः || भ्रातरं दयितो भ्रातुः सौभ्रात्रमनुदर्शयन् |
transliteration: taṁ vrajantaṁ priyo bhrātā lakṣmaṇo'nujagāma ha | snehād vinayasampannaḥ sumitrānandavardhanaḥ || bhrātaraṁ dayito bhrātuḥ saubhrātram anudarśayan ||
translation: As Rama was departing, his beloved brother Lakshmana, endowed with humility and increasing the joy of his mother Sumitra, followed him out of affection, demonstrating true brotherly love.
commentary_full: In this verse, the deep bond of brotherhood between Rama and Lakshmana is beautifully portrayed. As Rama sets out for the forest, Lakshmana ('priyaḥ bhrātā')—his loving and devoted brother—chooses to accompany him. 'Snehāt anujagāma' shows that his decision is driven purely by affection and love, not obligation. 'Vinayasampannaḥ' highlights Lakshmana’s humility and respectful nature, while 'Sumitrānandavardhanaḥ' indicates that his noble actions bring joy and pride to his mother, Sumitra. The phrase 'bhrātaraṁ dayito bhrātuḥ' emphasizes the mutual love between the brothers, and 'saubhrātram anudarśayan' reflects the ideal of perfect fraternity—selfless, loyal, and unwavering. Lakshmana’s choice to share Rama’s hardships rather than remain in comfort illustrates the highest form of devotion and familial duty. This moment strengthens the emotional core of the Ramayana, showcasing that dharma is not only about duty to truth and society but also about loyalty and love within relationships.
commentary_summary: Lakshmana, out of deep love and humility, follows Rama into exile, exemplifying perfect brotherly devotion and loyalty.
theme: The ideal of selfless brotherly love and unwavering loyalty

speaker: Narrator
text_sanskrit: रामस्य दयिता भार्या नित्यं प्राणसमा हिता || जनकस्य कुले जाता देवमायेव निर्मिता | सर्वलक्षणसम्पन्ना नारीणामुत्तमा वधूः || सीताप्यनुगता रामं शशिनं रोहिणी यथा |
transliteration: rāmasya dayitā bhāryā nityaṁ prāṇasamā hitā || janakasya kule jātā devamāyeva nirmitā | sarvalakṣaṇasampannā nārīṇām uttamā vadhūḥ || sītāpy anugatā rāmaṁ śaśinaṁ rohiṇī yathā |
translation: Sita, the beloved wife of Rama, dear as his very life and ever devoted, born in the family of Janaka, as if divinely created, endowed with all auspicious qualities and the foremost among women, followed Rama like Rohini follows the Moon.
commentary_full: In these verses, Sita is introduced as the ideal woman and devoted wife. She is described as 'rāmasya dayitā bhāryā'—Rama’s beloved consort, and 'prāṇasamā'—as dear to him as life itself. 'Nityaṁ hitā' signifies her constant goodwill and unwavering support. Born in the noble lineage of King Janaka ('janakasya kule jātā'), she embodies purity and virtue. The phrase 'devamāyeva nirmitā' suggests that she appears as though fashioned by divine power, reflecting her extraordinary grace and perfection.
